[p. 247]

The opening with this praise (*tahmid*) stands in the same position as the khutbah (sermon), which opens the discourse on the important matter at hand.

Since the sending down of the Qur'an upon the Prophet ﷺ is the greatest of Allah the Exalted's blessings upon His believing servants, because it is the means of their salvation in their everlasting life, the means of their success in this present life through good living, orderly affairs, and sovereignty over people, and a blessing upon the Prophet ﷺ himself in that He made him the intermediary of this, its conveyor and its explainer, for this reason Allah the Exalted deserves the most complete praise, both in its informative and its performative sense. The phrase "al-hamdu lillah" (all praise is for Allah) has already been shown, at the beginning of Surat al-Fatihah, to establish that He deserves the most complete praise.

Here it is a declarative sentence. Allah informed His Prophet and the Muslims that the one who deserves praise is Allah the Exalted and no other. He therefore followed the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalalah*) with a relative clause (*al-wasf bil-mawsul*), to draw attention to the content of the relative clause, and because the relative pronoun conveys the reason for the statement.

[p. 248]

Describing the Prophet ﷺ with the attribute of servanthood to Allah brings his station near and honours him, by way of the elevation of rank implied in the sending down of the Book upon him, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1].

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) means the Qur'an. Every portion of the Qur'an that is sent down is "the Book." So what is meant here by "the Book" is what was sent down from the day of the mission at the cave of Hira' until the day this surah was revealed. What is revealed after this verse is included in it, and its extent is increased accordingly.

The clause ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridah*) between "the Book" and the circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) that comes from it, which is ﴿upright﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. The "wa" (and) is parenthetical. It is also permissible for the clause to be a circumstantial clause, with the "wa" being circumstantial (*haliyyah*).

"Al-'iwaj" (crookedness), with the 'ayn vowelled with a kasra or a fatha, and with the waw vowelled with a fatha, is literally the deviation of a physical body from its straight shape; it is the opposite of straightness. It is used figuratively for deviation from what is correct and from meanings that are acceptable and praiseworthy.

The position of the most accomplished linguists is that the form with a kasra on the 'ayn and the form with a fatha on it are equivalent in both the literal and the figurative senses. It has been said that the form with a kasra on the 'ayn is restricted to the figurative sense, and al-Zamakhshari (author of *al-Kashshaf*) followed this view. But Allah's words refute it, when He mentioned the levelling of the mountains: ﴿so He will leave it a smooth flat plain, in which you will see no crookedness or curvature﴾ [Ta-Ha: 106]. The readers unanimously recited it with a kasra on the 'ayn. It is also reported from Ibn al-Sikkit that the form with a kasra is more general, used in both the literal and the figurative senses, while the form with a fatha is restricted to the figurative sense.

What is meant by "crookedness" here is the crookedness of the meanings of its speech, through their contradicting what is correct, their contradicting one another, their being far from wisdom, and their failing to hit the intended target.

The purpose of this parenthetical or circumstantial clause is to refute what the polytheists hurled at the Qur'an, saying "he forged it," "fables of the ancients," and "the words of a soothsayer," since such things cannot be free of crookedness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa': 82].

[p. 248 continues]

The pronoun in "lahu" (for it) refers to "al-Kitab" (the Book).

The verb "ja'ala" (to make) was made transitive with the preposition "li" (for) rather than "fi" (in), because the non-physical crookedness is suited to the preposition of specification (*harf al-ikhtisas*), not to the preposition of location (*harf al-zarfiyyah*). Location belongs to the relations of physical bodies, whereas the sense of specification is more general.

So the meaning is that it possesses the complete attributes of books: soundness of meanings and freedom from error and contradiction. This is an attribute of perfection of the Book in itself, and it entails that it is fit to be benefited from. It is thus like its description as ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Qayyiman" (upright) is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "al-Kitab" or of its pronoun in the preposition "li." For if it is made a circumstantial qualifier of one of them, the attribute is established for the other as well, since they are one and the same thing. So there is no benefit in what they have lengthened upon concerning its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*).

"Al-qayyim" is an intensive form (*sigha mubalaghah*) from the figurative sense of "qiyam" (standing, upkeep), which is used to mean the continuous care of something and the constant maintenance of its well-being. This is because caring for something entails "standing" to observe it and being alert to its conditions, as was mentioned earlier at the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿the Ever-Living, the Sustainer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255] in Surat al-Baqarah.

What is meant by it here is that it is upright over the guidance of the community and its reform. So the meaning is that its perfection extends to benefit others. Its position is thus like its description as ﴿a guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Combining His words ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ with His words "qayyiman" is like the combining of ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] and ﴿a guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. It is not an emphasis of the negation of crookedness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 2–3:

﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾

"Li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) is connected to "anzala" (He sent down), and the pronoun of the subject refers back to the Name of Majesty (Allah), i.e., "so that Allah may warn of a severe punishment from Him." The first object of "yundhira" is omitted in order to generalize,

Page 249
or the verb is treated as if it were intransitive, since the intended thing warned of is the severe punishment, to make it appear awesome, and to threaten the polytheists who deny that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah.

Ba's (punishment, severity) means intensity of pain, and it is also applied to strength in war, because it causes pain to the enemy. It has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the patient in misfortune and adversity and in time of battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended meaning here is the severity of the situation in this worldly life, and this is what the Qur'an names "ba's." Al-Tabari followed this interpretation. This is a hint of a threat to the polytheists with what they will encounter of killing and captivity at the hands of the Muslims. That is a punishment "from Him," exalted is He, because it is by His decree and by His command to His servants to carry it out. So the use of "min ladunhu" here applies to both its literal and its figurative meanings.

Making the warning with the worldly punishment as the reason for sending down the Book does not imply that the reasons for its revelation are limited to that, because a single act may have many reasons, some of which are mentioned while others are left out.

I preferred to interpret the severe punishment as the punishment of this world only in order to avoid the difficulty that arises from repeating the verb in ﴿and warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4], as will come later.

It is also permissible that "ba'" be understood as the punishment of the Hereafter, since it is a severe punishment, and "min ladunhu" would then be used in its literal sense. Most exegetes explained it in this way.

It is also permissible that the severe punishment includes both the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of this world. Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qurtubi followed this view, and the use of "min ladunhu" would then carry both its literal and figurative meanings. As for the punishment of the Hereafter, this is clear; as for the punishment of this world, it is because part of it is by killing and captivity, which are acts of people, but Allah commanded the Muslims to do them, so they are "from Him."

The omission of the object of "yundhira" is because the context indicates it, since it is evident that He warns those who did not believe in this Book or in the one to whom it was sent down, and because its counterpart indicates it in His saying, ﴿and give good news to the believers﴾.

* * *

Page 250
﴿and give good news to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever﴾. It is joined to His saying, ﴿to warn of a severe punishment﴾, so it is another reason for the sending down of the Book, prompted by the mention of warning, so that the warning remains directed at others.

His saying, ﴿that they will have a good reward﴾, is connected to "yubashshira" with the preposition removed before "anna," i.e., "with the fact that they will have a good reward." The mention of faith and righteous deeds is to indicate that the deserving of that reward is by the occurrence of these two matters. The Qur'an, for the most part, does not address the state of faith occurring together with some or many righteous deeds, and its ruling has many proofs.

Al-Muk th (lingering) means settling in a place. It likens what they have of pleasures and agreeable things to the container in which their state settles, to indicate that the good reward surrounds them and does not leave them for the blink of an eye. So His saying, "abadan" (forever), is not an emphasis of the meaning of "makithin" (abiding), but rather the combination of both conveys encompassing and permanence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 4:

﴿And warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers.﴾ [al-Kahf: 5] This is another justification for the sending down of the Book to His servant. It is placed as a continuation of His saying ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], on the basis that the warning intended here is a specific warning, in contrast to what He gave as good news to the believers. This is a warning of a recompense in which they will abide forever, namely the punishment of the Hereafter. If you follow the view that the "severe punishment" in His saying ﴿a severe punishment﴾ [al-Kahf: 2] is restricted to the punishment of this world, as has been mentioned earlier, then this warning is different from what precedes it. If you follow the view that the "punishment" includes both punishments, then the repetition of the verb ﴿warn﴾ is for emphasis, and its conjunction (with what precedes) is based on the fact that its object has an additional attribute beyond the meaning of the object of the earlier verb ﴿warn﴾, by which the group warned with both warnings is identified. This refers back to the implied ﴿those warned﴾ in His saying ﴿to warn of severe punishment﴾ [al-Kahf: 2] and dispenses with mentioning it. This reason was raised by the context of mentioning the good news before it. The object of the warning has been omitted here, relying on its counterpart, the object of the good news.

By ﴿those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ here is meant the polytheists who claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah. It does not mean the Christians who said that 'Isa is the son of Allah, the Exalted; because the Meccan Qur'an did not address the refutation of the People of the Book, even though they were eligible to enter the general scope due to the unity of the cause.

The expression of them by the relative pronoun and its clause is because they had become known for this statement among their peoples and among the Muslims, as a condemnation of them for this statement, and as an indication that they deserved what they were warned of because of it and because of other things, since causes are multiple. So the content of the relative clause is one of the reasons for what they were warned of.

Al-walad (the child): a noun for one who is born, male or female, and it is used equally for the singular and the plural. It was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him﴾ [Yunus: 68] in Surat Yunus.

The clause ﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾ [al-Kahf: 5] is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿those who say﴾. The pronoun governed by the preposition bi (in "bihi") refers back to the statement understood from "qalu" (they said).

The min (in "min 'ilm") is for emphasizing the negation. The benefit of mentioning this circumstance is that it is more grave in their disbelief, namely that they speak a falsehood for which they have no basis of doubt. Thus "knowledge" is used for the cause of knowledge, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 117].

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to a verbal noun derived from the verb "qalu," i.e., they have no knowledge of that statement.

The conjunction of ﴿nor did their fathers﴾ [al-Kahf: 5] is to cut off their argument, because they used to say ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]. So when their fathers had no proof for what they say, they are not worthy of being imitated by them.

[p. 252]

It is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence begun afresh without grammatical connection to what precedes it), expressing a dismal judgment on that shocking statement.

The reason the sentence is separated from the one before it is that it differs from it in form: it is a non-declarative (*insha'iyyah*) sentence, whereas the preceding one is declarative (*khabariyyah*).

The verb *kabura* (كَبُرَتْ), with the *ba'* vowelled with a *damma*, originally means reporting that a thing is large in its bulk. It is used figuratively, by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*), for intensity and strength in a description of any quality, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy. Here it is used to express wonder at how grave this statement is in its monstrousness, as indicated by the context (*qarinat al-maqam*). That the purpose is to express wonder is shown by the accusative of *kalimatan* (كَلِمَةً) as a specification (*tamyiz*, an accusative noun clarifying the scope of a verb or statement). The specification here can bear no meaning other than that it specifies the relation of the wonder. For this reason, the grammarians cited this verse as an example of the occurrence of the original *fa'ula* (فَعُلَ) form, and of the form converted to express praise or blame, with the meaning of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* (نِعْمَ وبِئْسَ), according to context.

The pronoun in His saying *kaburat* (كَبُرَتْ) refers to the word (*kalimah*) that is indicated by the specification.

The word *kalimah* is applied to speech in general, which is a common usage. Among its instances is God's saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], and the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "The truest word a poet has ever spoken is the word of Labid:

"Surely everything other than God is vanity."

The clause *takhruju min afwahihim* (تَخْرُجُ مِن أفْواهِهِمْ), "that comes out of their mouths," is an adjectival clause describing *kalimatan*. Its purpose is to convey their boldness in uttering it and their impudence in saying it.

The use of the present tense verb is to bring the image of its coming out of their mouths before the mind, as if imagining its atrocity. It also implies that such speech has no source other than the mouths, because, given its impossibility, it is received by mouths, uttered by them, and heard by ears, but reason does not comprehend it, since reason does not accept the impossible. Rather, it is accepted by the mere imitator (*muqallid*) without reflection.

[p. 253]

*Al-afwah* (الأفْواهُ) is the plural of *fam* (فَمٍ) on the pattern *af'al*. This is because the original form of *fam* is *fawh* (فَوَهٌ) with two fatḥahs on the pattern *jamal*, or *fih* (فِيهٌ) on the pattern *rih*. The *ha'* at its end was deleted because of its heaviness together with the paucity of the word, such that the speaker finds no consonant on which his tongue can rely. Also, because the letter before it is a heavy letter, namely the moving *waw*, when the word remained ending in a moving *waw*, it was changed into an *alif* because of its movement and the openness of what precedes it, so it became *fa* (فًا). A noun does not occur on two letters one of which is a tanwin (تَنْوِين, the nunation or doubled vowel ending). So the nunated *alif* was replaced by a sound consonant, namely the *mim*, because it resembles the *waw* which is the original in the word, since both are labial. Thus it became *fam* (فَمٌ). When they made it plural, they returned it to its original form.

The clause *in yaquluna illa kadhiban* (إنْ يَقُولُونَ إلّا كَذِبًا), "they say nothing but a lie," is a confirmation (*mu'akkidah*) of the content of the clause *takhruju min afwahihim*. This is because the thing that the tongues utter, and which has no reality in the external world or in fact, is falsehood. That is, it comes out of their mouths in the manner of falsehood, so their saying that is nothing but a lie, meaning that it has no attribute except the attribute of falsehood.

This is when the speech derived from *yaquluna* is taken to be specifically their saying ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. But you may take *yaquluna* in a general sense within a context of negation, meaning that no statement issues from them except falsehood. In that case it becomes a restriction relative to a particular domain (*qasr idafi*), meaning what they say concerning the Qur'an and Islam, or what they say of their beliefs that contradict what Islam brought. Then the clause *in yaquluna* becomes a concluding summary (*tadhyil*).

[p. 254]

﴿Then perhaps you will destroy yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this message﴾ is a consequence (*tafri'*) of the clause ﴿and to warn those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾ [18:4], in that they are deniers and disbelievers, as indicated by the phrase ﴿those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾.

The original meaning of *la'alla* (perhaps) is the expression of hope and anticipation, but it is used to express denial and warning by way of *al-majaz al-mursal* (figurative usage based on a non-metaphorical relation), because both hope and denial are associated with anticipating something disliked.

Here it is used to warn the Messenger (ﷺ) against falling into distress and sorrow over the disbelief of those among his people who do not believe. This carries the sense of consolation, because they are of little concern.

*Al-bākhi'* (the one who destroys himself) means the one who kills himself. This is how Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr explained it. Al-Bukhari explained it as "one who destroys," and this explanation goes back to Abu 'Ubayda.

There is a difference of opinion about its derivation. It is said to derive from *al-bikhā'* (with the single *bā'*), on the pattern of *kitāb*, which is a vein concealed in the nape of the neck. When the slaughterer reaches the *bikhā'*, that is the deepest slaughter. This was said by al-Zamakhshari in his commentary on the words ﴿perhaps you will destroy yourself﴾ [26:3] in Surat al-Shu'ara'. Al-Zamakhshari alone mentioned this derivation, in *al-Kashshaf*, *al-Fa'iq* and *al-Asas*. Ibn al-Athir said in *al-Nihaya*: "I searched the books of language and medicine and did not find *al-bikhā'* with the single *bā'*," meaning that al-Zamakhshari was alone in this derivation and in affirming *al-bikhā'* as the name of this vein. I say: al-Zamakhshari is sufficient as an authority for what he established. Al-Mutarrizi in *al-Mughrib* and the author of *al-Qamus* followed him in this. Thus *al-bakh'*, in origin, is that the slaughterer carries the cutting to the nape, and then it was applied to killing accompanied by anger.

*Al-athār* is the plural of *athar*, which is what the walker or rider leaves behind in sand or earth from the places where their feet and their mount's hooves tread. *Athar* also refers to what the people of a dwelling leave behind when they depart from it, such as the trivial tools with which they handled their affairs, like tent pegs and ashes.

The particle *'alā* (upon/over) indicates figurative elevation (*al-isti'lā' al-majāzī*). So the meaning may be: "Perhaps you will destroy yourself because of their turning away from you, as a traveller turns away from the place where he was." In this case *'alā* indicates cause (*al-ta'līl*).

It may also be that the meaning is an image (*tamthīl*) of the state of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his intense eagerness that his people follow him, and in his grief at their aversion. It also depicts their state of aversion and turning away as that of someone separated from his family and loved ones, who sees the traces of their dwellings and grieves at their parting. In this case the particle *'alā* is situated in a position of circumstance (*ḥāl*) relative to the pronoun of address, and the sense of *'alā* is figurative elevation, which is the intensity of attachment to the place.

It seems that this statement reached the Messenger (ﷺ) at the last of the times when he still hoped for their belief, as a hint that they would not come to believe, and as a preparation for his soul to bear the opposition he would meet from them, out of mercy from his Lord. For this reason He said ﴿if they do not believe in this message﴾ using the present tense, which implies occurrence in the future, meaning: if their unbelief continues.

The demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishāra*) and its explanation (*bayān*) intend the Qur'an. Because it is present in minds, it is as if it were present at the place where the verse was revealed, so it is pointed to with this consideration, and it is explained as "this message."

*Al-ḥadīth* means news. The application of the name *al-ḥadīth* to the Qur'an is based on its being information from God to His Messenger, since *al-ḥadīth* is a long speech containing reports and stories. It is called *ḥadīth* because it contains a matter that is *ḥadīth*, meaning something that has occurred and is new, that is, new reports that the addressee does not know. So *al-ḥadīth* is *faʻīl* in the sense of *mafʻūl*. See what comes under His words ﴿God has sent down the best discourse﴾ [39:23] in Surat al-Zumar.

*Asafan* (in grief) is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*) relating to *bākhi'un nafsaka* (destroying yourself), meaning killing it because of the intensity of sorrow. The conditional clause is inserted between the two objects, and it has no answer, because what precedes the conditional clause is sufficient in place of the answer.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 7–8:

[p. 256]

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren, dry wasteland.﴾ The connection of the placement of this verse here is obscure; the commentators have found it difficult to explain. Some of them remain silent about it, and some attempt to explain it with something that adds nothing beyond silence.

What appears is that it is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the disregard of the polytheists: that God has granted them respite and given them the worldly life, perhaps they would be thankful to Him, but they have been insolent toward the blessing. So God will strip the blessing from them, and their lands will become barren. This is an allusion that there will befall them the drought of the seven years, which the Messenger of God asked his Lord to place upon the polytheists, like the years of Joseph (peace be upon him).

This has a connection with His saying ﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾ [18:2].

The position of (inna, "indeed") at the beginning of this sentence is that of giving the reason for the consolation contained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces﴾ [18:6].

From this there arises a reminder to some of them of the power of God, exalted is He, especially of what is among it the bringing of things into existence and their opposites, from the life of the earth and its death, which resembles the life and death of people, and which resembles the spiritual life and spiritual death of faith and disbelief, blessing and retribution. All of these are lessons for whoever takes heed from change, and who moves from one state to another, so that he does not trust in his strength and might; so that he may measure things by their likenesses and present himself to the standard of virtues and the goodness of outcomes.

The argument from the condition of the earth on which people live was preferred, because it is closer to their senses and their attachments, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created? And at the sky, how it was raised? And at the mountains, how they were set up? And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ [88:17–20], and He said: ﴿And in the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾ [51:20].

[p. 257]

The composition of this statement has come in the style of inimitability, gathering many meanings that the wording can accommodate from various intended aspects. The report that the creation of what is on the earth is an adornment combines a favor upon people and a reminder of the marvelous workmanship of God, in that He set this world upon the most perfect pattern, suited to what souls love of adornment and ornamentation. Favor of this kind is frequent, such as His saying: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [16:6], and He said: ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires: women and sons, and heaped-up piles of gold and silver, and branded horses, and livestock, and tilled land﴾ [3:14].

Things are not an adornment except that life is diffused within them, by which their growth and flourishing come about. This adornment remains upon the face of the earth since man saw it, and its continuance is by the continuance of its kinds, even if passing befalls their individuals, which are replaced by other individuals of their kind. This includes a favor through the diffusion of life in earthly existents.

Among the necessary implications of this adornment is that it awakens minds to consider the existence of its Originator, and probes the depths of souls regarding the measure of gratitude to its Creator and the One who made it for them. Thus some fulfil the right of gratitude, some fall short in it, and some deny and disbelieve the blessing of this Benefactor, attributing it to other than its Originator. Also among its necessary implications is that it stirs desires to pluck and enjoy it, so that various modes of enjoying it are provoked, and the desires conflict over taking exclusive possession of it, which leads to people overpowering one another and transgressing against one another. This is what created their need for the laws, to regulate for them the conditions of their dealings. For this reason He gave the reason for making what is on the earth an adornment with His saying: ﴿that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾, i.e., who is most excellent in goodness of the deed of the heart, which turns to faith and disbelief, and the deed of the body, which manifests in compliance with the truth or swerving from it.

So people, taken together, differ in the goodness of their deeds, and from the degrees of this difference in goodness one knows by way of implication the degree of the absence of goodness altogether, which is the state of disbelief and evil deeds, as came in the hadith: "The likeness of the hypocrite who recites the Qur'an is like..., and the likeness of the hypocrite who does not recite the Qur'an..."

[p. 258]

Al-balw (testing, trial) means examination and experiment. It has already been mentioned at His saying ﴿There every soul will know what it has sent before﴾ [10:30] in Surat Yunus. Here it is used metaphorically for the attachment of God's actual knowledge, exalted is He, to the known object upon its occurrence, indicated by the rational and transmitted proofs that show the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of everything before its occurrence. He is therefore independent of testing and experiment. The benefit of this metaphor is the transition from it to the metonymy for the manifestation of that to all people, so that the righteous is not confused for its opposite. It is like the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"I advanced while the spear swayed between us, to know which of them is a coward and which of them is brave."

His saying ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren, dry wasteland﴾ completes the lesson and confirms the annihilation of the world. His saying "jā'ilūn" (will make) is an active participle intended to refer to the future, i.e., We will make everything that is upon the earth non-existent, so that upon the earth there will be nothing but dry, bare dust unfit for life upon it. That is the annihilation of the world, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day the earth will be changed into other than the earth﴾ [14:48].

Ṣaʻīd is dust, and juruz is barren and bare. The explanation of the meaning of ṣaʻīd will come at His saying ﴿and it becomes a slippery ṣaʻīd﴾ [18:40] in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 7–8:

[p. 256]

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren, dry wasteland.﴾ The connection of the placement of this verse here is obscure; the commentators have found it difficult to explain. Some of them remain silent about it, and some attempt to explain it with something that adds nothing beyond silence.

What appears is that it is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the disregard of the polytheists: that God has granted them respite and given them the worldly life, perhaps they would be thankful to Him, but they have been insolent toward the blessing. So God will strip the blessing from them, and their lands will become barren. This is an allusion that there will befall them the drought of the seven years, which the Messenger of God asked his Lord to place upon the polytheists, like the years of Joseph (peace be upon him).

This has a connection with His saying ﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾ [18:2].

The position of (inna, "indeed") at the beginning of this sentence is that of giving the reason for the consolation contained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces﴾ [18:6].

From this there arises a reminder to some of them of the power of God, exalted is He, especially of what is among it the bringing of things into existence and their opposites, from the life of the earth and its death, which resembles the life and death of people, and which resembles the spiritual life and spiritual death of faith and disbelief, blessing and retribution. All of these are lessons for whoever takes heed from change, and who moves from one state to another, so that he does not trust in his strength and might; so that he may measure things by their likenesses and present himself to the standard of virtues and the goodness of outcomes.

[Page 259]

﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ (Am) is used for *idrab intiqali* (a transitional turn, meaning "rather"), moving from one purpose to another. Since this is one of the aims for which the surah was revealed, this transition is not abrupt (*iqtidab*). Rather, it is like the move from the preamble and introduction to the main subject.

Moreover, the reason for the transition to it is connected with God's saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this message﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. Among the things that turned the polytheists away from faith was their denial of resurrection after death. So the mention of the people of the cave, and their being raised after sleeping for many years, served as an example of the possibility of resurrection.

[Page 259 continues]

Here, (am) is *am al-munqati'a*, meaning "rather." It always requires an implied interrogative, and an interrogative particle is understood after it. Sometimes it appears explicitly after it, as in the verse of Ufnun al-Taghlibi:

*How did they repay ʿĀmir with evil for their deed, or how do they repay me with evil for good?*

The implied interrogative after (am) here is exclamatory (*ta'jibi*), like the one in the verse.

The implied meaning here is: "Do you think that the companions of the cave were a wonder among Our signs?", that is, more wondrous than the rest of Our signs. The causing of the living to die after their life is greater than the wonder of the people of the cave being made to sleep, because in their sleep life was kept in their bodies, whereas in the death of the living there is no preservation of any part of life in them, despite their numbers and spread. This is an indirect rebuke of those who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to explain the story of the people of the cave in order to learn what wonder it contained. They asked about a wonder and disbelieved in what is more wondrous, namely the annihilation of the world. They turned away from mentioning the perishing of the world and said: ﴿There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24]. That is, "There is no life except our worldly life, not the life of the Hereafter, and time destroys us, and it remains."

In this there is a call to the minds of those who ask about wonderful stories, redirecting them from occupying themselves with the marvels of tales to the fact that it is better for them to take admonition from the lessons and causes they contain and their effects. For this reason, the account of their condition begins with God's saying: ﴿When the youths retreated to the cave and said, "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair"﴾ [al-Kahf: 10]. Thus He informed people of the steadfastness of their faith in God and their hope in Him. And with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance﴾ [al-Kahf: 13] and the verses that follow, which indicate that they rejected polytheism and called its adherents foolish, there is an implicit message that those who hear should follow their guidance.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the intended audience is his people who asked about the story, and the People of the Book who incited them to ask about it and seek its explanation. It appears that those who taught the Quraysh to ask about the people of the cave were some Christians who had ties

[Page 260]

with the people of Makkah, from among the merchants who came to Makkah, or from among the monks in the monasteries located on the route of the Quraysh caravan from Makkah to Syria, which was the summer journey. The point of wonder is His saying "among Our signs," meaning among the many signs they witnessed, which they did not find wondrous, restricting their amazement to such extraordinary events. So the meaning is interpreted as: the people of the cave are not the only wonder among the other signs. Rather, the wonders of God's creation are many, some of them more wondrous than the condition of the people of the cave, and some of them equal to it.

So the meaning of (min) in His saying "among Our signs" is partitive (*tab'id*): the story of the people of the cave is not unique in being wondrous among the other signs. It is like saying: "He asked So-and-so, and he is the most knowledgeable among us," meaning the one uniquely knowledgeable among us.

You may also take it as the figurative sense of location (*zarfiyyah majaziyyah*): "they were a wonder in Our signs," meaning the rest of the signs are not a wonder. This is a rebuke of their poor judgment, as they focus their attention on rare things, while before them are things more deserving of attention.

He described the companions of the cave as "wonder," although it is actually their condition among their people that is wondrous. So there is an omitted *mudaf* (a genitive construction) indicated by the context. He described their condition by the verbal noun (*masdar*) for emphasis, while the intended meaning is "wondrous."

The *kahf* (cave) is a split in a mountain that is wide in its middle. If it is not wide, it is a *ghar* (cave/grotto).

The *raqim* is of the form *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, from *raqm*, which means writing. So the *raqim* is a written record that was with the companions of the cave in their cave. It is said that they wrote in it what they believed of monotheism. It is also said that it was the book of their religion, a religion that existed before Jesus (peace be upon him). It is said that it was the religion of Jesus. It is also said that they wrote in it the cause that drove them to take refuge in the cave, fleeing from the disbelief of their people.

The Qur'an began its account of them with the point of true lesson and the good example from it: their turning to their Lord and His response to them.

[Page 261]

The verse alludes to the story of a group of righteous people from past nations who remained steadfast upon the religion of truth at a time when disbelief and falsehood had spread. They withdrew into seclusion to avoid mixing with the people of disbelief, and they took refuge in a cave where they settled, fleeing from the trial in their religion. God honored them by casting sleep upon them, and they remained in it for a long period. Then He awakened them, and they saw the extinction of those whom they feared for their religion. After they became certain of this, He returned them to their sleep, which was beyond the normal custom. He kept them alive until a term known to God, or He caused them to die and preserved their bodies from decay as an honor to them.

People knew their news, but they did not come upon their identities, nor did they find their inscription. Therefore they differed about their affair. Some of them affirm that their story occurred, and some deny it.

Since the meanings of the verses cannot be clarified except by knowing what they allude to from the story of the people of the cave, it is necessary to mention what is authentically reported by the leading historians, despite the differences among them. Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned a summary of this, without dwelling on what belongs to the additions of exaggerators and storytellers.

What most reports state is that in a town called (Ibsus), with an initial *alif* and a silent *ba*, and an *u* sound after it, followed by another unpointed *sin*, which was one of the frontier towns of (Tartus), between Aleppo, the lands of Armenia, and Antioch.

It is not (Ephesus), with *fa'* and a sister of *qaf* — the well-known city in the lands of Greece for the fame of the Temple of Jupiter there. That city is in Greece, and to its people Paul wrote his famous epistle. Some historians and exegetes confused the two. The town in question is near Marash in the lands of Armenia. The Christian religion had entered those regions, and the dominant religion there was the worship of idols in the Eastern Roman manner before the conversion of Constantine. Among the people of Ibsus was a group of righteous Christians who opposed idol worship. They lived in the time of the emperor Decius (also called Diqyanus), who reigned around the year 237. His reign lasted one year. He was fanatically devoted to the Roman religion and deeply hostile to Christianity. He openly showed his aversion to the Roman religion and threatened them with torture. They agreed to leave the city for a mountain two *farsakhs* away from it, called (Bunjalus), in which was a cave where they took refuge. There they devoted themselves to worshipping God alone. When the news of their flight reached the king, and that they had taken refuge in the cave, he sent after them. God cast a sleep upon them, and the king's men thought them dead. It is also said that he ordered the mouth of their cave to be sealed with a wall, but that this did not apparently take effect, for if a wall had been built over the mouth of their cave, those among them who were raised could not have come out. Perhaps what prevented the execution of the king's order was that his reign did not last long, as it did not exceed one year. They remained in their sleep for a long time, which Ibn al-ʿIbri estimated at two hundred and forty years. Their awakening occurred during the reign of Theodosius the Younger, and the Qur'an mentioned that it was three hundred years.

Then God made them a sign for themselves and for people. He raised them from their resting place, and they did not know how long they had remained. They sent one of them to the city, which was Ibsus, with coins to buy food for them. The people wondered at his appearance and his coins, and he wondered at what he saw of the change in conditions. The news of them spread among the people of the city. Theodosius the Younger went out with bishops, priests, and patriarchs to the cave. They looked at them, spoke with them, and believed in their sign. When they departed from them, they died in their places. It was a sign by which the religion of Christ was strengthened.

What is in the book of al-Tabari is that those who went to see the companions of the cave were the two leaders of the city, (Aryus) and (Atyus), and those with them from the people of the city. It is also said that when the people saw them, the two governors of the city wrote to the king of the Romans, who came, saw them, and ordered that a mosque be built over them. They did not mention whether the construction of the mosque was carried out or not. It is not mentioned that the cave was later found again. Perhaps it was sealed by an earthquake or something similar, as a favor from God to His companions. Although the false reports about its location in various places in the lands of the Muslims, from the ends of the earth, are many, and in the south of the Tunisian region there is a place called

[Page 263]

"the Cave," and in other places in the countryside of that region there are shrines they call "the Seven Sleepers," believing that the people of the cave were seven. You will learn the source of these illusions.

In the *Tafsir* of al-Alusi, from Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "We fought with Muʿawiyah in the expedition of al-Madiq toward the Romans. We passed by the cave in which were the companions of the cave. Muʿawiyah said: 'If only they were uncovered for us so we could look at them.' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'That is not for you. God has prevented that from one better than you.' He said: ﴿Had you looked at them, you would have turned from them in flight﴾ [al-Kahf: 18]. Muʿawiyah said: 'I will not stop until I learn their condition.' So he sent men and said: 'Go, enter the cave and look.' They went, and when they entered it, God sent a wind upon them that drove them out."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of ʿIkrimah that Ibn ʿAbbas campaigned with Habib ibn Maslamah. They passed by the cave, and there were bones in it. A man said: "These are the bones of the people of the cave." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Their bones decayed more than three hundred years ago."

In the *Tafsir* of al-Fakhr, on the authority of al-Qaffal, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi the astrologer: al-Wathiq sent him to learn the condition of the companions of the cave. He traveled to the Romans, and the king of the Romans sent with him groups of people to the place where they were said to be. He said: "The man assigned to that place frightened me from entering upon them. I entered and saw hair on their chests. I realized that it was deception and trickery, and that people had treated those corpses with drying agents to preserve their bodies from decay, such as coating them with aloe and other substances." End of quotation.

His saying "he traveled to the Romans" is based on their belief that the cave was near the city of (Ephesus), with *fa'* and a sister of *qaf*. This is an error arising from the similarity of the names of the two cities, as we pointed out just above. The city of Ephesus, in the time of al-Wathiq, was still under the rule of the Roman emperors at Constantinople. For this reason, some historians said that when the Roman emperor learned of the mission sent by the caliph al-Wathiq, he ordered that a guide be assigned to accompany the mission to facilitate what they needed.

[Page 264]

As for the city of (Ibsus), with *ba'* (the unpointed letter), it was at that time part of the realm of Islam.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: In al-Andalus, in the region of Granada, near a village called (Lushah), there is a cave containing dead people, and with them a dog in a state of decay (rimmah). Most of them have had their flesh stripped away, and some of them are still intact. The earlier centuries have passed, and we have found no knowledge of their circumstances, but people claim that they are the Companions of the Cave. I entered among them and saw them in the year 504 [AH], and they were in this state, and over them there was a mosque. Near them is a Roman structure called (al-Raqim), as if it were a rounded palace—thus it is written with an unpointed ḥāʾ; perhaps it means "circular, like a ring"—and some of its walls remain. It lies in a desolate, rugged stretch of land. And above the capital (ḥaḍrah) of (Aghirnatah), on the side facing the qiblah, are the remains of an ancient Roman city called the city of Diqyus, and in its remains we found strange things in its graves and the like. End of quote.

The story of the People of the Cave is connected to a great phase in the history of the emergence of the true religions, especially the phase of the spread of Christianity in the land.

Caves are widely mentioned as places of refuge and burial.

The Christians were persecuted in the lands, so they would flee from cities and villages to caves, taking them as dwellings. When one of them died, he was buried there. Perhaps when they killed them, they would place them in the caves in which they used to worship. For this reason there exists in Rome a great cave of this kind, which the Christians took for themselves there. They often took a dog with them to ward off wild beasts such as wolves and the like. The cave mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyya is none other than one of these caves.

However, what is mentioned concerning the occasion of the revelation of the surah—the Jews' knowledge of the People of the Cave, and their making that knowledge a sign of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ)—makes it unlikely that these People of the Cave were from the Christian religion, for the Jews shy away from every report that mentions Christianity. It is therefore possible that some Jews took refuge in some caves during the persecutions that befell the Jews, and they used to take refuge in caves. There is a place in the land of (Sakrah), near al-Marsa in the outskirts of Tunis, which contains artificial caves; some scholars of antiquities among the Christian monks in Tunis verified for me that they were hiding places for the Jews, where they concealed themselves from the persecution of the Carthaginian Romans against them.

It is also possible that people of both the Jewish and Christian religions have a report about a group of their righteous people known as the People of the Cave, or that they were one group whose story both the followers of each religion claimed for their own righteous people, and on that basis a disagreement arose over the naming of the land in which their cave was.

Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd al-Unuf: The People of the Cave were from a non-Arab (ʿajamiyyah) nation, and the Christians know their story and date their history by it. End of quote.

Some of this has already been discussed under the commentary on His words, "They ask you about the Spirit" (17:85), in Surat al-Isra'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 10:

﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave, they said: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and facilitate for us our affair into right guidance."﴾

(Idh) is an adverbial noun of time (zarf) governing the clause that follows it, and it is connected to "kānū" (they were), so that this clause is linked to the one before it.

It is also permissible for the adverbial to be connected to a deleted verb whose estimate is: "Remember" (udhkur). In that case the clause is a resumptive, explanatory beginning (isti'nāf bayānī) for the clause before it. Whichever is the case, the purpose is to summarize their story at the outset, as an alert that their story is not the most wondrous of God's signs, together with an alert that what God honored them with of care was indeed a strengthening (ta'yid) for them because of their faith. For this reason the statement ﴿they said: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself"﴾ is conjoined to it.

Page 266
Awā, ya'wā, ilā al-makān: he made it his dwelling. So al-ma'wā is the place. It has been discussed earlier at the words of the Most High ﴿Those—their refuge is the Fire, because of what they used to earn﴾ [Yunus: 8] in Surah Yunus.

Al-fityah (the youths) is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah) of fata (young man), who is the complete young man. It was discussed earlier at the words of the Most High in Surah Yusuf. The intended meaning of al-fityah is the People of the Cave. This is an instance of explicit mention in place of a pronoun, because the apparent requirement would be to say "idh awaw" (when they took refuge). It departed from that because of what the word fityah indicates of them being of close age, peers. He mentioned them with this description to hint at what it contains of the completion of manhood, expressed by futuwwah, which combines the meanings of sound judgment, steadfastness of heart, and defense of the truth. For this reason he departed from the pronoun and did not say "idh awaw ilā al-kahf."

The fa' in the clause ﴿fa-qālū﴾ indicates that when they took refuge in the cave, they immediately turned to God in supplication.

They called upon God to bestow upon them mercy from Him, and that comprises the good of this world and the next. That is, that He bestow upon them a great mercy befitting His care for their following the religion which He commanded. The addition of min ladunka with the verb of giving indicates this, because in min there is the sense of origination, and in ladun there is the sense of nearness and belonging to Him. This is more eloquent than if they had said "grant us mercy," because all creation is in the position of receiving mercy from God; but they asked for a special, abundant mercy at a time when its opposite was expected, and they intended security for their faith from trial, and so that they would not encounter hardship and pain in their estrangement, and that the enemies of the religion would not humiliate them, so that they would become a trial for the disbelieving people.

Then they asked God to decree for them circumstances whose outcome would be the attainment of what He had granted them of steadfastness upon the true religion and deliverance from the opposition of the polytheists. He expressed that decree by "tahy'ah" (facilitation), which is the preparation of the causes for the attainment of a thing.

The min in His words ﴿min amrinā﴾ is for origin (ibtidā'iyyah).

Page 267
Al-amr here: the affair and state in which they are, which is the totality of faith and holding fast to a place of seclusion away from the people of polytheism. God had prepared for them, among the states, that by which is their right guidance. Among that is turning their enemies away from pursuing them, and inspiring them to the location of the cave, and that its placement was in a suitable direction so that their bodies would remain intact, and that He made them sleep a long sleep so that the time in which the conditions of the city change would pass over them, and their guidance was achieved when they remained steadfast upon the true religion and witnessed it victorious and followed, and He made them a sign for people of the truthfulness of the religion, and of God's power, and of resurrection.

Al-rashad with two fathas: good, attaining the truth, benefit, and righteousness. It has been repeated in Surah al-Jinn with variation of these meanings. Al-rushd with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin is a synonym of al-rashad, and it has come to be specialized in good management of property. This word was not read here in the well-known readings except with a fatha on the ra', unlike His words ﴿Right guidance has become distinct from error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256] in Surah al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment﴾ [al-Nisa': 6] in Surah al-Nisa', where in both only a damma on the ra' was read.

The reason for preferring the fatha on the ra' and shin in this surah, in this place, and in His later words ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right conduct"﴾ [al-Kahf: 24]: the vocalization of the two letters in them is more suitable to the words occurring at the rhyme-endings of the verses. Do you not see that the majority read His words in this surah ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught as guidance﴾ [al-Kahf: 66] with a damma on the ra', because it is more suitable to the surrounding rhymes, which are ﴿from Our Presence knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 65], ﴿with me patience﴾, ﴿that which you do not encompass in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 68], ﴿and I will not disobey you in any matter﴾ [al-Kahf: 69], to the end of it. And there none read it with a fatha on the ra' and shin except Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 11–12:

[Page 268]
﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years.﴾ ﴿Then We awakened them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing what they had remained in terms of time.﴾ The connecting of this sentence with the particle fa' (so) is either based on the sentence of their supplication, which indicates that its content is the answering of their prayer, so God made their sleep an honour for them, by protecting them from torment at the hands of their enemies. And this confirmed that they were upon the truth, and He showed the people this after a long time.

Or it is based on the sentence ﴿when the youths took refuge﴾ [al-Kahf: 10], etc., which indicates that God hastened for them the attainment of what they sought, something that had not been within their calculation.

The verb ḍaraba here means "to place," as one says: "he placed a veil over him" (ḍaraba 'alayhi ḥijāban). From it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Abasement was struck upon them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 112]. Its detailed discussion has already preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to present an example, any example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26].

The object of "ḍarabnā" is omitted because it is evident, i.e., "We placed upon their ears a covering or a barrier against hearing," as one says: "he built upon his wife," its implied object being "he built a house." The striking upon the ears is a kināya (metonymy) for sleep, because deep sleep necessitates the absence of hearing, since sound hearing is not blocked except by sleep, unlike sound sight, which may be blocked by closing the eyelids.

This kināya is among the distinctive features of the Qur'an; it was not known before this verse, and it is among the aspects of its inimitability (i'jāz).

And ʿadadan is an adjective (naʿt) of sinīna, and "ʿadad" is used to mean abundance, i.e., "years of a great number." Its parallel is what occurs in the hadith of the beginning of revelation, in the saying of ʿĀʾisha: "He would go out to the cave of Ḥirāʾ and devote himself to worship therein for nights of countless number (al-layālī dhawāt al-ʿadad)," meaning many. The number has been left general here in accordance with the generality of the story.

[Page 269]
And al-baʿth (raising/awakening) here means waking, i.e., We woke them from their sleep with the wakefulness of one startled, as a camel is raised from its resting place. What makes this metaphor suitable here is that the purpose of this story is to establish resurrection after death, so mention of the word "baʿth" alerts that in this revival there is evidence for the possibility of resurrection and its manner.

Al-ḥizb: the group of people who agree upon one thing. The two parties (al-ḥizbān) are two factions: one of them is correct, and the other is mistaken in counting the period that passed over them. It has been said that they are two factions of the People of the Cave themselves, based on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿A speaker among them said: How long have you remained?﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. But this is far from the word "ḥizb," since the speaker was one, and the others were doubting; it is also far from the verb "aḥṣā," since the People of the Cave did not intend to count the duration of their stay upon awakening, but rather they thought it a short time. Therefore the correct view is that the two parties are two groups of people from their own city, who differed in their statements about the duration of their stay after they knew of their rising from their sleep: one of the two groups is correct, and the other is mistaken, and God knows which of them is correct and which is mistaken. So they are two parties on the two sides of correctness and error, as His saying "aḥṣā" indicates.

It is not appropriate to interpret the two parties as two groups of the People of the Cave about whom God said, ﴿A speaker among them said: How long have you remained? They said: We have remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], and so on.

Making God's knowledge of the state of the two parties the cause of His raising them is a kināya for the occurrence of disagreement regarding the estimation of their duration, for when they disagreed, God knew their disagreement with the knowledge of actualities, and this is a relation of knowledge that may be called "tanjīzī" (actualized), even if this does not occur according to the scholars of kalām.

This has been discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7], at the beginning of the surah.

"Aḥṣā" may be a past-tense verb, or it may be an elative noun (ism tafḍīl) formed from the quadriliteral on contrary to analogy. Al-Zamakhsharī in al-Kashshāf, following Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, preferred the first, to avoid forming an elative on non-analogical grounds due to its rarity; al-Zajjāj preferred the second. Although forming an elative from other than the triliteral is not analogical, it is common in eloquent speech and in the Qur'an.

The correct view is that "aḥṣā" is an elative noun, and the elative is directed to what is contained in the meaning of iḥṣāʾ of precision and accuracy. The meaning: that We may know which of the two parties is more exact in computing (iḥṣāʾ), i.e., counting, in that it is the one that matches reality and what truly is, while the rest is approximation and guessing at the unseen. This is what His saying, exalted is He, detailed: ﴿They will say: They were three﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and so on.

So "ayy" is an interrogative noun in the nominative as subject (mubtada'), and it suspends the verb "li-naʿlama" from operating; "aḥṣā" is the predicate of "ayy," and "amadan" is a specificative (tamyīz) of the elative, a tamyīz of relation (tamyīz nisba), i.e., the relation of the elative to what it describes, as in His saying, ﴿I am more than you in wealth﴾ [al-Kahf: 34]. Do not be troubled that it is not evident that this specificative is transferred from the subject, since it is not correct to say "the best of his time," for transference is a presumed matter intended for approximation.

The meaning: that the disorder of people in fixing the dates of events and the failure of their diligence become apparent, along with their conjecture when they undertake it, and the negligence of many people in determining events and their dates is known; both states are connected to one another.

[Page 271]

When His saying ﴿so that We may know which of the two parties best computed the time they remained﴾ [Al-Kahf: 12] implied that the account of the People of the Cave contains conjectures and guesses about the unseen, this stirred in the soul an eagerness to know the truth about their affair, from the origin of the story's existence to its details, from an informant whose truthfulness is not doubted. The sentence ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾ was therefore an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) following the sentence ﴿so that We may know which of the two parties best computed the time they remained﴾ [Al-Kahf: 12].

This is the beginning of a summary of the story and of attention to the lessons within it. He presented first what describes their steadfastness in faith, their defiance of their disbelieving people, and their entering the cave.

The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate in the sentence ﴿We relate to you﴾ conveys exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: it is We, and no other, who relates their stories in truth.

Here, "truth" (al-haqq) means truthfulness (al-sidq), and truthfulness is one kind of truth. An example of this is His saying ﴿It is fitting that I should not say about God except the truth﴾ [Al-A'raf: 105] in Surat al-A'raf.

The preposition "ba'" (bi-) indicates accompaniment (mulabasa), meaning: the story accompanied by truthfulness, not by conjectures.

Qasas (narrative) is the relating of a lengthy account, so a report delivered in scattered segments of speech is not a qasas. This was discussed at the opening of Surat Yusuf.

Naba' (report) is a piece of news that carries importance and has significance.

The sentence ﴿They were youths﴾ clarifies the qasas and the naba'. The opening of the sentence with the emphatic particle (inna) serves merely to express concern, not to reject denial.

The increase of guidance (ziyadat al-huda) may be a strengthening of the guidance of faith mentioned in His saying ﴿who believed in their Lord﴾, by opening their insight to think about the means of salvation through their faith, and by granting them success and steadfastness. All of this is guidance added to the guidance of faith.

It may also be a strengthening of the excellence of faith through the excellence of piety, as in His saying ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Ziyada (increase) is the abundance of the quantity of a specific thing, such as the abundance of the number of what is counted, the weight of what is weighed, or the population of a city.

The verb (zada, "increased") may be intransitive, as in His saying ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [Al-Saffat: 147], and it may be transitive, as in His saying ﴿so God increased them in sickness﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 10]. The increase is used metaphorically (isti'ara) for the intensification of a quality, as it is here.

Tying down the heart (ribt 'ala al-qalb) is used metaphorically for strengthening faith and removing hesitation regarding it. Since the term "heart" became commonly used for belief, the tying down (ribt) was borrowed for firmness in holding to it, as He said ﴿Had We not bound her heart so that she would be among the believers﴾ [Al-Qasas: 10]. From this comes the expression "he is ribt al-ja'sh" (firm of heart in the face of fear). Its opposite is said: "his heart trembled." And He said ﴿and hearts reached the throats﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 10], where trembling was borrowed for hesitation and doubt about the occurrence of something.

The verb "rabatna" is followed by the preposition of elevation ('ala) to express intensification in tightening, because the preposition of elevation is used metaphorically for the meaning of being in full control of the action.

The phrase ﴿when they stood up﴾ is an adverbial clause of time governing "tying down", meaning: the tying down occurred at the time of their standing up. That is, the resolve by which they stood up coincided with God's tying down of their hearts. In other words, had it not been for that, they would not have undertaken such an act or uttered such a statement.

The "standing up" (qiyam) may be literal, in that they stood before the polytheist king of the Romans, or they stood among their people as preachers announcing the corruption of the creed of polytheism. It may also be metaphorical for taking the initiative and daring to undertake a great deed, and for giving attention to the deed or statement, by likening that attention to a person rising from sitting to engage in some task, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

"Verily a fortress and a tribe from the Banu Asad
stood up and said: 'Our protection is not to be approached.'"

In this there is no standing after sitting; rather they may have said it while seated.

They referred to God by means of an idafa (genitive construction) to their pronoun, either because they had been known beforehand to worship God, who is transcendent above bodies and the attributes of created things, or because God was not known by a proper name among those polytheists, who claimed that the Lord of lords was Jupiter, represented by the planet Jupiter. Thus there was no way to identify the true God for them except through the idafa construction. Something similar is what God related of Moses' words to Pharaoh in His saying ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" He said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 23].

If the statement was directed to their polytheist people, they intended by it to proclaim their faith among their people and to show their indifference to the threats of the king and his people. In that case their position would be like the position of the Children of Israel when they said to Pharaoh ﴿No harm; indeed we will return to our Lord﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 50]. Or they intended by it to admonish their people without directly addressing them, drawing them in by way of allusion (ta'rid), in the manner of "I mean you, but listen, O neighbor"; and to be thorough in conveying the truth to them. This is the most evident reading if the standing is taken in its literal sense, and because the statement is attributed to the plural pronoun of them all, not to some of them. This differs from the attribution in His saying ﴿A speaker among them said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 19], which implies that the one addressed was another group. It is also evident that their statement was intended as an argument.

The phrase ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ is the predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtada'), serving to inform their people of this fact. The clause ﴿we shall never call upon any god besides Him﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf). Even if this statement was made among themselves in private as a preparation for His saying ﴿And when you separate from them﴾ [Al-Kahf: 16], and so on, the definition by idafa is used because it is the most serious way of identifying Him among them, and because it includes an honoring of themselves.

In this reading, the phrase ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a descriptive qualifier (sifa kashifa), and the clause ﴿we shall never call upon any god besides Him﴾ is the predicate of the subject.

They mentioned "calling upon" (du'a') rather than "worship" ('ibada), because du'a' includes all kinds of utterances: from applying the attribute of divinity to other than God, to calling upon other than God when asking for something.

The clause ﴿Indeed we would have said then an excessive lie﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) for what was conveyed by the emphasis of the negation with "lan" (never). The presence of the response particle within the clause indicates that it is a consequence of the preceding clause. The "lam" is the lam of oath.

Shatat (excess) means going to extremes in opposing the truth and what is right. It is derived from shatt (distance), meaning being far from one's place, because of the dislike that souls have for distance from it. It was therefore used metaphorically for excess in something hateful. The meaning is: "we would have uttered a statement that is excessive," namely attributing divinity to other than God.

In this reading, the phrase ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a descriptive qualifier (sifa kashifa), and the clause ﴿we shall never call upon any god besides Him﴾ is the predicate of the subject.

They mentioned "calling upon" (du'a') rather than "worship" ('ibada), because du'a' includes all kinds of utterances: from applying the attribute of divinity to other than God, to calling upon other than God when asking for something.

The clause ﴿Indeed we would have said then an excessive lie﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) for what was conveyed by the emphasis of the negation with "lan" (never). The presence of the response particle within the clause indicates that it is a consequence of the preceding clause. The "lam" is the lam of oath.

Shatat (excess) means going to extremes in opposing the truth and what is right. It is derived from shatt (distance), meaning being far from one's place, because of the dislike that souls have for distance from it. It was therefore used metaphorically for excess in something hateful. The meaning is: "we would have uttered a statement that is excessive," namely attributing divinity to other than God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 15:

﴿These are our people; they have taken besides Him gods. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? Who then is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie?﴾ This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) answering what the statement ﴿Indeed, we would have spoken, then, an enormity﴾ [al-Kahf: 14] necessarily raises in the mind of the listener, namely that he may ask who it is that utters this enormity, if there are among the hearers someone who does not know that, or by treating the non-questioner as if he were a questioner.

This sentence is part of the speech of the youths, as indicated by the pronoun in their words "besides Him" (dunihi), which refers to "our Lord."

The indication of their people by "these" (ha'ula') is meant to distinguish them by what he will report about them, and in this indication there is an implicit reproach expressing astonishment at their condition and an exposure of their handiwork; this is one of the implications of the purpose of distinction.

The clause "they have taken" (ittakhadhu) is a predicate of the demonstrative noun, and it is a predicate used for censure of them rather than for informing, since their taking gods besides Allah is known among the interlocutors, so informing about it would not convey the benefit of a report.

The meaning of "besides Him" (min dunihi) is "other than Him," and (min) is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), i.e., gods originating from other than Allah. Their people at that time were worshipping idols according to the creed of the Romans, and they did not believe in Allah.

The clause ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾ reinforces the preceding clause insofar as it is used for censure, since the content of this clause strengthens the censure against them.

(Law) is a particle of exhortation (tahdid); its reality is urging the attainment of what follows it. Since bringing an authority for the divinity of the idols they had taken as gods was impossible, as indicated by the fact that they denied it against them, the exhortation turned into rebuke and refutation, i.e., they took gods besides Allah for which there is no proof of their divinity.

The meaning of "for them" (alayhim) is "for their gods," by the indication of his saying ﴿they have taken besides Him gods﴾.

Sultan (authority) means proof and evidence.

Bayyin (clear) means evident in indication. The meaning of the speech is: since they did not bring an authority for that, they have founded their belief upon falsehood and error. For this reason, the clause ﴿Who then is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie?﴾ is made a consequence of it.

(Man) is interrogative, and it is a denial, i.e., there is no one more unjust than one who fabricates, and the meaning is that he is more unjust than others; the intended sense is not equality between him and others, as was mentioned previously in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114].

The meaning is that these people fabricated a lie against Allah, because they associated with Him others in divinity, and so they lied about Him in that, since they attributed to Him a quality contrary to reality.

The fabrication of lies (iftira' al-kadhib) was mentioned previously in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Then, if the speech from its beginning was addressed to their people, whom they had openly declared their faith to among themselves as previously mentioned, then the indication in their saying ﴿These are our people﴾ is on its apparent sense, and it was an escalation in the implicit admonition to them. If, however, the speech from its beginning revolved among themselves in their own circle, then the indication is to someone present in the mind, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So if these disbelieve in it﴾ [al-An'am: 89], i.e., the polytheists of Makkah.

[Page 276]

﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a useful provision in your affair.﴾ It is necessary that this be part of what some of them said to others, as counsel and sound advice. In relating the statements of speakers, it is not required that all the reported statements were uttered at one time. It is possible that they said this to one another after despairing that their people would turn back from their trial, at another occasion. It is also possible that it was said in the very same setting in which they addressed their people, by shifting the address from speaking to their people to speaking to one another, which is a kind of iltifat (shift in grammatical person or address). On the first possibility, the verb "i'tazaltumuhum" (اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهم, "you withdrew from them") is used to mean the intention of the act, like the verse ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. On the second possibility, the withdrawal had already occurred between the moment they addressed their people and the moment they addressed one another. On both possibilities, the Qur'an limited its relation of their statements to the most important purpose in showing their steadfastness, omitting whatever else had no bearing on the aim, since it is merely a narrative.

"Idh" (إذْ) here is for a figurative temporal sense, meaning causation.

I'tizal (الِاعْتِزالُ) means distancing oneself and separating from close contact with a thing. So the withdrawal from a people means ceasing to mix with them, and the withdrawal from what they worship means distancing oneself from worshipping idols.

The exception in His words "except Allah" (إلّا اللَّهَ) is disjunctive (munqati'), because the people did not worship Allah.

The "fa'" (الفاءُ) here is for consequence, following the clause ﴿and when you withdraw from them﴾, in view of its conveying the meaning: "you withdrew from their religion with a doctrinal withdrawal." Accordingly, a clause is implied after it, such as: "Withdraw from them with a withdrawal of separation, so take refuge in the cave." Or it is implied as: "And when you withdraw from their religion, and they torment you, then take refuge

[Page 277]

in the cave." Al-Farra' permitted that "idh" be construed with the meaning of a conditional, with "fa'awu" (فَأْوُوا, "take refuge") as its response. On the conditional reading, "i'tazaltumuhum" must necessarily be used to mean the intention of withdrawal.

"Awy" (الأوْيُ) has already been discussed above, meaning: so dwell in the cave.

The definiteness in "al-kahf" (الكَهْفِ, "the cave") may be the definiteness of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), in that the cave was already known to them, as a place where they had previously worshipped. It may also be the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-haqiqah), like the verse ﴿and I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], meaning: take refuge in any cave among caves. On this latter possibility, it would be an indication from them of the custom of the Christians mentioned at the beginning of these verses, or the habit of the persecuted among the Jews, as we have suggested there.

The "spreading" of mercy (نَشْرُ الرَّحْمَةِ) means that its attachment to those who are shown mercy becomes widespread. The continuous attachment of the attribute is likened to spreading a garment, in that it leaves nothing of the garment hidden. It has also been likened to unfolding. Its opposite is likened to folding and to gathering.

"Al-mirfaq" (المَرْفِقُ), with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa', is what one benefits from and uses for comfort. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it this way. With a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa', the rest of the readers read it so. Its "preparation" (تَهْيِئَتُهُ) is metaphorically used for honouring and caring for them, likened to preparing hospitality for a guest who is cared for. "Yanshur" (يَنْشُرْ) is in the jussive form as a response to the imperative. This is based on confidence in hope and supplication, and they expressed it as though it had already been achieved, out of their strong confidence in the gentle kindness of their Lord toward the believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 17:

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them on the left, while they were in a spacious chamber of it.﴾ He joined some of their circumstances to others.
