He moved on to mention it in connection with the indication of the fulfilment of their hope in their Lord, when some of them said to others: ﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you from your affair ease (mirfaq).﴾ [al-Kahf: 16].

Page 278
This is a great state, namely what Allah prepared for them in their affair of a place of ease (mirfaq), and that this was their reward for their being guided, and it is from the gentleness of Allah toward them.

The address is to an unspecified person, and the meaning is: "one who is able to see would see." This is common in usage, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

You see the birds of prey, having become confident in them, with a satisfaction from the choice young sheep and the slaughtered... (the verse as it stands)

The commentary has summarized from the account that when some of them said to others: ﴿So take refuge in the cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 16], they took refuge in it. The implied supplement is: they acted upon his advice, so they took refuge in the cave. This is indicated by His saying at the beginning of the story: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 10], so the latter part of the speech is returned to its beginning.

"Tazawwaru" is an imperfect verb derived from "al-zawr" with a fatha on the zay, meaning inclining. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on the zay followed by an alif and a fatha on the waw. Its origin is: "tatazawaru" with two ta's, and the ta' of the reflexive form (tafa'ul) was assimilated into the zay for lightness.

'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a light zay, by omitting one of the two ta's, namely the ta' of the imperfect, for lightness, relying on the nominative ending of the verb which indicates the imperfect. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (tazwarru) with a fatha on the ta', followed by a sakin zay, and a fatha on the waw, and a shadda on the ra', in the pattern of "tahmarru." All of these are forms derived from "al-zawar" with a vowel on the first letter, which is inclining away from a place. 'Antara said:

So it inclined from the impact of the spears in its chest.

That is, part of his body inclined toward another part and contracted.

The use of the imperfect verb indicates the repetition of this every day. And "tuqriduhum" means it turns away from them. The root of "al-qard" is cutting off, meaning that it does not enter into their cave.

Page 279
"Dhata al-yamin wa dhata al-shimal" [al-Kahf: 18] means "companion of," and it is an adjective of an elided noun indicated by the speech, i.e., the direction companion of the right. The discussion of "dhat" was previously made at His saying: ﴿So reconcile your differences (dhat baynikum)﴾ [al-Anfal: 1] in Surat al-Anfal.

The definiteness in (al-yamin, al-shimal) is a substitute for the omitted genitive, i.e., the right and left of the cave, which indicates that the mouth of the cave was open toward the north-east. So when the sun rises, it rises upon the side of the cave and its rays do not penetrate it, and when it sets, its rays are farther from the mouth of the cave than when it rises.

This is a wondrous arrangement which Allah facilitated for them in His wisdom, so that the inside of the cave would be in a state of moderation, and decay would not reach their bodies. That is among the signs of Allah's power.

"Al-fajwa" is the open space within the cave, such that they were not close to the mouth of the cave. In that space there is help in preserving this cave as it is.

* * *
﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾
The indication by His saying "dhalika" refers to what was mentioned from His saying ﴿And you would see the sun﴾.

"Ayat Allah" are the evidences of His power and His care for His friends and for those who support the religion of truth.

The sentence is parenthetical within the course of the story, to draw attention to its people, and the indication is for glorification.

* * *
﴿Whoever Allah guides is the one truly guided, and whoever He leads astray, you will not find for him any guardian (waliyyan) guiding him.﴾
"Murshidan" is an explanatory resumption in response to what the demonstrative implied of the glorification of the matter of the verse and its people.

Page 280
The generality of the conditional "man" includes those spoken of by the context of the situation. The meaning is that they were guided, because Allah guided them among those whom He guided, drawing attention to the fact that facilitating that for them from Allah is the effect of their being facilitated toward ease and guidance. So He conveyed the truth to them through their messenger, and granted them understandings that believe in the truth. The discussion of the parallel of "whoever Allah guides is the one truly guided" was previously made, and on the writing of "al-muhtad" without a ya' in Surat al-Isra'.

"Al-murshid" is the one who shows the bewildered the way of right guidance, which is reaching the sought good.

[Page 281]

﴿And you would think them awake while they are asleep, and We turn them to the right and to the left﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the rest of the story, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ). The address in it is like the address in ﴿And you see the sun﴾ [18:17]. This is a transition to the lesson in their condition for whoever might see them among people, with an incidental statement of their honour and of the great power of God regarding their affair. It is also an expression of wonder at their state for whoever might see them.

The meaning of "you would think them awake" is that they were in a state resembling wakefulness and different from sleep. It was said that their eyes were open.

The verb "you would think them" (taḥsabuhum) is in the present tense to indicate that this recurs over a long period.

*Al-Ayqāẓ* is the plural of *yaqiẓ*, on the pattern *kattif*, and also *yaqẓ* with the *qāf* vowelled, on the pattern *ʿaḍud*.

*Al-Ruqūd* is the plural of *rāqid* (sleeping).

*Al-Taqlīb* (turning) is changing the position of a thing from its outer side to its inner side. God says ﴿So he began to turn over his two hands﴾ [18:42].

[Page 281 continues]

﴿To the right and to the left﴾ means towards their right sides and their left sides. The meaning is that God caused them to undergo the condition of living, wakeful people, so their positions were changed from the right side to the left and the reverse. This was for a wisdom, which perhaps had an effect on keeping their bodies in a state of soundness.

The use of the present tense is to indicate renewal according to the narrated time, and it does not necessarily follow that they were in this state at the time the verse was revealed.

* * *

﴿And their dog stretched its two forelegs at the threshold﴾

This indicates that turning them to the right and to the left was an honour for them, by granting them the state of the living, and a care for them. For this reason the turning is not mentioned for their dog; rather it remained in its place, stretching its two forelegs, in the manner of a dog's sitting.

*Al-Waṣīd* is the entrance of the cave. It is likened to the door, which is *al-waṣīd*, because it is closed and shut.

The fact that the dog was not turned to its right or left shows that turning them was not among the causes of their preservation from decay; otherwise their dog would have been the same as them in that. Rather, it was an honour for them. It may be said that they did not perish, but as for their dog, it perished and became a scattered heap, with the bones of its forelegs spread out.

* * *

﴿Had you looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them﴾

The address is to an unspecified person, meaning: had you looked upon them, O listener, when they were in that state before God raised them, since the speech does not say that they remained so at the time the verse was revealed.

[Page 282]

The meaning is: had you looked upon them, and had you not known their story, you would have thought them to be thieves and highwaymen, since they were a group in a cave, and caves were hiding places for highwaymen, as Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said:

*I say to the Laḥyān when their waterskins have been emptied for them,*
*and my day is narrow of hole, its entrance narrow.*

So you would have fled from them, and terror would have seized you because of their evil, as in God's saying ﴿He felt a dread of them and was seized with fear﴾ [11:70]. The intended meaning is not terror from their essences, since nothing in their essences differs from the creation of people, nor is it fear from their being dead, since fear of the dead was not among the customs of the Arabs. Moreover, it has already been stated ﴿and you would think them awake while they are asleep﴾.

*Al-Iṭṭilāʿ* is looking over a thing and seeing it from a high place, because it is an *iftiʿāl* form from *ṭalaʿa*, meaning to ascend a mountain. The *iftiʿāl* form is used for intensifying the ascent. It was made to carry the meaning of looking over and so was followed by *ʿalā* (over). Then it was used metaphorically, as is well known, for seeing a thing that no one sees. This verb will be mentioned again at God's saying ﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ [19:78] in Surat Maryam. Moreover, the address being to the Prophet ﷺ is not what is intended; what appears in al-Kashshāf from Ibn ʿAbbās suggests that, but it is not correct.

*Firāran* (in flight) is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, a verbal noun specifying the type of action) explaining the kind of *wallaytа* (you would have turned).

*Mullitta* is in the passive voice, meaning that terror filled you. *Mallaʾa*, with the *lām* doubled, is the intensive form of *malaʾa*, and both readings are recited.

*Al-Malʾ* (filling) is the contained thing occupying the whole void of the container so that no room remains in the container for any increase of the contained. Thus the psychological attribute is represented by the contained thing, the human intellect is represented by the container, and the attribute's taking full possession of the soul, so that no thought of anything else mixes with it, is represented by filling the container with its contents. So in the phrase "you were filled" there is a figurative allegory (istiʿāra tamthīliyya). The opposite is God's saying ﴿and the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾ [28:10].

[Page 283]

*Ruʿban* (dread) is in the accusative as a specification of the relation (tamyīz al-nisba), transferred in meaning from the agent, because it is dread that fills. When the verb was made passive for the purpose of generality followed by detail, what should have been the agent became a specification. This is a wondrous construction, through which detail occurred after generality. It is not a specification transferred from the object, as might appear at first glance.

Dread (*ruʿb*) was mentioned previously in God's saying ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [3:151] in Surat Al ʿImrān.

Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathīr recited *wa-la-mullitta* with the *lām* doubled, for intensity in filling. The rest read it with the *lām* lightened, according to the basic form.

The majority read *ruʿban* with the *ʿayn* unvowelled (sakūn). Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb read it with the *ʿayn* vowelled (ḍamm).

[Page 284]

This is a continuation of the story, a part of it that contains a lesson for the People of the Cave themselves, so that they might know what God honoured them with: that He protected them from their enemies' hands, which would have inflicted humiliation on them, and that He informed them with certain knowledge (ʿilm al-yaqīn) of some of the manner of resurrection, since His knowledge is great. Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

The demonstrative in His words ﴿And thus﴾ refers to what was mentioned of their sleep and its manner. That is: just as We put them to sleep for centuries, We raised them up. The point of resemblance is that waking up is a sign of God's immense power, just as falling asleep is a sign.

It is also permissible that the resurrection mentioned is itself compared to something, for the sake of emphasizing wonder, as was previously stated in His words ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The discussion of the meaning of resurrection (baʿth) was given in the preceding verse, as was the discussion of the appropriateness of the word baʿth in this story, and of the causal clause in His words ﴿that they might ask one another﴾ when He said ﴿Then We resurrected them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing what they had stayed﴾ [al-Kahf: 12]. The meaning is: We raised them up, so they questioned one another.

The clause ﴿One of them said﴾ explains the clause ﴿that they might ask one another﴾. This exchange is called a questioning (tasāʾul) because it is a dialogue in which each seeks the opinion of the other in order to reach the determination of the duration. Those who said ﴿We stayed a day or part of a day﴾ are all of them except the one who said ﴿How long have you stayed?﴾

The answer is attributed to the pronoun of their group, either because they had agreed upon it, or to indicate distribution: some of them said, "We stayed a day," and some said, "We stayed part of a day." On this reading, the particle (aw, "or") may be for division in the saying, as shown by His subsequent words ﴿They said: Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾. That is, when they differed, they returned and gave up speaking by conjecture and entrusted the knowledge to God Most High, and that is from the perfection of their faith. Those who said ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾ may be all of them, which is the apparent meaning, or it may be the saying of some of them, which is attributed to them all because they considered it correct.

The consequence of their saying ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours﴾ follows from their saying ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾, because it means: abandon the debate about the length of the stay, for none knows it but God, and take up something else that concerns you. This is close to what is called the wise approach (al-uslūb al-ḥakīm, the method of responding to a questioner with something other than what he seeks, as an indication that another matter is more fitting for his situation). Had it not been for their saying ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾, their saying ﴿So send one of you﴾ would have been the very wise approach.

[Page 285]

Al-warq, with a fatḥa on the wāw and a kasra on the rāʾ, means silver. This is how the majority read it. It is also said warq with a fatḥa on the wāw and a sukūn on the rāʾ, and this is how Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Rawḥ from Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf read it. The meaning of warq here is a piece of minted silver, namely coins (dirham). It was said that they were dirhams of Diqyūs, the sultan of the Romans.

The demonstrative in ﴿this﴾ refers to specific coins that they had. The city is Absus, with a single bāʾ, and its mention was previously made at the beginning of the story.

The referent of ﴿which﴾ (ayyuhā) is any place in the city, since the city is a whole with many parts, among them the shops of the merchants. That is: let him look for which place in it has the purest food, meaning that its food is purer than the food of others.

The accusative ﴿food﴾ (ṭaʿāman) is a specification (tamyīz, a noun clarifying the sense of an adjective or comparative) for the attribution of (azkā, "purer") to (ayy, "which").

Al-azkā means the best and finest, because al-zakw is an increase in goodness and benefit.

Al-rizq means sustenance, and it was discussed previously at His words ﴿He said: No food will come to you that you are given, except I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ [Yūsuf: 37] in the Surah of Yusuf. The fāʾ (so) is for the consequence of their command to the one they send, that he should bring pure food and act with gentleness.

The imperative form in ﴿let him bring you﴾ and ﴿let him be gentle﴾ is addressed to an unspecified person whom they will appoint, that is: if you send him, he will bring you provision. It is also permissible that the one commanded is specified among them, and the vagueness is only in protecting their speech, not in the reported speech. On both readings, they are commanded to instruct him in this.

It was said that the letter tāʾ in the word ﴿and let him be gentle﴾ (walyatalaṭṭaf) is half of the letters of the Qur'an by count. There is also an opinion, which Ibn ʿAṭiyya restricted himself to, that the nūn in His words ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾ [al-Kahf: 74] is half of the letters of the Qur'an.

[Page 286]

Al-ish'ār means informing. It is an afʿāl form from shaʿara, of the pattern naṣara and karuma, shuʿūran, that is, to know. The hamza makes it transitive, like the hamza of aʿlama ("to inform") from ʿalima, which is the knowledge of recognition and is transitive to one object.

His words ﴿with you﴾ are connected to ﴿let him not make anyone aware﴾. So the object of the preposition is what is made known, that is, what is known. What is known is only a meaning among meanings, related to the pronoun in the genitive governed by the verb ﴿let him make aware﴾, in the category of attributing the judgment to the essence where some of its states are meant. The implied meaning is: let him not inform anyone of your presence. Here there is an omitted modifier, indicated by the implication of the context (dalālat al-iqtiḍāʾ), so it includes all their conditions: their number, their place, and other things. The nūn is for emphasizing the prohibition, as a warning against its consequences, which are contained in the clause ﴿If they come to know of you, they will stone you﴾, which comes as a cause for the prohibition and an explanation of the reason for emphasizing the prohibition with the nūn. So it stands in the position of cause and explanation, and both require separating it from what precedes it.

The clause ﴿If they come to know of you, they will stone you﴾ is the cause for the command to be gentle and the prohibition against making anyone aware of them.

The pronoun in ﴿they﴾ (innahum) refers to what the generality in His words ﴿let him not make anyone aware of you﴾ conveys, so ﴿anyone﴾ takes the meaning of all people, under the rule of an indefinite noun in the context of a quasi-prohibition.

Al-ẓuhūr originally means emergence without cover. It is also used for victory over a thing and for dominance over others, and this is what is meant here.

God Most High said: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private parts﴾ [al-Nūr: 31], and said: ﴿and God made him prevail over them﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 3], and said: ﴿you support one another against them in sin and aggression﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85].

Al-rajm means killing by throwing stones at the one stoned until he dies. It is a killing of degradation, humiliation, and torment.

[Page 287]

The clause ﴿they will stone you﴾ is the answer to the condition ﴿if they come to know of you﴾, and the two clauses of the condition and its answer together are evidence for the omitted predicate of (inna, "indeed"), since the condition and its answer indicate it.

The meaning of ﴿or make you return to their creed﴾ is: they will return you to the religion that is among their particular things. That is, their affair admits of no way out other than one of two matters: either returning you to their religion or killing you.

Al-milla means religion, and it was discussed previously in the Surah of Yusuf at His words ﴿Indeed, I have left the creed of a people who do not believe in God﴾ [Yūsuf: 37].

He emphasized the warning against returning to their creed by stating that it entails the negation of their success in the future, because of what the conditional particle (idhan, "then") indicates.

The word ﴿ever﴾ (abadan) is an adverb of the entire future. It is an emphasis on what the negation with (lan, "never") indicates of perpetuity or something close to it.

[Page 284]

This is a continuation of the story, a part of it that contains a lesson for the People of the Cave themselves, so that they might know what God honoured them with: that He protected them from their enemies' hands, which would have inflicted humiliation on them, and that He informed them with certain knowledge (ʿilm al-yaqīn) of some of the manner of resurrection, since His knowledge is great. Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260].

The demonstrative in His words ﴿And thus﴾ refers to what was mentioned of their sleep and its manner. That is: just as We put them to sleep for centuries, We raised them up. The point of resemblance is that waking up is a sign of God's immense power, just as falling asleep is a sign.

It is also permissible that the resurrection mentioned is itself compared to something, for the sake of emphasizing wonder, as was previously stated in His words ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The discussion of the meaning of resurrection (baʿth) was given in the preceding verse, as was the discussion of the appropriateness of the word baʿth in this story, and of the causal clause in His words ﴿that they might ask one another﴾ when He said ﴿Then We resurrected them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing what they had stayed﴾ [al-Kahf: 12]. The meaning is: We raised them up, so they questioned one another.

The clause ﴿One of them said﴾ explains the clause ﴿that they might ask one another﴾. This exchange is called a questioning (tasāʾul) because it is a dialogue in which each seeks the opinion of the other in order to reach the determination of the duration. Those who said ﴿We stayed a day or part of a day﴾ are all of them except the one who said ﴿How long have you stayed?﴾

The answer is attributed to the pronoun of their group, either because they had agreed upon it, or to indicate distribution: some of them said, "We stayed a day," and some said, "We stayed part of a day." On this reading, the particle (aw, "or") may be for division in the saying, as shown by His subsequent words ﴿They said: Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾. That is, when they differed, they returned and gave up speaking by conjecture and entrusted the knowledge to God Most High, and that is from the perfection of their faith. Those who said ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾ may be all of them, which is the apparent meaning, or it may be the saying of some of them, which is attributed to them all because they considered it correct.

The consequence of their saying ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours﴾ follows from their saying ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾, because it means: abandon the debate about the length of the stay, for none knows it but God, and take up something else that concerns you. This is close to what is called the wise approach (al-uslūb al-ḥakīm, the method of responding to a questioner with something other than what he seeks, as an indication that another matter is more fitting for his situation). Had it not been for their saying ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾, their saying ﴿So send one of you﴾ would have been the very wise approach.

[Page 285]

Al-warq, with a fatḥa on the wāw and a kasra on the rāʾ, means silver. This is how the majority read it. It is also said warq with a fatḥa on the wāw and a sukūn on the rāʾ, and this is how Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Rawḥ from Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf read it. The meaning of warq here is a piece of minted silver, namely coins (dirham). It was said that they were dirhams of Diqyūs, the sultan of the Romans.

The demonstrative in ﴿this﴾ refers to specific coins that they had. The city is Absus, with a single bāʾ, and its mention was previously made at the beginning of the story.

The referent of ﴿which﴾ (ayyuhā) is any place in the city, since the city is a whole with many parts, among them the shops of the merchants. That is: let him look for which place in it has the purest food, meaning that its food is purer than the food of others.

The accusative ﴿food﴾ (ṭaʿāman) is a specification (tamyīz, a noun clarifying the sense of an adjective or comparative) for the attribution of (azkā, "purer") to (ayy, "which").

Al-azkā means the best and finest, because al-zakw is an increase in goodness and benefit.

Al-rizq means sustenance, and it was discussed previously at His words ﴿He said: No food will come to you that you are given, except I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ [Yūsuf: 37] in the Surah of Yusuf. The fāʾ (so) is for the consequence of their command to the one they send, that he should bring pure food and act with gentleness.

The imperative form in ﴿let him bring you﴾ and ﴿let him be gentle﴾ is addressed to an unspecified person whom they will appoint, that is: if you send him, he will bring you provision. It is also permissible that the one commanded is specified among them, and the vagueness is only in protecting their speech, not in the reported speech. On both readings, they are commanded to instruct him in this.

It was said that the letter tāʾ in the word ﴿and let him be gentle﴾ (walyatalaṭṭaf) is half of the letters of the Qur'an by count. There is also an opinion, which Ibn ʿAṭiyya restricted himself to, that the nūn in His words ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾ [al-Kahf: 74] is half of the letters of the Qur'an.

[Page 286]

Al-ish'ār means informing. It is an afʿāl form from shaʿara, of the pattern naṣara and karuma, shuʿūran, that is, to know. The hamza makes it transitive, like the hamza of aʿlama ("to inform") from ʿalima, which is the knowledge of recognition and is transitive to one object.

His words ﴿with you﴾ are connected to ﴿let him not make anyone aware﴾. So the object of the preposition is what is made known, that is, what is known. What is known is only a meaning among meanings, related to the pronoun in the genitive governed by the verb ﴿let him make aware﴾, in the category of attributing the judgment to the essence where some of its states are meant. The implied meaning is: let him not inform anyone of your presence. Here there is an omitted modifier, indicated by the implication of the context (dalālat al-iqtiḍāʾ), so it includes all their conditions: their number, their place, and other things. The nūn is for emphasizing the prohibition, as a warning against its consequences, which are contained in the clause ﴿If they come to know of you, they will stone you﴾, which comes as a cause for the prohibition and an explanation of the reason for emphasizing the prohibition with the nūn. So it stands in the position of cause and explanation, and both require separating it from what precedes it.

The clause ﴿If they come to know of you, they will stone you﴾ is the cause for the command to be gentle and the prohibition against making anyone aware of them.

The pronoun in ﴿they﴾ (innahum) refers to what the generality in His words ﴿let him not make anyone aware of you﴾ conveys, so ﴿anyone﴾ takes the meaning of all people, under the rule of an indefinite noun in the context of a quasi-prohibition.

Al-ẓuhūr originally means emergence without cover. It is also used for victory over a thing and for dominance over others, and this is what is meant here.

God Most High said: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private parts﴾ [al-Nūr: 31], and said: ﴿and God made him prevail over them﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 3], and said: ﴿you support one another against them in sin and aggression﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85].

Al-rajm means killing by throwing stones at the one stoned until he dies. It is a killing of degradation, humiliation, and torment.

[Page 287]

The clause ﴿they will stone you﴾ is the answer to the condition ﴿if they come to know of you﴾, and the two clauses of the condition and its answer together are evidence for the omitted predicate of (inna, "indeed"), since the condition and its answer indicate it.

The meaning of ﴿or make you return to their creed﴾ is: they will return you to the religion that is among their particular things. That is, their affair admits of no way out other than one of two matters: either returning you to their religion or killing you.

Al-milla means religion, and it was discussed previously in the Surah of Yusuf at His words ﴿Indeed, I have left the creed of a people who do not believe in God﴾ [Yūsuf: 37].

He emphasized the warning against returning to their creed by stating that it entails the negation of their success in the future, because of what the conditional particle (idhan, "then") indicates.

The word ﴿ever﴾ (abadan) is an adverb of the entire future. It is an emphasis on what the negation with (lan, "never") indicates of perpetuity or something close to it.

﴿And thus We caused them to be found, so that they would know that the promise of God is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾. [He] moved on to the part of the story that is the lesson for the people of their time, through their condition and their benefit from the reassurance of their hearts regarding the occurrence of resurrection on the Day of Judgment, by way of bringing it near through direct observation, and the confirmation of the religion through the dignity (karamah) that appeared in its helpers.

The people who found them were believers like them, so their sign was a sign of firmness and strengthening of faith.

So the statement is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying ﴿And thus We raised them up﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], and so on.

The discussion of the comparison and the demonstrative in "wa-kadhalika" is like the discussion of the one before it just now.

[Page 288]

Al-ʿuthur ʿala al-shay' (finding upon a thing) means becoming aware of it and attaining it after searching. The report about the People of the Cave in that city had been circulating among its people, so God facilitated for the people of the city the finding of them, for the wisdom contained in His saying ﴿so that they would know that the promise of God is true﴾, and so on.

The object of aʿtharna is omitted, indicated by the generality of ﴿and let no one become aware of you﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Its estimated form is: "We caused the people of the city to find them."

The pronoun in "li-yaʿlamu" (so that they would know) refers to the omitted, estimated object, because the estimated is like the stated.

The promise of God is: the revival of the dead for resurrection. As for their knowledge that the Hour, that is the Hour of gathering, there is no doubt about it, if their knowledge of that comes from direct observation, by which the thoughts of hiddenness that afflict the believer in his belief are dispelled, when he cannot conceive the modality of the traditionally transmitted (samʿiyyah) doctrines, then it is not a doubt regarding the knowledge, but regarding the modality. This is what is reported concerning it: that it occurs only to a sincere believer (siddiq), and persists only in a heretic (zindiq).

* * *

﴿when they disputed among themselves regarding their affair﴾
The adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to aʿtharna, meaning: We caused them to be found at the time when they disputed regarding their affair. This was expressed in the form of the temporal adverb in order to indicate the continuity of the dispute over the affair of the People of the Cave with the finding of them, to the extent that they rushed to engage in [discussing] a dignity they would attribute to them. This is an idmaj (rhetorical embedding, idmaj: the inclusion of one matter within another in a single expression) of mention of a dispute that took place among those who had transgressed against them, concerning various matters gathered by His saying "their affair." The pronoun in "yatanazaʿun" (they dispute) and "baynahum" (among themselves) refers to what the pronoun in "li-yaʿlamu" referred to.

The pronoun in "amrahum" may refer to the People of the Cave, and "al-amr" here means "the matter/condition."

[Page 289]

Al-tanazuʿ means strong contention. That is, the people of the city dispute among themselves concerning the condition of the People of the Cave, such as: were they asleep or dead; will they remain alive or will they die; will they remain in that cave or return to dwelling in the city; and the duration of their stay.
It is also possible that the pronoun in "amrahum" refers to what the pronoun in "yatanazaʿun" referred to, meaning: their affair regarding what they would do with them.

The use of the present tense (al-mudariʿ) is to evoke the state of dispute.

* * *

﴿So they said, "Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them." Those who prevailed over their affair said, "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾
The description of their being found is omitted here, and their return to the cave is mentioned, because the purpose does not depend on mentioning it, since it is not a place of lesson; the return to their resting place and the death coming upon them is a matter customary for every living being.

The "fa-qalu" (so they said) is a consequence (tafriʿ) of "yatanazaʿun."

They only thought to build a structure over them because they feared, for them, the frequent visits of visitors who lacked decorum, lest they harm their bodies and garments by touching and turning them over, so they wished to build over them a structure whose door could be locked and guarded.

The clause ﴿their Lord knows best about them﴾ may be part of the quoted speech of those who said "build over them a structure," and the meaning is: their Lord knows best about their conditions regarding which we dispute, so this is a termination of the dispute over their affair. It may also be an interjected clause from the speech of God, the Exalted, in the course of narrating the dispute of those who were caused to find them, meaning: the Lord of the People of the Cave, or the Lord of those disputing over their affair, knows better than they do the reality of what they disputed about.

[Page 290]

Those who prevailed over their affair are the rulers of the affairs in the city. The pronoun in "amrihim" refers to what the pronoun in "fa-qalu" referred to, that is, those who prevailed over the affair of those who said: "build over them a structure."

They only saw that the structure should be a place of worship so that it would be an honor for them, and so that people's attention to their cave would continue. Taking places of worship over the graves of the righteous was a practice of the Christians, and the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade it, as in the hadith on the day of the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): ʿAʾishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "Had it not been for that, his grave would have been exposed," meaning it would have been exposed in the Prophet's Mosque, and it was not placed behind the wall of the chamber.

Taking mosques over graves and praying in them is forbidden, because that is a means (dhari'ah: a means leading to a prohibited end) toward worshipping the occupant of the grave, or resembles the act of those who worship the righteous of their religion. The means was specifically related to the dead because what befalls their companions of grief at their loss moves them to excess in what they reckon to be honoring them after their death; then the matter is forgotten, and people assume that this is due to a special quality in that deceased person. Building mosques over graves was a practice of the people of Christianity. If it was a law for them, then Islam has abrogated it (naskh: abrogation), and if it was an innovation (bidʿah) on their part in their religion, then it is more fitting to prohibit it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on surah 18, verse 22:

﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them their dog," and they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them their dog," guessing at the unseen. And they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few."﴾

When the story of the People of the Cave spread after the Qur'an was revealed concerning it, it became a topic of conversation in gatherings. It became a subject of conjecture about their number and about the length of their stay in the cave. Perhaps some of the Arab Christians (*al-mutanassirah*) related stories to them about this. The Qur'an drew attention to this and left the general public uninformed about it, for a wisdom: that the community should accustom itself to abandoning preoccupation with matters from which there is no benefit for the religion or for people. The use of the future tense (*sin al-istiqbal*) indicates that people will continue to engage in this discussion.

The pronoun in "yaqulun" (they say) refers to an unmentioned subject, because it is known from the context, meaning: "People say," or "the Muslims say," since there is no harm in this statement. Yet they were alerted that none of it has any proof behind it. The meaning of the particle *sin* (of the future) extends to the two verbs coordinated with the verb that is linked to *sin*. The arrival at the number eight does not imply that it is the actual number in reality.

God has informed us that a few of creation know their number, and they are those whom God made aware of it. At their head is Muhammad (ﷺ), because their story came through his tongue, so there is no doubt that God informed him of their number. It is narrated that Ibn 'Abbas said: "I am among the few."

It seems that people's opinions converged on the idea that their number is odd, out of a desire for good omen by the odd number. Otherwise, there is no proof for this over anything else. God called their statement "guessing at the unseen" (*rajman bil-ghayb*).

The literal meaning of *rajm* is throwing a stone or the like. It is used here metaphorically for throwing out speech without deliberation or verification. Zuhayr said:

*"Nor is he, concerning it, one who speaks by guesswork."*

The *ba'* in *bil-ghayb* is for transitivity. It is as if, when they spoke about an absent matter, they were throwing it at it.

Both the clause *"rabi'uhum kalbuhum"* (the fourth of them is their dog) and the clause *"sadisuhum kalbuhum"* (the sixth of them is their dog) are in the position of a qualifier of the numeral preceding them, or in the position of a second predicate of the omitted subject.

The clause *"wa thamimuhum kalbuhum"* (and the eighth of them is their dog) has a *waw* that is the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*). It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the omitted subject, or from the numeral which is the predicate of the subject. If the numeral is indefinite, its occurrence as a predicate of a definite subject makes it definite. Moreover, a circumstantial clause introduced by *waw* has been counted among the justifications for a circumstantial phrase coming from an indefinite noun. There is no basis for making the *waw* here enter a clause that is a qualifier of an indefinite noun, in order to emphasise the attachment of the qualifier to the qualified, as al-Zamakhshari (in *al-Kashshaf*) held, because that is not known in eloquent speech. Al-Sakkaki (in *al-Miftah*) and others refuted it.

Among the strange trials of innovation in the meanings of the Qur'an is the claim of someone who asserted that this *waw* is the *waw of eight* (*wawu al-thamaniyah*). This view is attributed in Arabic grammar books to some weak grammarians, and its originator was not identified. Ibn Hisham, in *Mughni al-Labib*, counted among those who held this view al-Hariri and some weak grammarians, such as Ibn Khalawayh, and al-Tha'labi among the exegetes.

I say: the earliest of these is Ibn Khalawayh, the grammarian, who died in 370 AH. He is the one meant by "some weak grammarians." I think Ibn Hisham took this description from the words of Ibn al-Munir in *al-Intisaf 'ala al-Kashshaf*, in the commentary on surah al-Tahrim, where it is reported from Ibn al-Hajib that al-Qadi al-Fadil believed that the *waw* in God's words ﴿thayyibatin wa abkaran﴾ (previously married women and virgins) [al-Tahrim: 5] in surah al-Tahrim is the *waw* which some weak grammarians called "the *waw* of eight." The qadi used to boast of extracting it in addition to the three well-known places. The first is in the eighth attribute in God's words ﴿wal-nahuna 'an al-munkar﴾ (and those who forbid wrong) [al-Tawbah: 112] in surah Bara'ah. The second is in His words "wa thamimuhum kalbuhum," and the third is in His words ﴿wa futihat abwabuha﴾ (and its gates will be opened) [al-Zumar: 73] in surah al-Zumar. Ibn al-Hajib said: "The qadi continued to admire this idea of his own until one day he mentioned it in the presence of Abu al-Jud, the grammarian, the reciter, who explained to him that he was mistaken in counting it among that category, and referred the explanation to the meaning which al-Zamakhshari mentioned, namely, that the need to describe the two attributes in a single qualified noun necessitates the use of the *waw* here..." until the end.

Ibn Hisham said in *al-Mughni*: "al-Tha'labi preceded al-Fadil in counting it among the places in his exegesis." I say: perhaps al-Fadil did not see it. Al-Tha'labi added God's words ﴿sab'a layalin wa thamaniyata ayyamin husuman﴾ (seven nights and eight days, continuous) [al-Haqqah: 7] in surah al-Haqqah, where he joined the numeral *thamaniyah* (eight) with the letter *waw*.

It is a remarkable coincidence that the reality of the number eight is connected to the five places mentioned in the Qur'an. Either it appears by its wording, as here and in the verse of al-Haqqah; or by reaching it, as in the verse of Bara'ah and the verse of al-Tahrim; or by its referent being counted as eight, as in the verse of al-Zumar. Noticing this may be counted among subtleties, but it does not reach the level of established knowledge. Since this is so, and there is no fixed rule for it, it is not far-fetched to count the verse of surah al-Tahrim among them, as al-Qadi al-Fadil did, because it coincides with the eighth in mention, even if it is not the eighth of the attributes of those described. The same applies to counting the verse of surah al-Haqqah. Such subtleties are like a flower: they are smelled, not rubbed.

The discussion of these was previously given under God's words ﴿wal-nahuna 'an al-munkar﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112] in surah Bara'ah.

The clause ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number."﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanation (*isti'naf bayani*) in response to what is raised by the clause ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them their dog"﴾ through its end, namely the expectation of specifying what can be relied upon concerning their number. So the answer is that knowledge of this is referred to the Knower of the unseen. The attribution of the superlative form (*ism al-tafdil*) to God, the Exalted, indicates that God's knowledge of their number is complete knowledge, while the knowledge of others is mere conjecture and guesswork, which may coincide with reality and may not.

The clause ﴿none knows them except a few﴾ is likewise a resumptive clause of explanation. This is because the report that God is the Most Knowing raises in the hearers' minds the question: "Could some people know their number with incomplete knowledge?" So the answer is that a few people know it, and they are without doubt those whom God informed of it by revelation. In any case, they are not described as the majority, because their knowledge is acquired from God, the Most Knowing of it.

* * *

[Page 294]

﴿So do not dispute about them except with an apparent dispute, and do not ask any of them for a ruling concerning them.﴾

This is a consequence of the disagreement about the number of the People of the Cave. That is, if some of the polytheists want to dispute about the number of the People of the Cave, on the basis of reports they received from the People of the Book, or in order to seek verification of their number, then do not dispute with them, because that is preoccupation with what has no benefit. This consequence, and what is conjoined to it, is a digression in the midst of the story.

*Tamari* (disputing) is a reciprocal form derived from *mirya*, which is doubt. The morphological pattern of reciprocity (*mufa'alah*) indicates that it is an act of doubt performed from both sides. It thus returns to the sense of argumentation about belief in order to refute it, and this leads to doubt about it. So *mira* was used in the sense of argumentation by way of metaphor (*majaz*), then it became common until it became a literal meaning (*haqiqah*) when it equalled the literal sense. The meaning of *mira* concerning them is the dispute about their number, as the context of the consequence requires.

The apparent dispute (*mira zahir*) is the one which cannot be denied, and whose discussion does not become lengthy. Such is God's words ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number."﴾ and His words ﴿none knows them except a few.﴾ For this is something that cannot be denied or rejected, because its proof is clear. Anything beyond this requires proof, and so it is not appropriate to be preoccupied with it, because its benefit is slight.

*Istifta'* (asking for a ruling) is seeking a *fatwa*. A *fatwa* is an informative statement about a matter of knowledge which not everyone knows. The meaning of "concerning them" is: concerning their affair, that is, the affair of the People of the Cave. The purpose of the prohibition against asking them is a *kinayah* (metonymy) for their ignorance of the affair of the People of the Cave. So the pronoun in "minhum" (from them) refers to what the pronoun in ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ refers to, namely the people of Makkah who asked about the affair of the People of the Cave.

Alternatively, it may be a symbolic *kinayah* (*kinayah ramziyyah*) for the Prophet's (ﷺ) knowledge of the reality of their affair, to the point that he is free from asking anyone, and that he does not inform the polytheists of what God taught him concerning the affair of the People of the Cave. In this case, *min* is causal (*ta'liliyyah*), and the pronoun governed by it refers to the questioners who were seeking to trap him, meaning: do not ask the knowledge of that because of the eagerness of the questioners that you inform them with certainty of the affair of the People of the Cave, for you have known it, and you were not commanded to teach them it. If the prohibition is not understood in this sense, its meaning does not become clear. Restricting it with "from them" is significant, and it is not correct to take the pronoun in "minhum" as referring to the People of the Book, because these verses are Meccan by the agreement of the narrators and the exegetes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 23:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ [al-Kahf: 24] This is an continuation of the parenthetical discourse (i'tiraḍ), and the reason for its placement here is what Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari related at the beginning of this surah, and al-Wahidi in the surah of Maryam: that when the polytheists asked the Prophet ﷺ about the People of the Cave and Dhu al-Qarnayn, he promised them an answer to their question the next day and did not say, "If Allah wills." So Jibril, peace be upon him, did not bring him the answer until after fifteen days, and it was said: after three days, as has been mentioned previously. That is, the delay of the revelation to him with the answer was a symbolic rebuke from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ, just as He rebuked Sulayman, peace be upon him, in what al-Bukhari related: "Sulayman said: 'Tonight I will go in to a hundred women, each of whom will bear a child who will fight in the way of Allah.' But none of them conceived except one, who bore half a boy." Then this was an explicit rebuke, for when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the People of the Cave, he promised an answer and forgot to say, "If Allah wills," just as Sulayman forgot. So Allah informed His Messenger of the story of the People of the Cave, then forbade him from promising to do something without qualifying it with the will of Allah.

The words ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ [al-Kahf: 24] are a genuine exception (istithna') from the preceding statement. There is disagreement among the exegetes regarding how it is structured. The implication of al-Zamakhshari's words is that it is part of the prohibition sentence, i.e., it is an exception from the ruling of the prohibition: "Do not say, 'Indeed, I will do that,' etc., unless Allah wills that you say it," and Allah's will is known from His permission for that. Thus the meaning becomes: "unless Allah permits you to say it." Accordingly, the verbal noun formed from "that Allah wills" is an exception from the general scope of the prohibited matters, and it is part of the speech of Allah the Exalted. The object of "Allah wills" is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, as is the nature of the verb of willing. The estimate is: "unless a statement that Allah has willed," so you are not forbidden from saying it.

The implication of the words of al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and al-Farra' is that it is an exception from the clause ﴿Indeed, I will do that tomorrow﴾, so it is an exception from the prohibited speech of the Prophet ﷺ, i.e., "except a statement accompanied by 'If Allah wills'." In this case the verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb is in the place of an accusative by removal of the preposition, which is the bā' of accompaniment. The estimate is: "except with ﴿that Allah wills﴾" [al-Kahf: 24], i.e., with that which indicates the mention of Allah's will. This is because accompanying the statement by the reality of the will is impossible, so it is known that what is meant is accompanying it with the mention of the will by the words "If Allah wills" and the like. Thus "the will" here means Allah's permission for him.

This verse has gathered a dignity (karamah) for the Prophet ﷺ from three aspects. The first: that He answered his request, and clarified for them what they had asked him, contrary to Allah's customary practice with the stubborn.

The second: that He taught him a great lesson of prophetic etiquette.

The third: that He did not teach him this except after answering his request, as a reassurance to himself that He would not hasten to forbid him from that before answering him, lest he suppose that the prohibition requires turning away from answering his question. Such is the manner of disciplining the beloved and honoured one. An example of this is what is in the Sahih: "Hakim ibn Hizam said: 'I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he gave me; I asked him again and he gave me; I asked him again and he gave me. Then he said: "O Hakim, this wealth is sweet and green. Whoever takes it with a generous soul, it will be blessed for him; and whoever takes it with a greedy soul, it will not be blessed for him, and he will be like one who eats but is never satisfied. The upper hand is better than the lower hand."' Hakim said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by the One who sent you with the truth, I will not ask anyone for anything after you until I depart this world.'" So Hakim understood that the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ saying this to him did not intend to prevent his request, but intended to adorn him with a good character. Therefore Hakim swore that he would not take from anyone other than the Messenger of Allah anything, and he did not say: "I will not ask you for anything after this time."

The construction of the verse is that the lam in His saying ﴿li-shay'in﴾ is not the lam by which the verb of saying is transitive to the addressee; rather it is the lam of cause, i.e., "Do not say, 'Indeed, I will do such and such,' on account of a thing you promise with it." So the lam is in the position of (fi, "in" / "concerning").

And "shay'" (thing) is a noun extremely general in its indefiniteness, whose meaning is determined by the context, i.e., the thing you intend to do.

The reference of the demonstrative in His saying "that" (dhalika) returns to "thing," i.e., "Indeed, I will do the reporting of a matter they ask him about."

And "ghadan" (tomorrow) is used in the sense of the future figuratively; the word "ghadan" is not intended to mean the day that follows his day, but it is used to mean the future time, just as "al-yawm" (today) is used to mean the present time and "al-ams" (yesterday) to mean past time. Zuhayr's verse combines them:

"I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but regarding the knowledge of what is in tomorrow, I am blind."

The apparent meaning of the verse is that its application is restricted to the report of a resolve to do an action in the future, excluding what is a speech of performative type, such as oaths. Therefore the jurists of the regions differed over whether this verse includes performative oaths and the like. The majority of them said: the mention of "unless Allah wills" is a release from the binding of the oath, which removes the obligation of expiation (kaffarah). Perhaps they took this from the meaning of "thing" in His saying ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that"﴾ etc.: that when you follow the oath with the words "unless Allah wills" or the like, the fulfilment of the oath is not obligatory. Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab, and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam related from Malik that His saying ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do"﴾ etc. was intended only as a reminder of Allah at the time of forgetfulness, and it is not an exception; that is, the ruling of the exception (thunya) in oaths is not derived from this verse, but is from what was established by the Sunnah. For this reason Malik did not disagree with applying the exception in oaths, which is the saying "If Allah wills," and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i.

[Page 299]

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Kahf (18), verse 24:**

﴿Remember your Lord when you forget.﴾

This is coordinated with the prohibition. The meaning is: do not promise anything, and if you forget and say, "I will do it," then remember your Lord, that is, remember what He has forbidden you. By "remembrance" is meant recovery (tadarruk). Here it is derived from *al-dhikr* (with a dammah on the dhal), which is a metonymy for its necessary consequence, which is compliance (imtithal). As 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Better than the remembrance of Allah with the tongue is the remembrance of Allah at His command and His prohibition." The use of the title "Lord" (*rabb*), attached to the pronoun of the addressee, rather than the proper name of Majesty (*ism al-jalala*), is a sign of the utmost gentleness, which is not hidden.

The object of *nasiti* ("you forgot") is omitted because it is clear from the context. That is: when you forget the prohibition and say, "I will do it." Some of those who applied the verse ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ to the dissolution of oaths by means of the exception (*istithna'*) with the will of Allah made the words ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾ a concession (*tarkhis*) permitting the addition of the exception (*al-thunya*) upon recalling it. Among them were those who did not set a time limit for this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: there is no time limit, even if a long period passes between the oath and the exception. The majority of scholars hold that the words ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾ do not indicate the permissibility of delaying the exception, and they argue that the Sunnah has come contrary to this.

* * *

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this."﴾

When Allah fulfilled the promise of His Prophet ﷺ, which he had made to the polytheists that he would explain to them the matter of the People of the Cave, and He revealed it to him and made him aware of it, He followed that with a reproach to him for undertaking to answer their questions about what lies outside the purpose of the message, without permission from Allah. He commanded him to mention the prohibition of his Lord and to resolve to train himself to withhold a promise by declaring what is asked of him to declare, without Allah having permitted him to do so. Here He commanded him to inform those who asked him that he was not sent to occupy himself with such matters, and that he hopes Allah will guide him to what is closer to right guidance than explaining such stories. Although this story contains admonition and guidance, the guidance found in explaining the Sharia is greater and more important. The meaning is: say to them, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this."

The clause ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me"﴾ etc. is coordinated with the clause ﴿so do not dispute about them﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. It is also possible that the clause ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me"﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾, meaning: remember His command and His prohibition, and say within yourself: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this," that is, call upon Allah with this.

*Rashadan* ("right guidance") is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification) of the comparative relation from the phrase ﴿to what is closer than this﴾. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) specifying the type of the verb ﴿will guide me﴾, since right guidance is a type of guidance.

Thus, *'asa* ("perhaps") is used to express hope, out of good manners. The demonstrative "this" refers to what was mentioned of the story of the People of the Cave, by the indication that this statement occurs as a parenthetical interjection within it.

It is also possible that the meaning is: hope from Allah that He will guide you, so that He reminds you not to promise to explain anything without the permission of Allah.

*Rashad* (with two fathahs) means guidance and good. It has already been discussed at His words, exalted is He, in this surah: ﴿and prepare for us from our affair right guidance﴾ [al-Kahf: 10].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 25:

Page 300
﴿And they remained in their cave for three hundred years, and they added nine﴾ This is a return to the rest of the story, after the interjection (al-i'tiraD) intervened between them with His words ﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] up to His words "rashadan" (guidance).

It is permissible that the clause "wa-labithu" (and they remained) is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon their saying in His words ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], meaning: "And they say: They remained in their cave," so that the position of His words ﴿Say, "My Lord is most knowing of their number"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] is like the position of His earlier words ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. In that case, this is not a report of the duration of their stay. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited (wa-qalu labithu fi kahfihim) to the end, and that is an explanation of this conjunction.

It is also permissible that the conjunction is upon the whole story, and the sense is: "And thus We caused them to be found" to the end, "and they remained in their cave three hundred years and nine years."

Depending on the two views, the meaning differs in His words ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained"﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], as will come. Furthermore, the apparent meaning is that the Qur'an reported the duration of the People of the Cave's stay in their cave, and that the intended stay is their first stay before awakening. This suits the preceding discussion of the stay in His words ﴿A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord is most knowing of how long you remained"﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. We have previously mentioned, at His words ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription...﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] etc., that the Christian historians claim the duration of the People of the Cave's sleep was two hundred and forty years. It was also said: the intended stay is from the time of their last death until the time of the revelation of this verse.

The meaning is: their stay is estimated as three hundred and nine years. He expressed this number as three hundred years plus an addition of nine, so that it is known that the estimate is in lunar years, which suit the history of the Arabs and Islam, with an indication that this quantity coincides with solar years, by which the history of the people to whom the People of the Cave belong is reckoned, namely the people of the lands of the Romans. Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd al-Unuf:

Page 301
"The Christians know the story of the People of the Cave and date by it." I say: The Jews who taught the Quraysh the question about them reckon the months by the lunar calculation and reckon the years by the solar cycle. The difference between the days of the lunar year and the days of the solar year amounts to one full lunar year in every thirty-three solar years, so the difference over a hundred solar years is three extra lunar years. Thus Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted it from al-Naqqash the exegete. By this the subtlety of the expression of the nine years as an "addition" becomes apparent, and this is from the scientific aspect of the Qur'an and its scientific miraculousness, which the general Arabs had no knowledge of.

Al-Jumhur read "thalathami'atin" with tanwin, and "sinin" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for the number, according to the view of those who forbid the accusative of the specification after "mi'a," or it is a specification (tamyiz) according to those who permit that.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the mi'a construct-annexed to "sinin," considering it a specification of "mi'a." The specification of "mi'a" in the plural has occurred, which is rare but eloquent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 26:

﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears! They have no protector other than Him, and He does not share His command with anyone."﴾ If the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 25] are a report from Allah about the duration of their stay, then His words ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained"﴾ serve to put an end to the dispute over the duration of their stay, which was disputed among the People of the Book; that is, Allah knows better than you about the duration of their stay.

If the words ﴿and they remained﴾ are a quotation of the statement of the People of the Book about the duration of their stay, then His words ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained"﴾ are a committing of that knowledge to Allah, like His words ﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22].

The unseen of the heavens and the earth is that whose knowledge is hidden from people, among the existing things of the heavens and the earth and their conditions. The lam in ﴿lillahi﴾ indicates ownership, and placing the prepositional predicate first indicates exclusivity, meaning: to Allah alone and not to other than Him, refuting those who claim knowledge of the account of the People of the Cave and the like.

﴿Absir bihi wa asmi'﴾ are two forms of exclamation expressing amazement at the all-encompassing extent of His knowledge, exalted is He, of the hidden things among what is seen and what is heard, which is a knowledge in which no one shares.

The plural pronoun in His words ﴿ma lahum min dunihi min waliyyin﴾ refers to the polytheists with whom the discourse is being conducted. It is a refutation of the guardianship of their gods, by way of stating the universality of the negation through the inclusion of the superfluous (min) before the indefinite noun in negation.

Likewise His words ﴿wa la yushriku fi hukmihi ahadan﴾ are a rejection of their claim that Allah took their gods as partners to Him in His dominion.

The majority of reciters read ﴿wa la yushriku﴾ with the verb in the nominative (yushraku) and with the third-person ya', and the pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty in His words ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing"﴾. Ibn 'Amir read it with the second-person ta' and the jussive form of (yushrik), with (la) as a prohibitive particle, and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning his community, or the address is to everyone who receives it.

Here ends the story of the People of the Cave along with what was interwoven within it, and the exegetes have greatly multiplied the narrations of fabricated reports concerning it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 27:

﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will not find any refuge other than Him.﴾ It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], with what it contains of His saying ﴿They have no protector other than Him, and He does not make anyone a partner in His command﴾ [al-Kahf: 26].

Page 303

The purpose of this is a rebuttal of the polytheists, for at that time nothing would become clear to them without their moving on to seek something else. They asked about the People of the Cave and about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and they asked the Prophet ﷺ to make some of the Qur'an praise them, and similar things, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you away from that which We have revealed to you, to fabricate other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ [al-Isra: 73], in Surat al-Isra.

The meaning is: do not concern yourself with them, even if they dislike the recitation of some of what has been revealed to you; and recite all that has been revealed to you, for none can alter it. Since He had promised them an answer concerning the Spirit and concerning the People of the Cave, and Allah fulfilled His promise to them by clarifying one of the two questions, cutting off their excuse, He appended to that an order to His Prophet to recite the Qur'an as it was sent down to him, and that none can alter the words of Allah, and so that he would not make them covet an answer to some of what they asked by hoping that he would answer them about everything they requested.

The original sense of negation with (لا) which denotes the genus (لا النافية للجنس) is that it negates the existence of its noun; what is meant here is the negation of permission for anyone to alter the words of Allah.

Tabdil (التبديل): change by addition and subtraction, that is, by concealing part of it, by omitting the recitation of what they do not wish to hear of the nullification of their polytheism and error. This indicates that they criticized some of what the story contained in the Qur'an, as His saying ﴿They will say: they were three﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] and His saying ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years﴾ [al-Kahf: 25] indicate.

A similar instance was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and none can alter the words of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 34], in Surat al-An'am.

So the imperative in His saying "wa-tlu" (and recite) is a metaphor (kinaya) for continuity, and ﴿mā ūḥiya﴾ (what has been revealed) conveys generality, meaning every part of what has been revealed to you. The implication of the relative clause is that what has not been revealed to him he does not recite, namely what they proposed he should say in praise of them and granting them a share of approval.

Page 304

Tilawa (التلاوة): recitation (القراءة). It was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqara: 102] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His saying ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal: 2] in Surat al-Anfal.

Al-multahad (الملتحد): a noun of place of the mimi form, which comes in the pattern of the passive participle of its verb. Al-multahad is the place of ilhad (الالتحاد), and ilhad is inclining toward a side. It came in the form of the iftiʿal pattern because its origin is the effort of inclining; and from the form of effort it is understood that it is a flight from something disliked, toward which the fearful person strives to take refuge. Therefore al-multahad carries the meaning of a refuge (الملجأ). The meaning is: you will not find anything that saves you from His punishment. The purpose of this is to despair them of what they had hoped for.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 28:

﴿And keep yourself patient along with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life.﴾ This is among the appendages of the answer to their question about the People of the Cave. It is connected to His saying ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 27], and it was previously mentioned in Surat al-An'am at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾ [al-An'am: 52], that the chiefs of the polytheists had claimed that were it not for the fact that among the believers there were people of humble means in this world, and slaves whom they would not consider their equals, and who did not deserve to sit with them, they would have come to sit with the Prophet ﷺ and listen to the Qur'an. So they proposed to him that he should drive them away from his side whenever the chiefs of Quraysh attended him. God answered them with what is in Surat al-An'am, what is in this surah, and what is here, which is more emphatic, since He commanded him to remain with them by His saying ﴿keep yourself patient﴾, that is, restrain yourself with them, a restraint of constancy. Patience (al-sabr) is binding oneself to a place such that one does not leave it; from this comes the name al-masbūrah, which is the animal tied up to be made a target for shooting. And because the verb isbir (keep patient) is given the sense of constancy (al-mulazamah), the adverbial phrase introduced by (ma'a, with) is attached to it.

Al-ghadāh (the morning) is read by the majority with an alif after the dal; it is the name of the time between dawn and sunrise. Al-'ashiyy is the evening. The intended meaning is that they call upon God in supplication that runs through the whole of the day and night. Al-du'a' (supplication) is intimate address and request, and what is meant by it includes the prayers.

The expression of them by the relative pronoun (alladhina) is to indicate the reason for the command to remain with them, that is: because they are deserving of that, on account of their turning to God; they are the most fitting to be accompanied and kept company with. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿bi-l-ghadwah﴾ with a sukun on the dal and a fatha-ended waw after the dal, and it is synonymous with al-ghadāh.

The clause ﴿seeking His countenance﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The countenance of God is a metaphor for His turning toward the servant.

Then he emphasised the command to keep company with them by forbidding even the slightest turning away from them.

The apparent meaning of ﴿and let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾ is a prohibition to the two eyes from passing beyond those who call upon their Lord, that is, from exceeding them, that is, from going away from them. The intended meaning is turning away. For this reason the verb ('adw, passing beyond) is given the sense of turning away, so it is construed with (ʿan, from) to its object, whereas its proper construction was to take the object directly; one says 'adāhu when he exceeds it. The prohibition addressed to the two eyes is a prohibition to their owner, so it reverts to the sense: "and do not let your eyes pass beyond them," and this is a wondrous brevity.

The clause ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the kāf of address; since the annexed noun is part of the annexed-to noun, that is: let not the desire for adornment be the cause of turning away from them, for they have no adornment of fine clothing or bearing.

This statement is an indirect rebuke to the foolishness of the chiefs of the polytheists, who made their concern and care the outward matters, and neglected consideration of realities and inner nobility; so they were arrogant toward sitting with the people of virtue, sound intellects and luminous hearts, and made their concern the outward forms.

* * *

﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire, and whose affair has become excess.﴾
This is a comprehensive prohibition against engaging in anything that the polytheists command him. The purpose of the prohibition is to establish a principle for the actions of the Messenger and the Muslims in the face of the desires of the polytheists, and to despair the polytheists of obtaining from the Prophet ﷺ anything they desire.

The relative (man) in the phrase ﴿man﴾ (whoever) refers to every person who has the attribute of the relative clause. It was said that it was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, who asked the Prophet ﷺ to drive away the poor Muslims from his assembly whenever he sat with him and his peers among the chiefs of Quraysh.

What is meant by the heart being made heedless is that it is made unmindful of reflection upon the Oneness of God, so that polytheism became current in it; for that arises from the creation of minds of narrow insight, driven by desire and habit.

The root of al-ighfal (making heedless) is the production of heedlessness (al-ghaflah), which is the forgetfulness of remembering a thing. What is meant here is a particular heedlessness, namely the continuous heedlessness derived from attributing the making heedless to God, Exalted is He, as a metaphor for His being in the natural constitution of those hearts; and what is by nature does not change.

This meaning is reinforced by the clause ﴿who follows his desire﴾, for the following of desire happens through insight, not through obliviousness. So heedlessness is a creation in their hearts, while the following of desire is an acquisition from their own capacity.

Al-furut, with two dammas, means injustice and transgression; it is derived from al-furuh, which is precedence, because injustice precedes in evil.

Al-amr means the affair and the state.

The addition of the verb of being (kāna) is to indicate the firm establishment of the predicate in the subject, that is: the state of firm establishment of excess and transgression against the truth.

[Page 307]

﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord. So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve. Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them. And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal that scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.﴾ After Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say what would nullify their twisted suggestions, and as an indirect way of making them despair of such things, He commanded him to state plainly to them that he would not deviate from the truth that had come to him from Allah, that he would convey it without any leniency, that he did not desire their belief in part while rejecting the rest, and that he would not lower himself to share their desires by surrendering a portion of the truth he had been brought. Their belief and their disbelief are left to themselves. They should not suppose that by promising to believe they can coax the Prophet (ﷺ) into giving up some of what has been revealed to him.

"Al-Haqq" (the truth) is the predicate of an omitted subject that is understood from the context, meaning "this is the truth." The expression "your Lord" serves as a reminder of the obligation to affirm His oneness.

The imperatives in ﴿فَلْيُؤْمِن﴾ and ﴿فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ express equality (al-taswiyah), by which is meant a threat and a promise.

Belief is mentioned before disbelief because their belief is what is desired.

The subject of the verb "will" (mashi'ah) in both places is a pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun "man" (whoever) in both places.

The verbs "yu'min" and "yakfur" are used in the future sense, meaning: whoever wishes to bring about one of the two matters, even if by way of persisting in one of them in which he is presently engaged, since the resolve to persist in it is a renewal of its occurrence.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory type (isti'naf bayani), because what the discourse implies, namely leaving belief and disbelief to their own selves and what that entails of threat, both of these stir in souls the question of what one who wills and persists in disbelief will face. It is answered that disbelief has a grave end for them.

By "the wrongdoers" are meant the polytheists. Allah says: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a great wrong﴾ (Luqman: 13).

The tanwin on "nāran" (a Fire) is for awe and magnification.

Al-Surādiq (السُّرادِقُ) with a damma on the sin is said to be the tent (al-fustat), that is, the pavilion. It is also said that al-surādiq is al-hujzah (with a damma on the ha and a sukun on the zay), that is, the barrier that surrounds the tent and prevents access to it. It may be of the same kind as the fustat, made of leather or cloth, and it may be something else, such as a trench. It is a word arabicized from Persian, originally (surātāq). They said: there is no single noun in the Arabic language whose third letter is an alif and which is followed by two letters. Here, al-surādiq is an imaginative element (takhyil) in a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyyah), comparing the Fire to a house, and it is attributed to it to emphasize how completely the house of punishment encloses them. The surādiq normally belongs to the dwellings of the affluent, so attributing it to the house of punishment is a mocking metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah).

Al-istighathah (seeking relief) is the request for ghawth, which is rescue from hardship, and the easing of pain. The word ﴿they ask for relief﴾ includes seeking relief from the heat of the Fire, by asking for something that will cool them, such as pouring water on their faces, as in the verse of al-A'raf: ﴿And the companions of the Fire call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour upon us some of the water"﴾ (al-A'raf: 50). It also includes seeking relief from the intense thirst that arises from the heat, so they ask for drink. The mention of two descriptions of this water in the words ﴿which scalds the faces; wretched is the drink﴾ points to the inclusion of both matters.

Al-ighathah (relief) is used metaphorically to mean an increase in what they sought relief from, by way of mockery. This is from the type of affirming a thing by means of something resembling its opposite.
