Al-muhl (المُهْلُ), with a damma on the mim, has many meanings. The most fitting here is that it is the dregs of oil, for these increase its burning. Allah says: ﴿On the day when the sky will be like molten metal﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 8).

The comparison is in the blackness of the color and the intensity of the heat, so it only increases their heat. For this reason the verse is followed by ﴿which scalds the faces﴾, and this is a fresh resumptive clause (isti'naf ibtida'i).

[Page 308]

The face is the most painful of the organs from the heat of the Fire. Allah says: ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 104).

The clause ﴿wretched is the drink﴾ is also a fresh independent resumptive clause, to denounce that water as a drink, just as it was denounced as a bath. In contrast, the praised water is mentioned in Allah's words: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾ (Sad: 42).

The object of the dispraise in bi'sa (wretched) is omitted, and it is understood from what precedes it. The implied sense is: "Wretched is the drink, that water."

The clause ﴿and evil is the resting place﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿which scalds the faces﴾, so it is also a resumptive clause, to express the dispraise of that Fire for what it contains.

Al-murtafaq (the resting place) is the place of reclining. It is a noun of place derived from a solid noun, since it is derived from al-mirfaq (the elbow), which is the joint of the upper arm and forearm. It was named mirfaq because a person finds ease (rifq) through it when he is exhausted and leans on it. When the limb was named by it, its derivation was forgotten and it became like a solid noun. Then al-murtafaq was derived from it, so al-murtafaq is the place where one leans. This was discussed in the surah of Yusuf.

It is characteristic of al-murtafaq that it is a place of rest, so applying it to the Fire is mockery, just as the term relief (al-ighathah) was applied to what increases their punishment, and just as al-surādiq was applied to their place.

The verb sā'a (evil) is used in the manner of bi'sa (wretched) and acts in its function, so the word murtafaqan (as a resting place) is a specification (tamyiz). The object of the dispraise is omitted, as was mentioned in the phrase ﴿wretched is the drink﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good in deed.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustaʾnafah) in the mode of explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani), in which the state of the listeners among the believers is taken into account. For when they hear what has been prepared for the polytheists, their souls long to know what has been prepared for those who believed and renounced polytheism. So they are informed that their deed is held in regard by their Lord. This also follows the Qur'an's habit of following a threat with a promise, and intimidation with encouragement.

The clause opens with the emphatic particle (inna) to establish its content. The particle (inna) is repeated in the clause that reports about the subject of the preceding clause, for greater care and affirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated others with Allah—indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 17], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you"﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 8]. Similar to it is the verse of Jarir:

Indeed the caliph, indeed Allah has clothed him
in the garment of kingship, by which the rings of rule are drawn.

The placement of the second (inna) in this verse is more eloquent than in Jarir's line, because the clause in which it occurs in this verse has an independent content, in that it conveys a ruling that encompasses both the subject of the report and others who are similar to those reported about in their deed. That generality, in itself, is a ruling worthy of emphasis, so that it may be realised for its possessors through the particle, unlike the line of Jarir.

As for the verse in Surat al-Hajj, the length of the separation required the emphatic particle, out of eagerness to convey emphasis.

Al-idaʿah (ḍayaʿah, "waste/loss") means making a thing lost. Its literal sense is the perishing of a thing from where it is expected to be found. It is used figuratively for the non-benefiting from an existing thing, as if it had been lost and perished. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195] in Surat Al 'Imran, and He said: ﴿And Allah would not waste your faith﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in al-Baqarah. It is also used for preventing someone from obtaining something and benefiting from it, by likening the one prevented to what is lost, in despair of his ever obtaining it, as in this verse; that is, "Indeed, We do not deprive one who does good in deed of the reward of his deed." Among its uses is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120].

[Page 311]

﴿They shall have gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow. They shall be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they shall wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein upon couches. How excellent a reward, and how fair a resting-place!﴾ The sentence is resumed as an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani, a sentence that answers an implied question raised by what precedes it), because what was stated in general terms, that their reward will not be lost, leads the listener to expect an explanation of this reward.

The opening of the sentence with the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) serves to draw attention to the fact that those referred to deserve what follows the demonstrative, on account of the attributes mentioned before it, namely that they believed and did righteous deeds.

The lam in ﴿lahum jannatu 'adnin﴾ is the lam of ownership (lam al-milk), and "min" is for the starting point (li'l-ibtida'). The direction "beneath them" is made the source of the flowing of the rivers. A similar verse has already occurred in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72], in the surah of Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).

As for "'adn" (Eden), it has already been discussed in the words of the Exalted, ﴿and goodly dwellings in gardens of Eden﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72], in the surah of Bara'ah.

And ﴿min tahtihim﴾ has the same status as ﴿min tahtiha﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72], because the area beneath their gardens is an area beneath them.

The reason for choosing to attach "taht" (beneath) to their pronoun rather than to the pronoun of the gardens is to add further confirmation of the meaning conveyed by the lam of ownership. Thus several elements that affirm its content are gathered in this statement: emphasis twice, the mention of the demonstrative, the lam of ownership, the governing of the directional noun by "min", and the attachment of the directional noun to their pronoun. The purpose of all this is an allusion intended to enrage the polytheists, so that the good tidings for the believers may be established in the most complete manner.

[Page 312]

The clause ﴿yuhallawna﴾ (they shall be adorned) stands in the position of a qualifier for "gardens of Eden".
Al-tahliyah means adornment, and al-hilyah means ornament.

The verb has been attributed to the passive voice, because they find themselves adorned by the creation of Allah the Exalted.

Al-asawir is the plural of siwar (bracelet) in an irregular pattern. It has been said that it is the plural of asawira, which is itself the plural of siwar; the form of "plural of plural" is used to indicate the variety of forms of the ornaments with which they are adorned, for ornament may be set with various kinds of rubies.

The "min" in ﴿min asawira﴾ is considered superfluous (mazidah) for emphasis according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, and its justification will come in the surah of al-Hajj. It may also be for the starting point (li'l-ibtida'), and this is the only correct reading according to those who forbid its being superfluous in affirmative statements.

The siwar is an ornament of gold or silver encircling the place of the forearm. It is a word arabicised from Persian according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun). In Persian it is "dustuwarah", with a final ha', as in the book of al-Raghib (al-Mufradat), and it is written without a ha' in Taj al-'Arus.

As for His saying ﴿min dhahabin﴾ (of gold), the "min" here is explicative (li'l-bayan), and the statement is elliptical: that is, "of gold and silver", just as in the verse of the surah of al-Insan the mention of silver is made sufficient in place of the mention of gold, in His saying ﴿and they shall be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 21]. Each of the two metals has its own particular beauty.

Al-libas is the covering of the body with a garment, whether a shirt, a waist-wrap, or a cloak, and all of these serve as protection from heat and cold and for adornment.

Al-thiyab is the plural of thawb, which is a piece of woven cloth.

The green colour is the most balanced of colours and the most beneficial to the sight, and it was a distinctive mark of kings. Al-Nabigha said:

They preserve bodies whose delight is ancient, with garments of pure lining, green at the shoulders.

[Page 313]

Al-sundus is a kind of garment, namely a thin brocade worn directly against the skin to protect it from the coarseness of al-istabraq.
Al-istabraq is a thick brocade woven with threads of gold, worn over the garments that are directly against the skin.

Both words are arabicised. As for the word sundus, there is no disagreement that it is arabicised; they have differed only regarding its origin. A group said its origin is Persian, while the verifiers said its origin is Indian. In the Indian language it is "sandun", with a nun at the end. A group of the notables of India came to Alexander bearing a gift of this brocade. The Romans changed its name to "sundus", and the Arabs took it from them and said "sundus". Thus it is arabicised from Roman, but its original root is Indian.

As for al-istabraq, it is arabicised from Persian. Its origin in Persian is "istabarh" or "istabar" without a ha', or "istaqrah" or "istafrah". Ibn Duraid said it is Syriac, arabicised, and its origin is "isturuwah". Ibn Qutaybah said it is Roman, arabicised. For this reason its hamzah is a hamzat qat' (a firm, pronounced hamzah) according to all, and some scholars of lexicography mentioned it in the chapter on the letter hamzah, and this is the more correct view. Its plural is aba'iq by analogy, though they diminutivised it as "ubayriq", treating the sin and the ta' as if they were augmentations.

In al-Itqan of al-Suyuti, from Ibn al-Naqib: "If the eloquent of the whole world gathered and wished to abandon this word and bring a word that stands in its place in eloquence, they would fail."

That is because when Allah the Exalted urges His servants to obedience through promise and warning, and the promise is of what rational people desire, this is confined to places, food, drink, garments and the like, in which natures agree or differ. The most elevated garment in this world is silk, and silk, the heavier its cloth, the more elevated it is. When it is wished to mention this, the best is to mention it by a single word laid down for it explicitly, and that is none other than al-istabraq, and there is no single word in Arabic that indicates what the word istabraq indicates. This is the substance of his discourse, with some lengthening.

The "min" in His saying ﴿min sundusin﴾ (of fine silk) is explicative (li'l-bayan).

Here he placed the mention of the ornaments before the garments, because that came as a qualifier of the gardens from the outset, and the displays of ornament were more radiant to the gardens. So he mentioned the ornaments first and delayed the garments, because garments are more closely connected with the people of the garden than with the displays of the garden. The reverse is found in the surah of al-Insan in His saying ﴿upon them garments of fine green silk﴾ [al-Insan: 21], because the discourse there proceeded according to the attributes of the people of the garden.

The clause ﴿muttaki'ina fiha 'ala al-ara'ik﴾ (reclining therein upon couches) stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yalbasuna" (they wear).

Al-ittika' is the sitting posture of ease and luxury. It was discussed at the words of the Exalted, ﴿and she prepared for them a banquet﴾ [Yusuf: 31], in the surah of Yusuf, peace be upon him.

Al-ara'ik is the plural of arikah, which is the name for a combination of a bed and a canopy (hajalah). The hajalah is a tent of cloth set up in a house, in which a woman sits or sleeps; for this reason women are called "rabbat al-hijal" (mistresses of the canopies). When a bed is placed within it for reclining or lying down, it is an arikah. A man sits in it and sleeps with a woman there, and this is a distinctive mark of the people of luxury.

The clause ﴿How excellent a reward﴾ is a resumed statement of praise (istinaf madh). The object of the verb of praise is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, and the estimated meaning is: "How excellent a reward are the described gardens."

Joined to it is a second verb of evaluation, which is ﴿and how fair a resting-place﴾, because "husuna" and "sa'a" are used in the manner of "ni'ma" and "bi'sa", and they act in the same way as them. For this reason the estimated meaning is: "And how fair are the gardens as a resting-place." This is the counterpart of His saying, in describing the state of the people of the Fire, ﴿and how evil a resting-place﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

Al-murtafaq here is used in its literal meaning, unlike its counterpart mentioned earlier.

[Page 315]

﴿Present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We made two gardens of grapevines, and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them fields of crops. Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them. He had abundant fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him: "I have more wealth than you and greater support in men." He entered his garden while wronging himself, and said: "I do not think this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will come. And even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find something better than these as a resting place."﴾

This is an continuation of the statement ﴿Say: The truth is from your Lord﴾ (al-Kahf 18:29) and what follows. After explaining what He has prepared for the people of polytheism, and mentioning what He has prepared in contrast for those who believed, He struck a parable for the condition of the two groups through a story in which God manifested His support for the believer and His humiliation of the disbeliever. This parable therefore bears a resemblance to the parable of the People of the Cave (ashab al-kahf) from an era closer to the knowledge of the addressees than the era of the People of the Cave. So He struck a parable for the two groups, the polytheists and the believers, with the example of two men, one of whose condition was pleasing and enticing, and the condition of the other was contrary to that. The outcome for the one with the enticing condition was ruin and loss, while the outcome for the other was success. This was to show both groups what arrogance, self-admiration and tyranny drag their possessor into of calamities, and what the humble believer who knows God's laws (sunan) in the world attains of admonition and reflection upon consequences, so that he becomes disposed to righteousness and success.

The preposition "li-" (for/to) in His saying ﴿lahum﴾ may be connected to the verb ﴿wadrib﴾ (present), as in His saying: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves﴾ (al-Rum 30:28). It may also be connected to the word ﴿mathalan﴾ (a parable) in the manner of a circumstantial complement (hal), meaning "a likeness for them", i.e., for the two groups, as in His saying: ﴿So do not strike forth parables for God﴾ (al-Nahl 16:74). The more apparent view is that it is contested between ﴿daraba﴾ (struck) and ﴿mathalan﴾ (a parable).

The pronoun in His saying ﴿lahum﴾ refers, according to the first view, to the polytheists of Makkah, although no prior mention of them has occurred. According to the second view, it refers to the community of disbelievers and believers.

Then, if the condition of these two men being used as an example was a known condition, the discourse is an illustration of a perceptible condition by a perceptible condition. Al-Kalbi said: The two men referred to were two brothers from the Banu Makhzum of the people of Makkah, one of whom was a disbeliever, namely al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad (with a shin, and it is also said with a sin) ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and the other was a Muslim, his brother, Abu Salamah 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Asad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth. In al-Isabah it occurs as "Ibn Hilal," and he was the husband of Umm Salamah before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married her.

The exegetes did not mention where the two gardens were. Perhaps they were in al-Ta'if, for there are gardens there belonging to the people of Makkah.

And from Ibn 'Abbas: They were two brothers from the Children of Israel. Their father died and left them wealth. One of them bought land and made two gardens in it, and the other gave his wealth in charity. What happened to them in this world was what God related in this sura. He also related their destiny in the Hereafter by what God related in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another. A speaker among them will say: "I had a companion who used to say, 'Are you indeed among those who affirm?'"﴾ (al-Saffat 37:50) and what follows. Thus their story is known from what was revealed about it in the Qur'an in Surat al-Saffat, before Surat al-Kahf.

If the condition of the two men is a hypothetical condition, as some exegetes permitted, reported from them by Ibn 'Atiyyah, then the discourse in every case is an illustration of the perceptible by the perceptible, because that state is imagined and conceived. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This form which God mentioned is one that a person can hardly imagine more beautiful in terms of people's earnings. On this view, this parable is like what is in His saying: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and for the strengthening of their souls is like a garden on a height﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:265) and what follows.

[Page 317]

The more apparent meaning from the context of the discourse and the construction of the sentences, such as His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while conversing with him: "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust?"﴾ (al-Kahf 18:37) and so on, is that "qala" (said) came without being joined by "fa" (then), and this is characteristic of the narration of actual conversations. Likewise His saying: ﴿He had no company to help him other than God, nor was he able to defend himself﴾ (al-Kahf 18:43), indicates that this parable is a known story. Moreover, that is more effective for lessons and admonition, like the admonitions regarding the fate of past nations.

The meaning of ﴿We made for one of them﴾ is: We decreed for him the causes of that.

The mention of the garden, grapevines and date palms has preceded in His saying: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:266), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of ﴿hafafnahuma﴾ (We surrounded them) is: We enclosed them. It is said: "hafahu bi-kadha," when one makes him encircle it, i.e., surround it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the angels circling around the Throne﴾ (al-Zumar 39:75). Because "hafa" is transitive to one object, when one wishes to make it transitive to a second, it is made transitive to it by the preposition "bi-," like "ghashiyahu" and "ghashsha-hu bi-kadha" (he covered him with such). Among the excellences of gardens is that they are surrounded by fruit-bearing trees.

The meaning of ﴿We placed between them crops﴾ is: We inspired him to place between them. The apparent meaning of the discourse is that these crops were a separation between the two gardens: the two gardens bordered a field of crops, so the whole was one plot of land. The mention of crops has preceded in Surat al-Ra'd.

And ﴿kilta﴾ (both) is a word denoting totality applied to a dual, explained by the noun it is attached to. It is thus a singular noun denoting two things, like "zawj" (pair). Its masculine form is "kila." Sibawayh said: the original of "kila" is "kilaw," and the original of "kilta" is "kilwa." The lam of the root was deleted from "kilta," and the ta' was substituted for the deleted lam, so that the ta' indicates feminine gender. The predicate of "kila" and "kilta" may be singular, taking account of its wording, and this is more eloquent, as in this verse. It may also be dual, taking account of its meaning, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

[Page 318]

"Both of them, when the race between them grew intense, have stopped, and both of their nostrils [are] sweating."

The word ﴿ukulaha﴾ (its produce) was recited by the majority with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf. It was recited by 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf with a damma on the hamza and a damma on the kaf, meaning the fruit, which has preceded.

The clause ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce﴾ is an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses. The meaning is: the two gardens bore abundant fruit, to the extent that they resembled one who gives from his own hand.

The meaning of ﴿and did not fall short in anything﴾ is: they did not diminish from it, i.e., from their produce, anything; that is, they did not fall short of the amount that trees give in a time of abundance. So there is conciseness in the discourse through the deletion of a modifier, and the estimated meaning is: "and did not wrong in terms of the measure of its equivalents." The word "wrong" (zulm) is used metaphorically for "shortfall" in the manner of an illustrative figure, by likening the state of the owner of the two gardens, in perfecting their condition and awaiting their fruiting, to the state of one who has a right to an abundant yield; when the two gardens do not bring forth what is expected of them, they resemble one who withholds from a rightful claimant his right and wrongs him. Thus "wrong" is used for the reduction of yield, and its negation is used for fulfilling the due of fruiting.

Tafjir (causing to gush forth) has been discussed at His saying: ﴿until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ (al-Isra' 17:90), in Surat al-Isra'.

The word "nahar" (river), with the ha' vowelled, is a dialectal variant of "nahr" with the ha' sukun, and it has been discussed at His saying: ﴿He said: "Indeed God will test you with a river"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:249), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And he had fruit﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿li-ahadihima﴾ (for one of them). "Thumur" (wealth), with a damma on the tha' and the mim, means abundant wealth of varied kinds, of gold and silver, livestock, gardens and fields. It derives from "thummira malahu," with the mim doubled and in the passive form, said: "thammara Allahu malahu" when it increased (i.e., God multiplied his wealth). Al-Nabighah said:

"When he saw that God had multiplied his wealth, and established what he had, and mended his poverty..."

It is derived from the name of the fruit by way of metaphor or figurative usage, since profits and surplus wealth resemble the fruit of trees, and this metaphor became so common that it became literal. Al-Nabighah said:

"Enough. Let all the people be ransom for you, but I do not multiply [wealth] of money or of children."

[Page 319]

The majority recited ﴿thumurun﴾ with a damma on the tha' and a damma on the mim. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. 'Asim recited it with a fatha on the tha' and a fatha on the mim.

They said: it is the plural of "thimar" (fruits), which is itself the plural of "thumur," like "kutub" the plural of "kitab" (book). So it denotes many kinds of what gains produce, as has preceded just now in the plural "asawir" from His saying: ﴿bracelets of gold﴾ (al-Kahf 18:31). From al-Nahhas, with his chain of transmission to Tha'lab from al-A'mash: that al-Hajjaj said: "If I hear anyone recite (wa-kana lahu thumurun), i.e., with a damma on the tha', I will cut out his tongue." Tha'lab said: I said to al-A'mash: "Shall we take by that?" He said: "No, and not the delight of the eye." And he used to recite "thumurun," i.e., with two dammas.

The meaning is: the owner of the two gardens had property, i.e., other than the two gardens. The fa' (then) is for the sequencing of the clause "he said" upon the preceding clauses, because what the preceding clauses contained is of such a nature that it gives rise to self-conceit, to which his Lord responds with such speech.

The word "companion" (sahib) here means "one who accompanies in mention," in that the parable's report brings them together. Or it may be meant to refer to "one who is involved in dispute," as in the statement of al-Hajjaj addressing the Kharijites: "Are you not my companions in al-Ahwaz?"

The companion here means the other of the two men, i.e., he said, the one who had no gardens, in a dialogue between them. The purpose did not depend on mentioning where this speech took place or its cause, since there was no need for it in the admonition.

The clause ﴿while conversing with him﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qala" (he said). "Muhawarah" means the exchange of speech between speakers.

[Page 320]

The separate pronoun of the third person refers to the owner of the two gardens, and the object pronoun in "yuhawiruhu" refers to the companion of the owner of the two gardens. The lord of the two gardens was conversing with his companion, and the act of conversing indicates that his companion had admonished him concerning faith and righteous deeds, so he answered him with boasting and arrogance, like the people of haughtiness and contrariness, who turn away from disputing in the manner that is best toward displays of greatness and pride.

The word ﴿a'azz﴾ (greater in might) means more mighty, and "izza" (might) is the opposite of humiliation; it is the abundance of a man's clan and his bravery.

The "nafar" is the clan of a man who go forth with him, and by it here he means his children, as indicated by its contrast in his companion's reply, in His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ (al-Kahf 18:39). The word "nafaran" is in the accusative as a specification of the relation of ﴿a'azz﴾ to the speaker's pronoun.

The clause ﴿and he entered his garden﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qala" (he said), i.e., he said that while he had entered his garden accompanied by his companion. That is, he entered his garden with his companion, as indicated by His saying: ﴿He said: "I do not think this will ever perish"﴾, because speech is only addressed to another, i.e., he said to him. It is also indicated by His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while conversing with him﴾ (al-Kahf 18:37). And the occurrence of the answer to His saying: ﴿I have more wealth than you and greater support in men﴾ occurred within the course of the dialogue taking place between them in that garden.

The meaning of ﴿while wronging himself﴾ is: while he was a polytheist, denying the Resurrection, insolent regarding God's blessing upon him.

The reason the word "garden" is singular here, though there are two gardens, is that entering occurs only into one of them, since upon first entering one enters only one of them before moving from it to the other. So he entered only one of the two gardens.

"Zann" (supposition) here means belief, and when the supposition of that is negated, the supposition of its opposite is established. "Tabid" means perish and vanish.

The reference by "this" is to the garden in which they are, i.e., I do not believe that it will collapse and be obliterated.

[Page 321]

"Abad" (ever) is meant to express a long duration, i.e., it remains lasting like its likes, nothing that would destroy it befalling it. This is his self-deception through his wealth, and self-deception through the firmness, strength and stability of the trees of that garden, and the convergence of the causes of its growth and permanence around it, from water and shade.

He moved from reporting his belief in the permanence of that garden to reporting his belief in the negation of the establishment of the Hour.

There is no necessary connection between the two beliefs. Rather, he intended to belittle his believing companion and to rebuke him. For this reason he followed it with his words ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than these as a destination﴾, mocking his companion. The pronoun in ﴿minhuma﴾ ("from them both") refers to the two gardens, returning to the beginning of the speech. This is a stylistic variation in relating his words. According to the reading of the majority, ﴿minhuma﴾ is in the dual. [Page 315]

﴿Present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We made two gardens of grapevines, and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them fields of crops. Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them. He had abundant fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him: "I have more wealth than you and greater support in men." He entered his garden while wronging himself, and said: "I do not think this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will come. After explaining what He has prepared for the people of polytheism, and mentioning what He has prepared in contrast for those who believed, He struck a parable for the condition of the two groups through a story in which God manifested His support for the believer and His humiliation of the disbeliever. The outcome for the one with the enticing condition was ruin and loss, while the outcome for the other was success. This was to show both groups what arrogance, self-admiration and tyranny drag their possessor into of calamities, and what the humble believer who knows God's laws (sunan) in the world attains of admonition and reflection upon consequences, so that he becomes disposed to righteousness and success.

Then, if the condition of these two men being used as an example was a known condition, the discourse is an illustration of a perceptible condition by a perceptible condition. In al-Isabah it occurs as "Ibn Hilal," and he was the husband of Umm Salamah before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married her.

The exegetes did not mention where the two gardens were. Perhaps they were in al-Ta'if, for there are gardens there belonging to the people of Makkah.

And from Ibn 'Abbas: They were two brothers from the Children of Israel. Their father died and left them wealth. One of them bought land and made two gardens in it, and the other gave his wealth in charity. What happened to them in this world was what God related in this sura. He also related their destiny in the Hereafter by what God related in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another. On this view, this parable is like what is in His saying: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and for the strengthening of their souls is like a garden on a height﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:265) and what follows.

[Page 317]

Moreover, that is more effective for lessons and admonition, like the admonitions regarding the fate of past nations.

The meaning of ﴿We made for one of them﴾ is: We decreed for him the causes of that.

The mention of the garden, grapevines and date palms has preceded in His saying: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:266), in Surat al-Baqarah.

Among the excellences of gardens is that they are surrounded by fruit-bearing trees.

The meaning of ﴿We placed between them crops﴾ is: We inspired him to place between them. The apparent meaning of the discourse is that these crops were a separation between the two gardens: the two gardens bordered a field of crops, so the whole was one plot of land. The mention of crops has preceded in Surat al-Ra'd.

Its masculine form is "kila." Sibawayh said: the original of "kila" is "kilaw," and the original of "kilta" is "kilwa." It may also be dual, taking account of its meaning, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

[Page 318]

"Both of them, when the race between them grew intense, have stopped, and both of their nostrils [are] sweating."

The word ﴿ukulaha﴾ (its produce) was recited by the majority with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf. It was recited by 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf with a damma on the hamza and a damma on the kaf, meaning the fruit, which has preceded.

The clause ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce﴾ is an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses. The meaning is: the two gardens bore abundant fruit, to the extent that they resembled one who gives from his own hand.

The meaning of ﴿and did not fall short in anything﴾ is: they did not diminish from it, i.e., from their produce, anything; that is, they did not fall short of the amount that trees give in a time of abundance. The word "wrong" (zulm) is used metaphorically for "shortfall" in the manner of an illustrative figure, by likening the state of the owner of the two gardens, in perfecting their condition and awaiting their fruiting, to the state of one who has a right to an abundant yield; when the two gardens do not bring forth what is expected of them, they resemble one who withholds from a rightful claimant his right and wrongs him. Thus "wrong" is used for the reduction of yield, and its negation is used for fulfilling the due of fruiting.

The clause ﴿And he had fruit﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿li-ahadihima﴾ (for one of them). "Thumur" (wealth), with a damma on the tha' and the mim, means abundant wealth of varied kinds, of gold and silver, livestock, gardens and fields. It derives from "thummira malahu," with the mim doubled and in the passive form, said: "thammara Allahu malahu" when it increased (i.e., God multiplied his wealth). Al-Nabighah said:

"When he saw that God had multiplied his wealth, and established what he had, and mended his poverty..."

It is derived from the name of the fruit by way of metaphor or figurative usage, since profits and surplus wealth resemble the fruit of trees, and this metaphor became so common that it became literal. Al-Nabighah said:

"Enough. Let all the people be ransom for you, but I do not multiply [wealth] of money or of children."

[Page 319]

The majority recited ﴿thumurun﴾ with a damma on the tha' and a damma on the mim. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. 'Asim recited it with a fatha on the tha' and a fatha on the mim.

They said: it is the plural of "thimar" (fruits), which is itself the plural of "thumur," like "kutub" the plural of "kitab" (book). So it denotes many kinds of what gains produce, as has preceded just now in the plural "asawir" from His saying: ﴿bracelets of gold﴾ (al-Kahf 18:31). The companion here means the other of the two men, i.e., he said, the one who had no gardens, in a dialogue between them. The purpose did not depend on mentioning where this speech took place or its cause, since there was no need for it in the admonition.

The clause ﴿while conversing with him﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qala" (he said). "Muhawarah" means the exchange of speech between speakers.

[Page 320]

The word ﴿a'azz﴾ (greater in might) means more mighty, and "izza" (might) is the opposite of humiliation; it is the abundance of a man's clan and his bravery.

The "nafar" is the clan of a man who go forth with him, and by it here he means his children, as indicated by its contrast in his companion's reply, in His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ (al-Kahf 18:39). The word "nafaran" is in the accusative as a specification of the relation of ﴿a'azz﴾ to the speaker's pronoun.

It is also indicated by His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while conversing with him﴾ (al-Kahf 18:37). And the occurrence of the answer to His saying: ﴿I have more wealth than you and greater support in men﴾ occurred within the course of the dialogue taking place between them in that garden.

The meaning of ﴿while wronging himself﴾ is: while he was a polytheist, denying the Resurrection, insolent regarding God's blessing upon him.

The reason the word "garden" is singular here, though there are two gardens, is that entering occurs only into one of them, since upon first entering one enters only one of them before moving from it to the other. So he entered only one of the two gardens.

"Zann" (supposition) here means belief, and when the supposition of that is negated, the supposition of its opposite is established. "Tabid" means perish and vanish.

The reference by "this" is to the garden in which they are, i.e., I do not believe that it will collapse and be obliterated.

[Page 321]

The clause ﴿while conversing with him﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qala" (he said). "Muhawarah" means the exchange of speech between speakers.

[Page 320]

The separate pronoun of the third person refers to the owner of the two gardens, and the object pronoun in "yuhawiruhu" refers to the companion of the owner of the two gardens. The lord of the two gardens was conversing with his companion, and the act of conversing indicates that his companion had admonished him concerning faith and righteous deeds, so he answered him with boasting and arrogance, like the people of haughtiness and contrariness, who turn away from disputing in the manner that is best toward displays of greatness and pride.

The word ﴿a'azz﴾ (greater in might) means more mighty, and "izza" (might) is the opposite of humiliation; it is the abundance of a man's clan and his bravery.

The "nafar" is the clan of a man who go forth with him, and by it here he means his children, as indicated by its contrast in his companion's reply, in His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ (al-Kahf 18:39). The word "nafaran" is in the accusative as a specification of the relation of ﴿a'azz﴾ to the speaker's pronoun.

That is, he entered his garden with his companion, as indicated by His saying: ﴿He said: "I do not think this will ever perish"﴾, because speech is only addressed to another, i.e., he said to him. It is also indicated by His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while conversing with him﴾ (al-Kahf 18:37). And the occurrence of the answer to His saying: ﴿I have more wealth than you and greater support in men﴾ occurred within the course of the dialogue taking place between them in that garden.

[Page 321]

This is his self-deception through his wealth, and self-deception through the firmness, strength and stability of the trees of that garden, and the convergence of the causes of its growth and permanence around it, from water and shade.

He moved from reporting his belief in the permanence of that garden to reporting his belief in the negation of the establishment of the Hour.

There is no necessary connection between the two beliefs. Rather, he intended to belittle his believing companion and to rebuke him. For this reason he followed it with his words ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than these as a destination﴾, mocking his companion. The indication of the mockery is his saying ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever occur﴾. This is like the statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "I will surely have wealth there, and then I will pay off your debt from it."

He emphasized his speech with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid), intensifying the mockery.

The accusative of ﴿munqalaban﴾ is a tamyiz (specification accusative) of the relation of the predicate (tamyiz nisbat al-khabar). Al-munqalab means the place to which one turns, i.e., the place to which one returns.

According to the reading of the majority, ﴿minhuma﴾ is in the dual. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read ﴿minha﴾ in the singular, in conformity with his words ﴿and he entered his garden﴾ and ﴿lest this [garden] perish﴾.

[Page 315]

﴿Present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We made two gardens of grapevines, and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them fields of crops. Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them. He had abundant fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him: "I have more wealth than you and greater support in men." He entered his garden while wronging himself, and said: "I do not think this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will come. And even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find something better than these as a resting place."﴾

This is an continuation of the statement ﴿Say: The truth is from your Lord﴾ (al-Kahf 18:29) and what follows. After explaining what He has prepared for the people of polytheism, and mentioning what He has prepared in contrast for those who believed, He struck a parable for the condition of the two groups through a story in which God manifested His support for the believer and His humiliation of the disbeliever. This parable therefore bears a resemblance to the parable of the People of the Cave (ashab al-kahf) from an era closer to the knowledge of the addressees than the era of the People of the Cave. So He struck a parable for the two groups, the polytheists and the believers, with the example of two men, one of whose condition was pleasing and enticing, and the condition of the other was contrary to that. The outcome for the one with the enticing condition was ruin and loss, while the outcome for the other was success. This was to show both groups what arrogance, self-admiration and tyranny drag their possessor into of calamities, and what the humble believer who knows God's laws (sunan) in the world attains of admonition and reflection upon consequences, so that he becomes disposed to righteousness and success.

The preposition "li-" (for/to) in His saying ﴿lahum﴾ may be connected to the verb ﴿wadrib﴾ (present), as in His saying: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves﴾ (al-Rum 30:28). It may also be connected to the word ﴿mathalan﴾ (a parable) in the manner of a circumstantial complement (hal), meaning "a likeness for them", i.e., for the two groups, as in His saying: ﴿So do not strike forth parables for God﴾ (al-Nahl 16:74). The more apparent view is that it is contested between ﴿daraba﴾ (struck) and ﴿mathalan﴾ (a parable).

The pronoun in His saying ﴿lahum﴾ refers, according to the first view, to the polytheists of Makkah, although no prior mention of them has occurred. According to the second view, it refers to the community of disbelievers and believers.

Then, if the condition of these two men being used as an example was a known condition, the discourse is an illustration of a perceptible condition by a perceptible condition. Al-Kalbi said: The two men referred to were two brothers from the Banu Makhzum of the people of Makkah, one of whom was a disbeliever, namely al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad (with a shin, and it is also said with a sin) ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and the other was a Muslim, his brother, Abu Salamah 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Asad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth. In al-Isabah it occurs as "Ibn Hilal," and he was the husband of Umm Salamah before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married her.

The exegetes did not mention where the two gardens were. Perhaps they were in al-Ta'if, for there are gardens there belonging to the people of Makkah.

And from Ibn 'Abbas: They were two brothers from the Children of Israel. Their father died and left them wealth. One of them bought land and made two gardens in it, and the other gave his wealth in charity. What happened to them in this world was what God related in this sura. He also related their destiny in the Hereafter by what God related in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another. A speaker among them will say: "I had a companion who used to say, 'Are you indeed among those who affirm?'"﴾ (al-Saffat 37:50) and what follows. Thus their story is known from what was revealed about it in the Qur'an in Surat al-Saffat, before Surat al-Kahf.

If the condition of the two men is a hypothetical condition, as some exegetes permitted, reported from them by Ibn 'Atiyyah, then the discourse in every case is an illustration of the perceptible by the perceptible, because that state is imagined and conceived. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This form which God mentioned is one that a person can hardly imagine more beautiful in terms of people's earnings. On this view, this parable is like what is in His saying: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and for the strengthening of their souls is like a garden on a height﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:265) and what follows.

[Page 317]

The more apparent meaning from the context of the discourse and the construction of the sentences, such as His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while conversing with him: "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust?"﴾ (al-Kahf 18:37) and so on, is that "qala" (said) came without being joined by "fa" (then), and this is characteristic of the narration of actual conversations. Likewise His saying: ﴿He had no company to help him other than God, nor was he able to defend himself﴾ (al-Kahf 18:43), indicates that this parable is a known story. Moreover, that is more effective for lessons and admonition, like the admonitions regarding the fate of past nations.

The meaning of ﴿We made for one of them﴾ is: We decreed for him the causes of that.

The mention of the garden, grapevines and date palms has preceded in His saying: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:266), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of ﴿hafafnahuma﴾ (We surrounded them) is: We enclosed them. It is said: "hafahu bi-kadha," when one makes him encircle it, i.e., surround it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the angels circling around the Throne﴾ (al-Zumar 39:75). Because "hafa" is transitive to one object, when one wishes to make it transitive to a second, it is made transitive to it by the preposition "bi-," like "ghashiyahu" and "ghashsha-hu bi-kadha" (he covered him with such). Among the excellences of gardens is that they are surrounded by fruit-bearing trees.

The meaning of ﴿We placed between them crops﴾ is: We inspired him to place between them. The apparent meaning of the discourse is that these crops were a separation between the two gardens: the two gardens bordered a field of crops, so the whole was one plot of land. The mention of crops has preceded in Surat al-Ra'd.

And ﴿kilta﴾ (both) is a word denoting totality applied to a dual, explained by the noun it is attached to. It is thus a singular noun denoting two things, like "zawj" (pair). Its masculine form is "kila." Sibawayh said: the original of "kila" is "kilaw," and the original of "kilta" is "kilwa." The lam of the root was deleted from "kilta," and the ta' was substituted for the deleted lam, so that the ta' indicates feminine gender. The predicate of "kila" and "kilta" may be singular, taking account of its wording, and this is more eloquent, as in this verse. It may also be dual, taking account of its meaning, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

[Page 318]

"Both of them, when the race between them grew intense, have stopped, and both of their nostrils [are] sweating."

The word ﴿ukulaha﴾ (its produce) was recited by the majority with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf. It was recited by 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf with a damma on the hamza and a damma on the kaf, meaning the fruit, which has preceded.

The clause ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce﴾ is an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses. The meaning is: the two gardens bore abundant fruit, to the extent that they resembled one who gives from his own hand.

The meaning of ﴿and did not fall short in anything﴾ is: they did not diminish from it, i.e., from their produce, anything; that is, they did not fall short of the amount that trees give in a time of abundance. So there is conciseness in the discourse through the deletion of a modifier, and the estimated meaning is: "and did not wrong in terms of the measure of its equivalents." The word "wrong" (zulm) is used metaphorically for "shortfall" in the manner of an illustrative figure, by likening the state of the owner of the two gardens, in perfecting their condition and awaiting their fruiting, to the state of one who has a right to an abundant yield; when the two gardens do not bring forth what is expected of them, they resemble one who withholds from a rightful claimant his right and wrongs him. Thus "wrong" is used for the reduction of yield, and its negation is used for fulfilling the due of fruiting.

Tafjir (causing to gush forth) has been discussed at His saying: ﴿until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ (al-Isra' 17:90), in Surat al-Isra'.

The word "nahar" (river), with the ha' vowelled, is a dialectal variant of "nahr" with the ha' sukun, and it has been discussed at His saying: ﴿He said: "Indeed God will test you with a river"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:249), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And he had fruit﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿li-ahadihima﴾ (for one of them). "Thumur" (wealth), with a damma on the tha' and the mim, means abundant wealth of varied kinds, of gold and silver, livestock, gardens and fields. It derives from "thummira malahu," with the mim doubled and in the passive form, said: "thammara Allahu malahu" when it increased (i.e., God multiplied his wealth). Al-Nabighah said:

"When he saw that God had multiplied his wealth, and established what he had, and mended his poverty..."

It is derived from the name of the fruit by way of metaphor or figurative usage, since profits and surplus wealth resemble the fruit of trees, and this metaphor became so common that it became literal. Al-Nabighah said:

"Enough. Let all the people be ransom for you, but I do not multiply [wealth] of money or of children."

[Page 319]

The word ﴿ukulaha﴾ (its produce) was recited by the majority with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf. It was recited by 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf with a damma on the hamza and a damma on the kaf, meaning the fruit, which has preceded.

The clause ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce﴾ is an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses. The meaning is: the two gardens bore abundant fruit, to the extent that they resembled one who gives from his own hand.

The meaning of ﴿and did not fall short in anything﴾ is: they did not diminish from it, i.e., from their produce, anything; that is, they did not fall short of the amount that trees give in a time of abundance. So there is conciseness in the discourse through the deletion of a modifier, and the estimated meaning is: "and did not wrong in terms of the measure of its equivalents." The word "wrong" (zulm) is used metaphorically for "shortfall" in the manner of an illustrative figure, by likening the state of the owner of the two gardens, in perfecting their condition and awaiting their fruiting, to the state of one who has a right to an abundant yield; when the two gardens do not bring forth what is expected of them, they resemble one who withholds from a rightful claimant his right and wrongs him. Thus "wrong" is used for the reduction of yield, and its negation is used for fulfilling the due of fruiting.

Tafjir (causing to gush forth) has been discussed at His saying: ﴿until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ (al-Isra' 17:90), in Surat al-Isra'.

The word "nahar" (river), with the ha' vowelled, is a dialectal variant of "nahr" with the ha' sukun, and it has been discussed at His saying: ﴿He said: "Indeed God will test you with a river"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:249), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And he had fruit﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿li-ahadihima﴾ (for one of them). "Thumur" (wealth), with a damma on the tha' and the mim, means abundant wealth of varied kinds, of gold and silver, livestock, gardens and fields. It derives from "thummira malahu," with the mim doubled and in the passive form, said: "thammara Allahu malahu" when it increased (i.e., God multiplied his wealth). Al-Nabighah said:

"When he saw that God had multiplied his wealth, and established what he had, and mended his poverty..."

It is derived from the name of the fruit by way of metaphor or figurative usage, since profits and surplus wealth resemble the fruit of trees, and this metaphor became so common that it became literal. Al-Nabighah said:

"Enough. Let all the people be ransom for you, but I do not multiply [wealth] of money or of children."

[Page 319]

The majority recited ﴿thumurun﴾ with a damma on the tha' and a damma on the mim. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. 'Asim recited it with a fatha on the tha' and a fatha on the mim.

They said: it is the plural of "thimar" (fruits), which is itself the plural of "thumur," like "kutub" the plural of "kitab" (book). So it denotes many kinds of what gains produce, as has preceded just now in the plural "asawir" from His saying: ﴿bracelets of gold﴾ (al-Kahf 18:31). From al-Nahhas, with his chain of transmission to Tha'lab from al-A'mash: that al-Hajjaj said: "If I hear anyone recite (wa-kana lahu thumurun), i.e., with a damma on the tha', I will cut out his tongue." Tha'lab said: I said to al-A'mash: "Shall we take by that?" He said: "No, and not the delight of the eye." And he used to recite "thumurun," i.e., with two dammas.

The meaning is: the owner of the two gardens had property, i.e., other than the two gardens. The fa' (then) is for the sequencing of the clause "he said" upon the preceding clauses, because what the preceding clauses contained is of such a nature that it gives rise to self-conceit, to which his Lord responds with such speech.

The word "companion" (sahib) here means "one who accompanies in mention," in that the parable's report brings them together. Or it may be meant to refer to "one who is involved in dispute," as in the statement of al-Hajjaj addressing the Kharijites: "Are you not my companions in al-Ahwaz?"

The companion here means the other of the two men, i.e., he said, the one who had no gardens, in a dialogue between them. The purpose did not depend on mentioning where this speech took place or its cause, since there was no need for it in the admonition.

The clause ﴿while conversing with him﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qala" (he said). "Muhawarah" means the exchange of speech between speakers.

[Page 320]

The separate pronoun of the third person refers to the owner of the two gardens, and the object pronoun in "yuhawiruhu" refers to the companion of the owner of the two gardens. The lord of the two gardens was conversing with his companion, and the act of conversing indicates that his companion had admonished him concerning faith and righteous deeds, so he answered him with boasting and arrogance, like the people of haughtiness and contrariness, who turn away from disputing in the manner that is best toward displays of greatness and pride.

The word ﴿a'azz﴾ (greater in might) means more mighty, and "izza" (might) is the opposite of humiliation; it is the abundance of a man's clan and his bravery.

The "nafar" is the clan of a man who go forth with him, and by it here he means his children, as indicated by its contrast in his companion's reply, in His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ (al-Kahf 18:39). The word "nafaran" is in the accusative as a specification of the relation of ﴿a'azz﴾ to the speaker's pronoun.

The clause ﴿and he entered his garden﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "qala" (he said), i.e., he said that while he had entered his garden accompanied by his companion. That is, he entered his garden with his companion, as indicated by His saying: ﴿He said: "I do not think this will ever perish"﴾, because speech is only addressed to another, i.e., he said to him. It is also indicated by His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while conversing with him﴾ (al-Kahf 18:37). And the occurrence of the answer to His saying: ﴿I have more wealth than you and greater support in men﴾ occurred within the course of the dialogue taking place between them in that garden.

The meaning of ﴿while wronging himself﴾ is: while he was a polytheist, denying the Resurrection, insolent regarding God's blessing upon him.

The reason the word "garden" is singular here, though there are two gardens, is that entering occurs only into one of them, since upon first entering one enters only one of them before moving from it to the other. So he entered only one of the two gardens.

"Zann" (supposition) here means belief, and when the supposition of that is negated, the supposition of its opposite is established. "Tabid" means perish and vanish.

The reference by "this" is to the garden in which they are, i.e., I do not believe that it will collapse and be obliterated.

[Page 321]

"Abad" (ever) is meant to express a long duration, i.e., it remains lasting like its likes, nothing that would destroy it befalling it. This is his self-deception through his wealth, and self-deception through the firmness, strength and stability of the trees of that garden, and the convergence of the causes of its growth and permanence around it, from water and shade.

He moved from reporting his belief in the permanence of that garden to reporting his belief in the negation of the establishment of the Hour.

There is no necessary connection between the two beliefs. Rather, he intended to belittle his believing companion and to rebuke him. For this reason he followed it with his words ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than these as a destination﴾, mocking his companion. The indication of the mockery is his saying ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever occur﴾. This is like the statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "I will surely have wealth there, and then I will pay off your debt from it."

He emphasized his speech with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid), intensifying the mockery.

The accusative of ﴿munqalaban﴾ is a tamyiz (specification accusative) of the relation of the predicate (tamyiz nisbat al-khabar). Al-munqalab means the place to which one turns, i.e., the place to which one returns.

The pronoun in ﴿minhuma﴾ ("from them both") refers to the two gardens, returning to the beginning of the speech. This is a stylistic variation in relating his words. According to the reading of the majority, ﴿minhuma﴾ is in the dual. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read ﴿minha﴾ in the singular, in conformity with his words ﴿and he entered his garden﴾ and ﴿lest this [garden] perish﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 37–38:

﴿His companion said to him, while he was arguing with him, "Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you as a man?" "But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord. And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, 'What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah'?"﴾ [al-Kahf: 39]

The speech of his companion is related with the verb of saying without a conjunction (ʿatf), to indicate that it takes the place of a dialogue and a reply, as we have mentioned more than once.

[Page 322]

The interrogative in His words ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you﴾ is used for the purposes of astonishment and denunciation, and it is not meant literally, because the companion knew that his companion was a polytheist, as shown by his words to him, ﴿and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. So by "disbelief" here is meant the polytheism that is part of his beliefs, which includes denying the resurrection. For this reason he is identified through the relative construction (al-mawsuliyya), because the content of the relative clause ought to turn anyone who perceives it away from associating others with Him, since they acknowledge that Allah is the One who created people, so no one other than Allah deserves to be worshipped.

Furthermore, knowledge of the first creation ought to turn a person away from denying the second creation, as He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15], and He said, ﴿It is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Thus the content of the relative clause is an allusion (taʿrid) to the ignorance of the one addressed.

His words "from dust" indicate the components of which the semen is composed, which are the constituents of nourishment extracted from the dust of the earth, as He, exalted is He, said in another verse, ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs from what the earth grows﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36].

Al-nutfa (the drop) is the man's water, derived from al-naṭf, which is flowing. And ﴿sawwaka﴾ means "He made your creation balanced," i.e., He made it proportionate in form and function.

The "min" (from) in His words ﴿from dust, then from a drop﴾ is initial (ibtidāʾiyya). His words ﴿lākinnā huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ were written in the Mushaf with an alif after the nun. The ten readers agreed on pronouncing the alif when pausing. As for continuous recitation (waṣl), the majority read it without pronouncing the alif, while Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu Jaʿfar, and Ruways from Yaʿqub read it with the alif pronounced in continuous recitation. The Mushaf's orthography permits both transmissions.

The word lākinnā is composed of lākin (with the nun sukun), which is a corrective particle (ḥarf istidrāk), and the first-person pronoun anā. Its original form is lākin anā, then the hamza was dropped for ease, as al-Zajjaj said, that is, by an irregular process and not for a morphological cause (ʿilla taṣrīfiyya). For this reason the hamza does not have the status of a fully present sound, so it does not prevent the assimilation (idghām) that is prevented by something deleted for a morphological cause, on the basis that what is deleted for a cause is equivalent to what is present. Its vowel was transferred to the quiescent nun of lākin as evidence of the deleted hamza, so two vowelled nuns came together, and their assimilation became obligatory, and it became lākinnā. It is not permissible that it be lākinna with the doubled nun and the fatha of the nun lengthened, because the doubled lākinna, one of the sisters of inna, requires that the noun after it be in the accusative, and there is nothing here that is an accusative pronoun. Nor is it permissible to consider the pronoun anā an accusative pronoun for the noun of lākinna, because the accusative first-person pronoun must be with the first-person yāʾ. Nor is it permissible to consider it the first-person plural pronoun, because that contradicts the singular pronouns that follow it in His words ﴿He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾.

(Fa-anā) is a subject (mubtadaʾ), and the sentence ﴿huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) with its predicate, and it is the predicate of anā, meaning: my matter is that Allah is my Lord. The predicate in His words ﴿huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ is used for affirmation, meaning: I acknowledge that He is my Lord, unlike you.

The place of the corrective particle is the contrast of what follows lākin with what precedes it, especially if the two men were brothers or close friends, as has been said, since it may be suspected that their beliefs are the same.

He reinforced the affirmation of his acknowledgment of the One Creator with four emphases: the two nominal sentences; the pronoun of the matter in His words ﴿lākinnā huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾; the definiteness of the predicate and the subject in the words "Allāhu rabbī," which conveys the restriction (qaṣr) of the attribute of Allah's lordship to the speaker himself, a restriction of specification (qaṣr idāfī) relative to his interlocutor, meaning: not you, since you worship gods other than Allah. The restriction is itself a doubled emphasis; then there is the verbal emphasis of the sentence in his words ﴿and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾.

The coordination of the clause ﴿And why, when you entered﴾ [al-Kahf: 39] with the clause ﴿Do you disbelieve﴾ is coordination of denunciation upon denunciation. The particle (lawlā) is for reproach, as is its usage when it enters upon a past verb, as in His words ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ [al-Nur: 13], meaning: it was incumbent upon you to say ﴿What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 39] instead of your saying ﴿I do not think this will ever perish, nor do I think the Hour will be established﴾ [al-Kahf: 35]. The meaning is: Do you disbelieve in Allah, and have you ingratefully rejected His blessing?

[Page 323]

As for the (mā) in His words ﴿What Allah wills﴾ [al-Kahf: 39], the best of what they have said about it is that it is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and it is the predicate of an omitted subject indicated by the circumstance of entering the garden, meaning: this garden is what Allah willed, that is, the thing Allah willed to give me.

And better than this in my view: that (mā) is an indefinite qualifying noun (nakira mawṣūfa), and the estimate is: this is a thing Allah willed, that is, for me.

The sentence ﴿there is no power except through Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 39] is an explanation (taʿlīl) for the fact that this garden is from the will of Allah, meaning: I have no power to bring it into being, or no one who brought it into being has power except through Allah. For all powers are a gift from Allah, exalted is He, and they do not take effect except with His help, through the soundness of the causes and the thinking and crafting instruments. Thus the generality found in the sentence ﴿there is no power except through Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 39] makes it like the cause and the proof that this garden is a particular instance of the products of human powers, which are given to people by the grace of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 39–41:

﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes a barren slope of bare earth,﴾ ﴿or its water will sink away, so you will never be able to find it.﴾

This is an independent sentence by which he returns to answering his companion regarding his statement ﴿I am more than you in wealth and stronger in men﴾ [al-Kahf: 34]. In it he admonishes him that he does not know whether the abundance of his wealth will turn into scarcity, or into utter ruin, and whether the little wealth of the other will become a great wealth.

The ya' of the first person has been dropped after the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) for lightness, and this is common.

The word (anā) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and therefore ״aqalla״ is in the accusative as a second object of ״tarunna״, and the pronoun is not counted. The word (ʿasā) expresses hope (rajāʾ), which is a request for a matter that is near to occurring, and perhaps by it he intended a supplication for himself and against his companion.

al-Ḥusbān: a verbal noun of ḥasaba, like al-Ghufrān. Here it is an adjective of a deleted noun, meaning a destruction that is ḥusbān, i.e., decreed by God, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a gift reckoned﴾ [al-Naba': 36]. It has been said: al-Ḥusbān is a collective noun for short arrows shot at one target, having no singular. It has also been said: it is the plural of ḥusbāna, which is the thunderbolt. It has also been said: it is a name for locusts. The four meanings are all suitable here. Al-samāʾ: the elevated atmosphere above the earth.

Al-ṣaʿīd: the surface of the earth. It was mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then perform tayammum with clean ṣaʿīd﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], and they interpreted it here with that meaning, so mentioning it here serves as a preparation for applying the attribute to it, which is "zalaqan" (slippery).

In Lisan al-ʿArab, from al-Layth: it is said of a garden, when it is ruined and its trees have gone, "it has become ṣaʿīdan," i.e., level land with no trees in it. End quote.

This, if it is correct, is the best meaning here, and describing it as zalaqan would be hyperbole for the complete absence of benefit from it. But I think that al-Layth devised this meaning from this verse; it is an explanation of the sense of the speech, not a clarification of the signification of the word ṣaʿīd. A parallel is His saying ﴿And indeed We will make what is upon it a barren ṣaʿīd﴾ [al-Kahf: 8] at the beginning of this surah.

Al-zalaq: the verbal noun of "zalaqat al-rijl" when the foot is unsteady and slips on the ground and does not stand firm. Describing the earth with it is hyperbole, i.e., possessing slipperiness, meaning it is made slippery.

Al-ghawr: the verbal noun of "ghāra al-māʾ," when water sinks into the earth. Describing it with the verbal noun is for emphasis, and for this reason He followed it with ﴿so you will never be able to find it [any] seeking﴾. He brought the particle of emphatic negation for added confirmation of this hope, which issued as a form of supplication.

Al-ṣaʿīd: the surface of the earth. It was mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then perform tayammum with clean ṣaʿīd﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], and they interpreted it here with that meaning, so mentioning it here serves as a preparation for applying the attribute to it, which is "zalaqan" (slippery).

In Lisan al-ʿArab, from al-Layth: it is said of a garden, when it is ruined and its trees have gone, "it has become ṣaʿīdan," i.e., level land with no trees in it. End quote.

This, if it is correct, is the best meaning here, and describing it as zalaqan would be hyperbole for the complete absence of benefit from it. But I think that al-Layth devised this meaning from this verse; it is an explanation of the sense of the speech, not a clarification of the signification of the word ṣaʿīd. A parallel is His saying ﴿And indeed We will make what is upon it a barren ṣaʿīd﴾ [al-Kahf: 8] at the beginning of this surah.

Al-zalaq: the verbal noun of "zalaqat al-rijl" when the foot is unsteady and slips on the ground and does not stand firm. Describing the earth with it is hyperbole, i.e., possessing slipperiness, meaning it is made slippery.

Al-ghawr: the verbal noun of "ghāra al-māʾ," when water sinks into the earth. Describing it with the verbal noun is for emphasis, and for this reason He followed it with ﴿so you will never be able to find it [any] seeking﴾. He brought the particle of emphatic negation for added confirmation of this hope, which issued as a form of supplication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 39–41:

﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes a barren slope of bare earth,﴾ ﴿or its water will sink away, so you will never be able to find it.﴾

This is an independent sentence by which he returns to answering his companion regarding his statement ﴿I am more than you in wealth and stronger in men﴾ [al-Kahf: 34]. In it he admonishes him that he does not know whether the abundance of his wealth will turn into scarcity, or into utter ruin, and whether the little wealth of the other will become a great wealth.

The ya' of the first person has been dropped after the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) for lightness, and this is common.

The word (anā) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and therefore ״aqalla״ is in the accusative as a second object of ״tarunna״, and the pronoun is not counted. The word (ʿasā) expresses hope (rajāʾ), which is a request for a matter that is near to occurring, and perhaps by it he intended a supplication for himself and against his companion.

al-Ḥusbān: a verbal noun of ḥasaba, like al-Ghufrān. Here it is an adjective of a deleted noun, meaning a destruction that is ḥusbān, i.e., decreed by God, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a gift reckoned﴾ [al-Naba': 36]. It has been said: al-Ḥusbān is a collective noun for short arrows shot at one target, having no singular. It has also been said: it is the plural of ḥusbāna, which is the thunderbolt. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 42–43:

﴿And his fruits were encompassed (by destruction), and he began to wring his hands over what he had spent upon it, while it lay in ruins upon its trellises, and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ ﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah, nor was he able to defend himself.﴾

His companion, the believer, was a righteous man, so Allah fulfilled his hope. Or he was a muhaddath (one who receives inspiration) of this community, or of the earlier nations, according to the disagreement over who is meant by the two men in the verse. Allah inspired him with knowledge of what He had decreed in the unseen of punishment in this world for the disbelieving, arrogant man.

The clause ﴿And it was encompassed﴾ is not connected by the particle fa' of consequence to the hope of his believing companion, since the purpose in this context is not to point to the believing man. Rather, the important matter is to alert that this is an event that befell the disbeliever as a punishment for his disbelief, so that the listeners may know that this is the recompense of those like him, and that it is not specific to the supplication of the believing man.

Ihata (encompassing) means seizing from every side, derived from the encirclement of an enemy around a people when he raids them. It has already been discussed in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿unless you are encompassed (by it)﴾ [Yusuf: 66] in Surat Yusuf, and His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord encompasses the people﴾ [al-Isra': 60] in Surat al-Isra'.

The meaning: all his wealth was destroyed, by Allah sending upon the garden and the crops a punishment from heaven, so that they became barren ground, slippery; his livestock perished and his properties were seized, or it was swallowed up by an earthquake or something similar.

The disagreement of the reciters concerning the word "thumur" has already been mentioned just above, at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And he had fruit﴾ [al-Kahf: 34].

Wringing the hands: it is a movement performed by one who is filled with regret, namely that one turns them upward and then in front of himself, in grief over the wealth he expended on establishing that garden. So it is a metonymy for regret, and similar to it is the saying "he struck the tooth out of remorse," and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119].

Al-khawiyah means the empty one, i.e., while it was empty of trees and crops. Al-'urush means the roof. (ʿalā) indicates elevation, and the clause ﴿upon its trellises﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in khawiyah.

The Qur'an employed this construction as a metaphor for complete ruin, which is the collapse of the building's roofs and walls. It was discussed in His saying ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town while it was in ruins upon its trellises﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259] in Surat al-Baqarah, where the pronoun is taken to refer to the walls of the town, by the indication of its contrast with "its trellises," since the town consists of dwellings composed of walls and roofs. Then this was made a metaphor for every total destruction in which no remnant of the destroyed thing remains.

The clause "and he says" is a narration of his remorse over what had passed from him, at a time when remorse no longer benefits him after the punishment has descended.

The present tense indicates the repetition of that statement from him.

The vocative particle is used to express lamentation, and (laytani) is a wish whose purpose is regret. The origin of the saying "O would that I..." is that it is a treatment of the word as though it were a rational being, as if he addresses the word "would" saying: "Come, for this is your time." Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿lest a soul say, "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah"﴾ [al-Zumar: 56].

This is regret over associating others with Allah in the past, and it indicates that he believed in Allah alone at that time.

His saying ﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾ is an admonition and a warning concerning the recompense for his saying ﴿and more powerful in manpower﴾ [al-Kahf: 34].

Al-fi'ah means the group. The clause "yansurunahu" is a qualifier: that is, he had no group of this description, for his group did not avail him against the punishment of Allah.

His saying ﴿nor was he able to defend himself﴾ means: nor would there be for him any victory or escape from the punishment.

The majority read "lam takun" with a feminine (ta') prefix, considering the feminine form of fi'ah in wording, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "yakun" with a yā' prefix. Both readings are permissible in grammar when the noun is not of true feminine gender.

This punishment encompassed him not merely because of disbelief, for Allah may grant many disbelievers enjoyment throughout their lives, give them respite, and draw them on gradually. Rather, this punishment encompassed him as a recompense for his transgression and for making his wealth and property a means of despising the poor believer. For when he took pride in those blessings and used them to deny Allah's promise, he deserved Allah's punishment by the removal of those blessings from him, just as the blessing was removed from Qarun when he said ﴿I was given it only on knowledge I possess﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. For this reason this parable became a lesson for the polytheists who made their blessings a means of exalting themselves above the gatherings of the call, since those gatherings included people they regarded as lowlier than themselves, and they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to drive them away from his assembly, as has been mentioned earlier.
