[Page 329]

﴿There, guardianship belongs to God, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾ This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement appended to what precedes it), because of the generality contained in this sentence, which arises from restricting guardianship (*wilayah*) to God Most High. That restriction confirms the sentences before it: ﴿And he will say, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ [al-Kahf: 42], ﴿And he had no party to help him other than God, nor was he one who could defend himself.﴾ [al-Kahf: 43]. This is because guardianship by its nature prompts one to help the one under guardianship, and it leads the one under guardianship to expect that his guardian will help him. Therefore, when the disbeliever saw what had befallen him as a consequence of his disbelief, he resorted to saying, ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord.﴾ [al-Kahf: 42], since he knew that the other gods had not availed him anything through their guardianship, just as Abu Sufyan said on the day he embraced Islam, "I have known that if there had been another god with Him, it would have availed me something." So the demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿the guardianship belongs to God﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*) concerning the demonstrative.

The demonstrative of distant place is used figuratively to indicate a strange situation, by likening the situation to a place because it encompasses its possessor, and likening its strangeness to distance because such situations are rare. The meaning is: in such a situation, guardianship is restricted to God. "Guardianship" (*al-wilayah*) is a generic noun defined by the definite article of genus (*lam al-jins*), which indicates that this genus is exclusive to God through the article, in the manner established in His saying, "All praise is due to God."

*Al-wilayah* with a fatha on the waw is the verbal noun of *waliya*, when one is entitled to *al-wala'* (allegiance/patronage). It was discussed under His saying, ﴿You have no guardianship over them until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], in Surat al-Anfal.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *al-Wilayah* with a kasra on the waw, and it is then a noun of the verbal noun, or a noun meaning authority and dominion.

The majority read *al-haqq* in the genitive, as an attribute of God Most High, as He is described by it in His saying, ﴿and they were returned to God, their true Lord (*mawlahumu al-haqq*)﴾ [Yunus: 30], in Surat Yunus. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *al-haqq* in the nominative, as an attribute of *al-wilayah*. Thus *al-haqq* carries the meaning of truth, because the guardianship of other than Him is falsehood and vanity.

Hujjat al-Islam (al-Ghazali) said: "The necessary existent in its essence is the Truth absolutely, for it is what is recognized by the intellect as truly existent. Thus, in terms of its essence it is called existent, and in terms of its relation to the intellect that perceives it as it is, it is called true." (end of quote)

By this, the reason for describing Him here as *al-Haqq* rather than with another attribute becomes clear, because it has become evident in such a situation that other than God has no reality, or has no permanence.

*Khayr* may mean "more excellent in outcome" (*akhir*), so that the preference (*tafdil*) is in excellence over the reward and outcome of others, for what comes to others as reward or outcome is either deceptive, leading to harm, or transient, whereas God's reward is pure and everlasting, and likewise His outcome.

It may also be that *khayr* is a noun opposite to *sharr* (evil), meaning that He is the one whose reward and outcome are good, while whatever else is other than Him is evil.

[Page 330]

The specification (*tamyiz*) is the specification of the attribution of goodness to God. *Al-'uqub*, with two dammas or with a sukun on the qaf, means *al-'aqibah*, i.e., the final end of the matter, which is what a person hopes for from his effort and work.

The majority read *'uquban* with two dammas and tanwin, while 'Asim, Hamzah and Khalaf read it with a sukun on the qaf and tanwin.

It is as if what that arrogant polytheist attained of gifts was attained only through apparent means and causes, and he did not attain it through God's care and honour. Therefore it was not good, and its outcome was evil for him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 45:

﴿And strike for them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it, and then it became dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is ever Able over all things.﴾

The greatest barrier between the polytheists and reflection upon the proofs of Islam was their absorption in pursuing this fleeting life and its delights, and the deception that deluded the tyrants among the people of polytheism, diverting them from employing their minds to understand the proofs of Tawhid (the oneness of God) and resurrection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Leave Me with those who deny, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], and He said: ﴿Because he possesses wealth and children. When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the former peoples."﴾ [al-Qalam: 14].

They used to think that this world would not come to an end. ﴿And they say, "There is none but our worldly life; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time."﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24]. And neither of the two men whose story has preceded was anything but one of the polytheists, when he said: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever occur﴾ [al-Kahf: 36].

So Allah commanded His Messenger to strike for them the example of the life of this world, whose splendor had deluded them.

The "life of this world" (al-hayah al-dunya) is applied to the duration of the survival of living species upon the earth and the earth remaining in its state. The application of the name "the life of this world" to that duration is because it is the period of the deficient life that is not everlasting, since its cessation is decreed; thus it is "dunya" (the lower/nearer).

The life of this world is also applied to the duration of the life of individuals, i.e., the life of each person. Describing it as "dunya," meaning "near," i.e., present and not awaited, is a metaphor for presence by nearness; the description serves to distinguish it from the Hereafter, which is the life after death.

The kaf in His saying "kama'in" (like water) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-hayah" (life), which is the mudaf ilayhi of "mathal" (example). That is: strike for them an example of it in the state that it is like water which We sent down.

This example applies to the life of this world in both of its senses, and both are intended by it. The pronoun in "lahum" (for them) refers to the polytheists, as indicated by the consistency of the plural pronouns in His following saying: (And We gathered them, and We left none of them behind, and they were presented [before your Lord] … but you claimed that We would not appoint for you an appointment).

The mingling of the plants (ikhtilat al-nabat) means their abundance and the intertwining of some of them with others, from the strength of fertility and flourishing.

The ba' in His saying "bihi" (with it) is the ba' of causation, and the pronoun refers to "ma'" (water); that is, the plants mingled because of the water, i.e., some plants mingled with others. The ba' is not for making the verb "ikhtalata" transitive to an object, since the meaning would not be clear upon that reading. Mentioning "the earth" after "the sky" is an embellishment of antithesis (tibaq).

"Asbaha" (became) is used in the sense of "sara" (became), which is a common usage.

Al-hashim (stubble) is a noun on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., broken and shattered; al-hashm means breaking and crumbling.

"Tadhruhu al-riyah" (which the winds scatter) means it disperses it in the air; al-dharw means throwing into the air. The state of this world with what is in it is likened to the state of a garden that remains for a time delightful and green, and then after a while its plants come to decay. The point of resemblance is the passage from a good state to a bad state. This is a likening of an intelligible matter to a sensible one, since the state being likened is intelligible, for people do not see the early signs of the contraction of the delight of life. Also, the condition of the worldly blessings coming forward in life together with youth, wealth, and the adornment of living for its people, then the contraction of that, the cessation of its benefit, and then its extinction into scattered pieces, is likened to the condition of rain bringing forth crops, their growth from it, their freshness and abundance, then their beginning to diminish and the absence of enjoyment of them, then their scattering into pieces in the air: a likening of a compound sensible matter to a compound sensible matter, with the point of resemblance as you have understood.

The clause ﴿And Allah is ever Able over all things﴾ is a parenthetical clause at the end of the speech. Its purpose is to remind of Allah's power to create things and their opposites, and to make their beginnings lead to their endings, and His arranging the causes of perishing upon the causes of subsistence; and that is a wondrous power. This has been conveyed in the most complete manner by the generality in His saying "over all things," and by that generality it resembles a concluding summary (tadhyil). Al-muqtadir: the one who is strong in power.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 18, verse 46:**

﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward, and better for hope.﴾

This is a parenthetical statement (iʿtirāḍ, a clause inserted between related parts of a discourse), intended as an admonition and a lesson for the believers. What the polytheists possess of blessings, of wealth and children, is nothing but the adornment of the worldly life, which you know to be passing away. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do not be deceived by the movement of those who disbelieve through the land. It is a brief enjoyment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 196]. And what God has prepared for the believers is better in the sight of God and better in hope. Taking pride in wealth and children is a well-known custom among the Arabs. Ṭarafa said:

*If my Lord willed, I would be Qays ibn ʿĀṣim,*
*And if my Lord willed, I would be ʿAmr ibn Marthad.*

*So I became a man of abundant wealth, and noble sons surrounded me,*
*Masters of the one who is made a master.*

﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾ are two adjectives applied to a deleted noun, meaning: the good deeds that are enduring, that is, those which have no passing away, i.e., there is no passing away of their good, which is their lasting reward. Thus they are better than the adornment of the worldly life, which is not enduring.

[Page 333]

The apparent arrangement of the two adjectives would require that *al-ṣāliḥāt* (the good) be placed before *al-bāqiyāt* (the enduring). Although both are adjectives of a deleted noun, the more familiar of the two as a description of that deleted noun is *al-ṣāliḥāt*, because it is widely used to say "the good deeds" and one does not say "the enduring deeds." Moreover, their enduring is contingent upon their being good. Therefore *al-ṣāliḥāt* is an adjective that took the place of the noun and largely replaced it in speech, until the word *al-ṣāliḥāt* came to function like a noun denoting a good deed. This occurs frequently in the Qur'an, where God, Exalted is He, says ﴿and did good deeds﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], and in their speech Jarīr said:

*How can I satirize, when a good woman from the family of Laʾm*
*keeps coming to me from behind the unseen?*

However, the apparent order is reversed here, and *al-bāqiyāt* is placed first, to draw attention to the fact that what was mentioned before it was separated from the good deeds, because it is not enduring. This refers to wealth and children, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but a brief enjoyment﴾ [al-Raʿd: 26]. This placement fulfills the requirement of concision, since it dispenses with a deleted statement whose implied meaning is: "that [wealth and children] is passing, or it is not enduring, and the enduring among the good deeds is better than it." His saying ﴿so it became dry stubble, which the winds scatter﴾ [al-Kahf: 45] conveys passing away by way of illustration, and it is an indication by inclusion (dalālat al-taḍammun). His saying "and the enduring" conveys the passing away of other things by way of implication (dalālat al-iltizām). Thus two non-corresponding indications are obtained, and these are more effective in the art of eloquence. Through the second of them there is an emphasis on the meaning of the first, so the speech came as concise and emphatic.

A parallel to this verse is the verse of Surah Maryam, His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward, and better for return﴾ [Maryam: 76]. It came immediately after His saying ﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say to those who believed: "Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?"﴾ [Maryam: 73], and ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, who were finer in furnishing and appearance﴾ [Maryam: 74], and so on.

The mention of wealth is given precedence over children because it comes more readily to people's minds, since both the young and the old, the youth and the elderly, and even one who already has enough children, desire it. For this reason it was also placed first in the verse of Ṭarafa mentioned just above.

[Page 334]

The meaning of ﴿and better for hope﴾ is that the hope of one who hopes in wealth and children is for the attainment of something uncertain in its attainment and limited to its own term. As for one who hopes for the reward of good deeds, he hopes for the attainment of something promised by the One whose promise is true, and he hopes for something from which benefit is obtained in both this world and the Hereafter, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Naḥl: 97]. Therefore His saying ﴿and better for hope﴾ is, with certainty and generality, a concluding remark (tadhyīl) following what precedes it.

[Page 335 begins]

**﴿And on the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We will gather them and leave none of them behind.﴾ ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have come to Us just as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would not appoint for you a appointed time."﴾**

This is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, conjunction of one clause to another) with the clause ﴿And present to them the parable of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf 18:45]. The word ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ (*yawma*, "the day") is in the accusative, governed by a implied verb whose estimated form is ﴿اذْكُرْ﴾ (*udhkur*, "remember"), as is customary in such constructions. Having first shown them, by way of admonition, that the bliss they enjoy is subject to decline, the verse then reminds them of what follows that decline, by depicting the state of the Resurrection and the punishment awaiting them there for their disbelief in it. This is a counterpart to its opposite, mentioned in His words ﴿And the lasting good deeds are better﴾ [al-Kahf 18:46].

It is also possible that the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*) depends on an implied word other than ﴿اذْكُرْ﴾, one indicated by the context of warning, such as: "They will see a terrifying or great matter," or something similar, which the listener himself would supply. The implied element is placed after the adverbial phrase and what is connected to it, for the purpose of emphasizing the awfulness of the Day and what occurs in it.

It is not permissible for the adverbial phrase to depend on the implied verb of speech (*fiʿl al-qawl al-muqaddar*) at His words ﴿You have indeed come to Us﴾, because that would not suit the position of this clause's conjunction with the one before it, and there would be no justification for placing the adverbial phrase before its governing element.

The setting in motion of the mountains (*taysīr al-jibāl*) means removing them from their places by a great earthquake. This is like His words ﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾ [al-Takwir 81:3], and His words ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by like clouds﴾ [al-Naml 27:88]. It has also been said that "setting in motion" is used to mean the scattering of their parts. In that case the meaning is: "On the Day We set in motion every mountain among the mountains," and this is like His words ﴿And the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [al-Qariʿa 101:5], and His words ﴿And the mountains will be crushed to powder, becoming scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqiʿa 56:5], and His words ﴿And the mountains will be set moving, becoming a mirage﴾ [al-Naba 78:20]. The cause is one, and the two modes are mutually implied. This is among the conditions of the dissolution of the order of this world and the arrival of the world of eternal life and the Resurrection.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿نُسَيِّرُ﴾ (*nusayyiru*, "We set in motion") with the first-person plural of majesty (*nūn al-ʿaẓama*). Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿تُسَيَّرُ الجِبالُ﴾ (*tusayyaru al-jibālu*, "the mountains are set in motion") with a feminine prefix and the verb in the passive voice, with ﴿الجِبالُ﴾ (*al-jibālu*, "the mountains") in the nominative.

The address in His words ﴿and you see the earth laid bare﴾ is not directed at a specific person. The meaning is: "whoever sees will see," like the line of Tarafa:

*You see two heaps of earth upon them, slabs, solid, of layered stone.*

This is a parallel to His words ﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾ [al-Kahf 18:49].

﴿البارِزَةُ﴾ (*al-bārizah*, "laid bare") means "manifest," that is, its surface is exposed, since nothing covers its face of trees, plants or animals. This is like His words ﴿Then they will be on the level ground﴾ [al-Naziʿat 79:14].

The clause ﴿And We gather them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relative to the pronoun in ﴿نُسَيِّرُ﴾ according to the reading of those who read with the *nūn* of majesty, or relative to the implied agent which the passive form of the verb requires, according to the reading of those who read ﴿تُسَيَّرُ الجِبالُ﴾ with the passive voice.

It is also possible to make the clause ﴿وحَشَرْناهم﴾ (*wa-ḥashharnāhum*, "and We gathered them") conjoined to the clause ﴿نُسَيِّرُ الجِبالَ﴾ on the interpretation of it as ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ (*naḥshuruhum*, "We will gather them"), by using the past tense verb to express the future, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence.

The verb ﴿المُغادَرَةُ﴾ (*al-mughādarah*) means leaving a thing and abandoning it, so that no action is connected to it. The pronouns of the third person in ﴿حَشَرْناهم﴾ (*ḥashharnāhum*), ﴿ومِنهم﴾ (*wa-minhum*) and ﴿وعُرِضُوا﴾ (*wa-ʿurriḍū*) refer back to what the pronoun of the third person in ﴿واضْرِبْ لَهم مَثَلَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ [al-Kahf 18:45] referred to.

[Page 336 begins]

The presentation of a thing (*ʿarḍ al-shayʾ*) is bringing it forward so that its condition and what it needs may be seen. From this comes the review of an army before the commander, so that he may see their condition and number. In a hadith: "The nations were displayed to me." Here it is used figuratively for bringing them forward, where they know that they will receive what God commands regarding them.

The row (*ṣaff*) is a group who stand one behind another, such that all of them appear and none of them hides another. Its origin is the verbal noun of ﴿صَفَّهم﴾ (*ṣaffahum*, "he arranged them in rows"), when he made them stand, and the term was applied to those arranged in rows. ﴿صَفًّا﴾ (*ṣaffan*, "in rows") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the *wāw* in ﴿عُرِضُوا﴾. This condition indicates that they were brought in the state of criminals, none of whom can be concealed, in order to instill terror in their hearts.

The clause ﴿وعُرِضُوا عَلى رَبِّكَ﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿وحَشَرْناهُمْ﴾, so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause relative to the accusative pronoun in ﴿حَشَرْناهم﴾. That is: "We gathered them when they had been presented," drawing attention to the swiftness of their presentation at the time of their gathering.

In His words ﴿عَلى رَبِّكَ﴾ (*ʿalā rabbika*, "before your Lord"), He shifted from the pronoun to the definite form by means of the genitive construction, instead of saying ﴿عَلَيْنا﴾ (*ʿalaynā*, "before Us"). The construction includes an honouring of the one addressed, to the effect that in this presentation and the threat it contains there is a share of support for the addressee, since they denied him when he informed them and warned them of the Resurrection.

The clause ﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونا﴾ is the content of an implied speech, indicated by the fact that the clause is an address to those presented, so the estimation of a speech verb is necessary. This clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the estimate is: "saying to them, 'You have indeed come to Us.'" This is by having them hear this speech from God, while they know that it comes from God. The address in His words ﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونا﴾ is directed at the referent of the pronoun in ﴿عُرِضُوا﴾.

The statement in His words ﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونا﴾ is used for threat, severe rebuke and reproach for their denial of the Resurrection. The coming (*al-majīʾ*) is a metaphor for presence. They are likened, at the time of their death, to absent persons, and their life after death is likened to the arrival of the absent one.

His words ﴿كَما خَلَقْناكم أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ﴾ ("just as We created you the first time") occupy the position of an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*, a verbal noun used to emphasize or specify the manner of the action) that indicates resemblance. That is: "You have come to Us with a coming like your creation the first time." So the second creation resembles the first creation, that is, this is a second creation. The *mā* (ما) is verbal (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning "as Our creating you the first time." He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf 50:15]. The purpose is an indirect rebuke of their error in denying the Resurrection.

The turning away (*iḍrāb*) in His words ﴿بَلْ زَعَمْتُمْ ألَّنْ نَجْعَلَ لَكم مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("But you claimed that We would not appoint for you a appointed time") is a transition from threat, and what accompanies it of indirect allusion to error, to an explicit declaration of error in the form of a denial. So the statement is used figuratively for error, and is not used to convey its original meaning.

The claim (*zaʿm*) is a mistaken belief, or a report exposed to falsehood. The appointed time (*mawʿid*) originally means the time of a promise of something, or the place of a promise. Here it means the time promised for life after death.

The meaning is: you held the false belief that there would never be for you an appointed time for the Resurrection after death.
