[Page 338]

The clause ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and they will be presented before your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 48], so it stands in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: "while the Book has been placed."

By "the Book" is meant the genus, that is, the records of the deeds of mankind were placed, because every person has a book, as other verses indicate, among them His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck, and We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book he will find spread open: "Read your book."﴾ [al-Isra': 13]. The singular pronoun in His saying "about what is in it" follows the singular form of the word "Book." It is reported from al-Ghazali that he said: "There will be a single book comprising everything that is scattered among the individual books of each person." He probably derived this from this verse. The statement of the condition of the criminals at the placing of the Book is a consequence of the placing of the Book.

The address in His saying "you will see" is to an unspecified addressee, not to the Prophet (ﷺ), because on that day the Messenger (ﷺ) is in lofty stations far removed from that place.

Ishfāq (apprehension) is fear of a matter that will occur in the future.

The use of the present tense in "they say" serves to bring the dreadful state vividly before the mind, or to indicate that they repeatedly say this. Its repetition is the habit of the terrified and frightened.

The call "Woe" (wayl) is a lamentation expressing anguish from woe. Its origin is a vocative that is used figuratively, by treating what is not addressed as if it were addressed, with the aim of making it present, as if one were saying: "This is your time, so come forth." Then this usage became common, until it came to be used merely for its purpose of calling, which is anguish and the like.

Waylah is the feminine form of wayl for emphasis, and it means evil condition and ruin, just as the word for "house" (dār) is made feminine as dārah, to indicate the spaciousness of the place. This has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿He said: "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31], in Surat al-'Uqud (Surah al-Ma'idah).

The interrogative in their saying "What is this Book's?" (mā li-hādhā al-kitāb) is used to express wonder. So "mā" is an interrogative noun, meaning "what," and "li-hādhā al-kitāb" is a qualifier of the interrogative "mā," because of the indefiniteness it contains, meaning: "What is established for this Book?"

The lām is for specification, like His saying: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not trust us with Joseph?﴾ [Yusuf: 11].

The clause "it leaves nothing" (lā yughādiru) stands in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, and it is the source of the wonder. The usage has been to attach the circumstantial qualifier to expressions like "mā laka" (what is the matter with you), so they say: "What is the matter with you that you do not do it?" and "What is the matter with you doing it?"

Mughādarah means leaving, and it has already been discussed a moment ago at His saying: ﴿and We left none of them behind﴾ [al-Kahf: 47].

"Ṣaghīrah" (small) and "kabīrah" (great) are two attributes of an omitted noun, which is indicated by the context, meaning: "an act or a trifle." What is meant here by smallness and greatness are the great deeds and the petty deeds. Greatness and pettiness vary according to clarity and obscurity, and they also vary according to strength and weakness.

[Page 339]

The mention of "small" is placed first because it is more important, since the wonder concerns its being counted. "Great" is coordinated with it to intend generality in the counting, because generality also provokes wonder: they wondered at the all-encompassing knowledge of the one who wrote the Book of all deeds.

The exception (istithnā') is from the general state of the small and the great, meaning: it leaves no small or great thing in any of its states except in the state of His counting them, that is, it leaves nothing uncounted. So the exception here is from the affirmation of a thing by something resembling its opposite, because if He has counted it, He has not left it. It thus returns to the meaning that He leaves nothing behind, and the literal sense of the exception is dropped.

So the clause "He has counted them" (aḥṣāhā) stands in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, and the link between it and the qualified element is the particle of exception. Iḥṣā' means counting, meaning: their deeds were enumerated and detailed.

The clause ﴿and they found what they had done present﴾ stands in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "they say," meaning: they only said that when their deeds were all presented to them at the placing of that Book, by a swift presentation through which each person came to know what was in his own book, in a manner that breaks the normal course of things.

The clause ﴿and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and they found what they had done present﴾, because of what the relative clause implies, namely that they found nothing other than what they had done. That is, nothing was imputed to them that they had not done, because God does not wrong anyone by holding him accountable for what he did not commit. He had already defined for them what they were not permitted to do, what they were commanded to do, and He had threatened and promised them. So there is no wrong to them in holding them accountable for what they did of the forbidden acts after that. The purpose is to convey this aspect of God's attributes, and therefore the clause is coordinated so as to be intended in its own right. Yet it also carries the meaning of a concluding statement (tadhyīl), because it contains an argument for the content of the preceding clause and a general scope that encompasses the content of the preceding clause and other things. Thus, from this standpoint, it is fit to be separated without a conjunction so as to function as a concluding statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 50:

[Page 340]
﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Then do you take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾ It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿and the day We set the mountains in motion﴾ [al-Kahf: 47], with the implied sense: "And mention when We said to the angels," as a variation (tafannun) in the purpose of admonition for which these sentences were brought, namely the reminder of the consequences of following desire and turning away from righteous deeds, and of the refutations of pride and self-admiration, of despising virtue, and of delighting in accidental things that do not bring their possessors any inner perfection. Just as they were admonished with the last days of the world, they are here reminded through admonition with the first days of it, which is the day of the creation of Adam. This is also a preparation and a prelude to His saying ﴿and the day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed"﴾ [al-Kahf: 52] and what follows, for associating partners was from the deception of Satan toward the children of Adam.

It also has a connection with the preceding verses, which were directed at those who boasted of their standing and wealth and despised the poor among the Muslims, and did not distinguish between true perfection and false vanity, as indicated by His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. So the story of Iblis's attitude toward Adam was an example for them. And because this story contains a reminder that Satan is the origin of misguidance, and that the loss of the losers on the Day of Resurrection returns to their following the steps of Satan and his allies, for this reason He placed upon both matters His saying, ﴿Then do you take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are an enemy to you?﴾

This story has been repeated in many places in the Qur'an, and in each place it includes something not included in the others, and in each place it is mentioned it has a lesson that differs from the lesson of the other. Its mention in Surat al-Baqarah, for example, is an informing about the beginnings of matters, while its mention here serves as an analogy for the present situation and a preparation for denunciation and rebuke. Draw an analogy from that.

[Page 341]
And "fasaqa" (he transgressed): he went beyond obedience to Him. Its origin is the saying of the Arabs, "fasaqat al-rutabah" (the date swelled and came out of its skin), and it was used figuratively for transgression. Abu 'Ubaydah said: fisq in the sense of going beyond obedience — Abu 'Ubaydah said: we have not heard this in anything from the poetry of the Jahiliyyah or its narratives; rather the Arabs spoke it after the revelation of the Qur'an, that is, in this verse and similar ones. Al-Mubarrad and Ibn al-A'rabi agreed with him. The term fisq is applied in several places in the Qur'an to grave disobedience, and it was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying, ﴿And He does not cause to go astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26].

The word "amr" in His saying ﴿from the command of his Lord﴾ is in the sense of "the commanded," that is, he abandoned and departed from what Allah had commanded him.

The shift in His saying ﴿from the command of his Lord﴾ to definition by way of the idafah (construct) rather than a pronoun is to magnify the defiance of Satan against the command of Allah: that it is the defiance of a servant against the command of one whose obedience is obligatory upon him, because He is his Owner.

Having reminded them of Satan's defiance and of his arrogance toward the origin of the human species, He drew from this the denunciation of taking him and his host as allies, because his arrogance toward Adam necessitates his enmity toward the species, and because his disobedience to the command of his Owner necessitates that no good is to be expected from him, and he is not worthy of being followed.

The interrogative is used for denunciation and rebuke of the polytheists, since they used to worship the jinn. Allah said, ﴿And they made the jinn partners with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 100]. For this reason He gave the reason for the prohibition by the clause of the circumstance, which is the clause ﴿while they are an enemy to you﴾.

"Dhurriyyah" means offspring, and the descendants of Satan are the devils and the jinn.

"Al-'Aduww" is a noun that applies to the singular and the plural. Allah said, ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, showing them affection﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and He said, ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4].

This noun was treated as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is on the pattern of the masdar, like "al-qabul" and "al-wuluʿ," and both are verbal nouns. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿So if he was from a people hostile to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 92], in Surat al-Nisa'.

[Page 342]
"Al-Waliyy" is one who takes charge, that is, one who takes a position of guardianship (wilayah) — with a fatha on the waw — which is nearness, and what is meant by it is nearness in meaning, namely friendship, kinship, or alliance. The "min" in "min dduni" is superfluous for emphasis, meaning: you take them as allies while distancing yourselves from Me. That is associating them in worship, for every state in which they worship the gods is a taking of them as allies instead of Allah.

The address in "a-tattakhidhunahu" and what follows is addressed to the polytheists who took him as an ally, and it is a warning to the Muslims against that.

The sentence ﴿Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah) for the inception of censure of Iblis and his descendants, in view of the polytheists' taking them as allies: that is, wretched is the exchange for the polytheists — Satan and his descendants. So His saying "badalan" (as an exchange) is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) explaining the omitted subject of "bi'sa," with the intent of dispensing with it by the specification, in the manner of summary followed by detail.

"Al-zalimun" (the wrongdoers) are the polytheists, and the explicit mention of "al-zalimin" in place of the pronoun is to expose them and because of the sense of wrongdoing (zulm) in the explicit noun, which is a censure of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 51:

﴿I did not call them to witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, nor was I one who would take the misleaders as helpers.﴾ This sentence serves as a justification (ta'lil) for the two sentences before it, namely ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me﴾ [al-Kahf: 50] up to His words "in exchange" (badalan). For since they did not witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, they were not partners with God in creation, all the more so; and therefore they were not worthy of being worshipped. This is an argument against the polytheists based on what they themselves acknowledge, for they acknowledge that God alone is the one who singularly created the heavens and the earth and the creation of all existing things.

Al-ishhad (calling to witness) means making another a witness, i.e., present. Here it is a metaphor (kinaya) for a specific kind of presence, namely presence for participation in the work or assistance in it. The negation of this witnessing necessarily entails the negation of partnership in creation and divinity by implication (bi-al-fahwa), i.e., a fortiori. For the creation of the heavens occurred before the existence of Iblis and his offspring. So this is an argument for the negation of their divinity through the priority of non-existence over their existence; and whatever is subject to non-existence is impossible to be eternal (qidam), and eternity is among the necessary attributes of divinity.

The pronouns of the third person in His saying "I did not call them" (ashhadtuhum) and "themselves" (anfusihim) refer to those being spoken of, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, just as the pronoun referred to them in His saying ﴿And they are an enemy to you﴾ [al-Kahf: 50].

The meaning of "themselves" (anfusihim) is "the selves of some of them," by the indication of the impossibility of a created being witnessing the creation of its own self. Thus the use of "selves" here is like its use in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and in His saying ﴿nor expel yourselves from your homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 84], meaning the selves of some of you. On this reading the pronouns are coherent and the intended meaning is established.

Know that God, exalted is He, created the heavens and the earth before He created their inhabitants for them, as indicated by His saying ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Fussilat: 9], ﴿And He placed firm mountains upon it from above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, alike for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 10], ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly﴾ [Fussilat: 11], ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. The people of pre-Islamic ignorance (jahiliyya) believed that there were jinn who exercised control over the earth, so when they descended into a frightening valley they would say: "I seek refuge in the mighty one of this valley," so that they would be safe from its harm.

Abu Ja'far read (ma ashhadnahum) with the royal "we" (nun al-'azama), and he read (wa ma kunta) with a fatha on the ta', in the second person, the address being to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is a report used in the sense of a prohibition.

By "the misleaders" (al-mudillin) are meant the devils (al-shayatin), because they led people astray by casting thoughts of error and corruption into souls, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you; and if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

The clause ﴿nor was I one who would take the misleaders as helpers﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the clause ﴿I did not call them to witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾.

The departure from the pronoun, by saying "wa ma kuntu muttakhidhahum ila al-mudillin," is to convey blame, and because a concluding clause should be an independent statement.

Al-'adud (helper), with a fatha on the 'ain and a damma on the dad (of the dictionary letter) in the most eloquent usage, and with fatha and sukun on the dad in the dialect of Tamim, and there are other weaker dialects. Ibn 'Atiyya attributed that Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the 'ain and a damma on the dad, as a dialectal form of 'adud; this is the narration of Harun from Abu 'Amr, and it is not well known. It means the bone between the elbow and the shoulder, and it is used figuratively for one who assists in work; one says: "So-and-so is my 'adud," and "I took support by him" (i'tadadtu bihi).

The meaning: it is not fitting for divine perfection that I should take those who lead to misguidance as helpers, so that I should make them partners with Me in My exercise of creation; for God is the bestower of guidance and the giver of understanding, so how could His helpers be sources of error? That is, one only helps another in work of the same kind, and one is only a companion to those of his own kind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 52:

﴿And [remember] the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed," so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of destruction.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], so it is estimated: "And mention the Day He will say, 'Call upon My partners'." Or it is coordinated upon the clause ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Kahf: 51], and the estimate is: "Nor did I make their partners witness [it] all, nor will their partners benefit them on the Day of Gathering." Thus it is a transition from nullifying the lordship of Satan and the jinn to nullifying the divinity of all the deities which the mass of polytheists worshipped, together with an explanation of the disappointment and despair that overtake them on that day. He followed, in nullifying their divinity, the method of the theological discourse (al-madhhab al-kalami), which is reasoning to the negation of a quiddity (al-mahiyyah) by the negation of its necessary attributes (lawazim). For when its benefit to those who worship it is negated, that entails the negation of its divinity. By this there is achieved a specification of their disappointment and their despair of salvation.

Page 345

The majority read "yaqulu" with the ya' of the third person, and the pronoun of the absent refers to God, Exalted, by the indication of the context. Hamzah read "naqulu" with the nun of majesty (nun al-ʿazamah).

The day on which this occurs is the Day of Gathering. The meaning: He says to the polytheists, as indicated by His saying ﴿whom you claimed﴾, that is, "whom you claimed to be My partners." He placed the description of them as partners before the verb of claiming, as mockery of those addressed and as rebuke to them. Then He followed it with what indicates their lie in what they asserted, by the verb "claimed," which indicates a false belief.

Al-nida' (calling) is the request for coming forward for help and intercession.

Al-istijabah (response) is speech indicating the hearing of the call and the beginning of turning toward the one who calls, with such words as "Here we are" (labbayk).

His command to them to call upon their partners is used in its literal meaning together with the intention of its implication, which is the manifestation of their falsehood, by the indication of the word "claimed." For this reason they had no choice but to call upon them, as He said ﴿so they called upon them﴾, because of their hope. When they call upon them, the disappointment of their hope becomes clear to them. Therefore He coordinated the verb of calling with the particle fa' (fa), which indicates immediate sequence, and expressed it in the past tense, to indicate the speed of its occurrence at that time, as if it had already passed.

Al-mawbiq: the place of perdition (al-wubuq), that is, destruction. It is said: waqaba, like waʿada, wajila and waritha. Here, al-mawbiq is intended to mean Hell (Jahannam). That is, when they called upon their idols by their names, God placed between their place and the place of their idols the mouths of Hell. It is also permissible that the clause ﴿and We will place between them a barrier of destruction﴾ be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "and We have placed between them a barrier of destruction," as a preparation for what follows it, His saying ﴿and the criminals will see the Fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 53].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 53:

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall into it, and they will find no escape from it.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And We have made between them a barrier of destruction (mawbiq)﴾ [al-Kahf: 52], meaning: We made the mawbiq, and the criminals saw it. The mention of "the criminals" here is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (izhar fi maqam al-idmar), to indicate what the word "criminals" conveys of their being characterized by that for which they deserved the punishment of the Fire. Likewise, "the Fire" (al-nar) is used in place of a pronoun referring to the mawbiq, to indicate that the mawbiq is the Fire; it is thus similar to an explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan).

The verb "ẓanna" (to think, to suppose) is used here in the sense of certainty (al-tahaqquq), which is one of its usages. Perhaps its choice here is a kind of mockery (tahakkum) of them: they judged it likely that this Fire had been prepared for them, whereas in fact they were certain of this.

Al-muwaqaʿa is a form of mufaʿala derived from al-wuquʿ (falling, occurring), which is coming into being, for the purpose of emphasis (mubalagha). That is, they are those who will fall into it, falling as a thing falls into a place that requires it, so it is as if it falls into them.

Al-masraf is the place of turning away (al-sarf), that is, escaping and passing beyond. There is an elision (ijaz) in the speech; its implied sense is: they tried to turn back or to turn away, but they found no escape from it, that is, no way of deliverance.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 54:**

﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people every kind of example. But mankind is ever most disputatious.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) with the preceding sentences in which examples were struck, namely His saying ﴿And strike for them an example: two men﴾ [Al-Kahf: 32] and His saying ﴿And strike for them the example of the life of this world﴾ [Al-Kahf: 45]. Since this had a persuasive effect on them, and they had no way to repel it, the discourse returned to highlighting the guidance of the Qur'an, a return that looks back to His saying ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf: 27] and His saying ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 29]. Thus it indicated to them that these examples which struck their ears are part of the guidance of the Qur'an, from which they had grown weary. The discussion of the parallel of this verse has already occurred at His saying ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ [Al-Isra: 89] in Surat al-Isra. However, a question arises here: why did this verse place one of the two complements of the verb of diversifying (taṣrīf) before the other? For here He put His saying "in this Qur'an" before His saying "for the people," the reverse of the verse of Surat al-Isra. We have pointed to this at the previous verse, namely that mention of the Qur'an is more important than mention of people in the primary sense. There is no reason to deviate from that here; rather the matter is the reverse, because the discourse is about highlighting the status of the Qur'an and that it descends with truth, not according to the desires of souls.

"The people" (al-nās) is a general term for everyone whom the Qur'an reaches throughout the subsequent ages. What is specifically intended is the polytheists, as indicated by the clause ﴿and mankind is ever most disputatious﴾. Its parallel is therefore the parallel of His saying ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ [Al-Isra: 89]. His saying ﴿and those who disbelieve dispute by falsehood in order to refute thereby the truth﴾ [Al-Kahf: 56] will come, and this resembles a general statement that was revealed upon a specific cause and specific indications.

The clause ﴿And mankind is ever most disputatious of things﴾ is a tadhyīl (a concluding statement that generalises the preceding point), and it indicates an omitted statement by way of brevity. The estimated sense is: "So they disputed concerning it, and mankind was ever more disputatious." The word "al-insān" (mankind) is a name for the species of the children of Adam, and the definite article in it is for defining the reality (lām al-ḥaqīqa), so it is broader in generality than the word "al-nās" (the people). The meaning is that they disputed. Disputation (jidāl) is a trait: among it is a blameworthy kind, which the discipline of Islam restrains from, and which remains in the character of the polytheists; and among it is a praiseworthy kind, as in His exalted saying ﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had reached him, he started disputing with Us concerning the people of Lot. Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, grieving, and turning back in repentance﴾ [Hud: 74]. Thus He indicated, by praising Abraham, that his disputation was praiseworthy. The intended meaning of "al-insān" is not the disbelieving human, as in His exalted saying ﴿Man says, "When I have died, will I be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66]. Nor is the intended meaning of "jidāl" disputation by falsehood, because this will come in His saying ﴿and those who disbelieve dispute by falsehood﴾ [Al-Kahf: 56], and so His saying here ﴿And mankind is ever most disputatious of things﴾ is a preparation for His saying after it ﴿and those who disbelieve dispute by falsehood﴾ [Al-Kahf: 56].

"Shay'" (thing) is a singular noun extremely broad in generality, and for this reason it is correct to make the elative (ism al-tafḍīl) grammatically annexed to it, meaning "the most of things." The elative here is stripped of comparison (maslūb al-mufāḍala), like His saying ﴿My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. It was used in this form only to intend hyperbole regarding the intensity of man's disputation and his inclination toward contention and dispute, even in matters where abandoning disputation would be better, to the extent that the intensity of the description in him resembles his excelling in the description over everyone else who might be described with it.

[Page 348]

We were compelled toward this interpretation of the elative because it is evident that other kinds of creatures on earth, apart from mankind, are not conceived to engage in disputation. Disputation is specific to mankind, because it is among the branches of speech, which is the distinguishing feature of the reality of humanity. As for the angels, their disputation is praiseworthy, like their saying ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [Al-Baqara: 30] up to His saying ﴿and we exalt You﴾ [Al-Baqara: 30]. As for the devils, they are more disputatious than mankind, but since the context did not turn toward them, they were not intended by the comparison in disputation.

"Jadalan" (disputatiously) is a specification (tamyīz) for the relation of the majority to mankind. The meaning is: "mankind was much in respect of disputation," that is, his disputation was much. This meaning is supported by what is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ (of al-Bukhari) from ʿAlī: "That the Prophet ﷺ came to him and Fatima at night and said, 'Will you not pray?' ʿAlī said, 'O Messenger of Allah, our souls are only in the hand of Allah; if He wills to raise us, He raises us.' He said: The Messenger of Allah turned away when I said that to him and did not return any reply to me. Then I heard him striking his thigh and saying, ﴿And mankind is ever most disputatious of things﴾." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ meant that the proper course for ʿAlī was to praise the Messenger of Allah's waking him to get up at night, to be eager for its repetition, and to be pleased with the reproach in the Messenger of Allah's words, and not to argue with what makes him love the continuation of his sleep. That is the reason for the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ astonishment at ʿAlī's (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) answer.

It is not appropriate to take the elative in the verse in its literal sense, by meaning that mankind is more disputatious than the devils and jinn, since disputation is conceivable in its literal sense for them; because this is an interpretation that is not intended in a context like this. And who informed us that the devils and jinn have the capacity for disputation?

"Jadal" (disputation) is contention through the exchange of speech, that is, it is the speech by which one attempts to nullify what the addressee holds of an opinion or resolve to which he is committed, by proof, by persuasion, or by falsehood. He, exalted, said ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabut: 46], and He said ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 1], and He said ﴿He disputes with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74], and He said ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [Al-Nisa: 107], and He said ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth after it has become evident﴾ [Al-Anfal: 6].

[Page 349]

What is intended here is disputation in its absolute sense, and especially that which is by falsehood, meaning that every human, by his nature, is eager to persuade the opponent of the rightness of his belief or action. The context of the discourse requires that the intended meaning be false disputation.

[p. 350]

This is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) with the preceding clause, ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for people every kind of example﴾ [al-Kahf 18:54], and its meaning is connected in the fullest sense with the meaning of the clause before it. Were it coordinated with the particle of consequence (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ), that would be what the apparent sense requires. The clause ﴿And man is, above all things, most given to dispute﴾ [al-Kahf 18:54] is regarded as an interjection (iʿtirāḍ) between them. Yet making this clause independent in its coordination shows concern for its content in itself, such that subordinating it to the content of the preceding clause would divert it from the position it deserves in the minds of the hearers, since it is intended to be an established truth in their souls. For this particular reason, in my view, the clause shifts from the pronoun to the explicit noun, with ﴿what prevented the people﴾ and ﴿when guidance had come to them﴾, rather than saying "what prevented them from believing when guidance had come to them." The aim is that the clause stand on its own, not relying on anything else, so that it constitutes an independent point deserving the minds' attention for its own sake, and not because it is a branch of something else.

Moreover, the generality of "the people" here is more comprehensive than the generality of "the people" in ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people﴾ [al-Kahf 18:54], for that embraces the people who hear the Qur'an in the times after the revelation of that verse, whereas this embraces all the people who refused to believe in God.

Likewise, the generality of the word "guidance" (al-hudā) includes the guidance of the Qur'an and of the divine books before it and all the sayings of the prophets. Thus this clause is an analogical comparison (qiyās tamthīlī), with the evidence of history and the circumstances of nations' reception of their messengers' calls.

[p. 350 continued]

The meaning, then, is: nothing prevents these polytheists from believing in the Qur'an that would prevent the like of it, but they are like the nations before them, who, when guidance came to them in its various forms, of books, signs, and direction toward goodness, did not accept it.

The "former ones" (al-awwalīn) means those nations who preceded them in error and obstinacy. It is also possible that it means their forefathers, that is, the custom of their forefathers, meaning their way and their religion, since every nation has a nation that preceded it.

"That there come to them" (an taʾtiyahum) is an emptied exceptive construction (istithnāʾ mufarragh), the subject of "prevented" (mana'a). "That they believe" (an yuʾminū) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "from believing."

The meaning of ﴿the custom of the former ones come upon them﴾ is that it alights upon them and befalls them, meaning it is cast into their souls and presented to them as attractive. The sense is that they resemble the creation of those before them among the people of error and imitate them, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did they bequeath it to one another? Nay, they are a people who are transgressors﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:53].

The "custom of the former ones" is their way of disbelief. The attribution of "custom" to them resembles the attribution of a verbal noun to its agent, meaning the custom which the former ones established. And attributing their prevention from belief to the coming of the custom of the former ones is a metaphor (istiʿāra).

The meaning is: nothing prevented the people from believing except what prevented the former ones before them, namely the habit of obstinacy and tyranny, and their way of denying the messengers and treating them with contempt.

Mentioning seeking forgiveness (istighfār) here after mention of belief is an instruction to them to hasten to cease disbelief and to repent to God for denying the Prophet and obstinately resisting him.

"Or" (aw) here has the sense of "until" (ilā), and the verb "there come to them the punishment" is in the subjunctive by an implied "that" (an) after "or." "Or" is connected in meaning to the verb "prevented." That is, the imitation of the custom of the former ones prevented them from belief until there comes to them the punishment as it came upon the former ones.

This is what appeared to me in the interpretation of this verse, and I consider it most fitting to the position of this verse relative to the one before it.

[p. 351]

As for all the exegetes, they interpreted the verse contrary to this in one word. They made the referent of "the people" the same as the referent in ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every kind of example﴾ [al-Kahf 18:54], that is, what prevented the polytheists from believing in God and His Messenger. They made the referent of "guidance" the same as the referent of "the Qur'an." They understood "the custom of the former ones" as the meaning of the custom of God regarding the former ones, that is, the past nations who denied, so that the attribution of "custom" to "the former ones" is like the attribution of a verbal noun to its object. It is God's practice concerning them, namely that He punishes them with the punishment of annihilation (istiʾṣāl).

They made the attribution of preventing belief to the coming of the custom of the former ones by way of an implied modifier, that is, the awaiting that the custom of God concerning the former ones should come upon them. The statement is thus sarcasm and an allusive threat of the punishment befalling the polytheists, meaning they will not believe except at the descent of the punishment of annihilation. This is in the sense of God's words: ﴿Do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: wait, and I too am waiting with you﴾ [Yūnus 10:102].

They made His words ﴿or the punishment come to them face to face﴾ a counterpart (qasīm) to His words ﴿unless the custom of the former ones come upon them﴾. So the particle "or" is for division, and the verb "there come to them" is in the subjunctive by coordination with the verb ﴿that the custom of the former ones come upon them﴾, namely by sudden annihilation, or the punishment comes to them face to face. They made "face to face" (qubulan) a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the punishment, meaning opposing. Al-Kalbī said: it is the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr. Perhaps he means that it is a punishment of confrontation, face to face, that is, the punishment of executioners with swords. Its meaning is that among the polytheists some tasted the punishment of the sword in the battles of the Muslims, and some died and so see the punishment of the Hereafter. According to this interpretation which they adopted, the sense of concluding statement (tadhyīl) is stripped from the verse, and it is confined to the meaning of threat.

The "coming" (al-ityān) is a metaphor for occurrence in the future, because of the presence of the verbal "that" (an) which renders the present tense to the future. It is a relative future, for each nation has the future of the custom of those before it.

"Custom" (sunna) is a habit familiar in some circumstance.

The attribution of their prevention from belief to the coming of the custom of the former ones or the coming of the punishment is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī). The meaning is: nothing prevented them except the cause of the coming to them of the custom of the former ones or the coming of the punishment. The cause of that

[p. 352]

is arrogance, obstinacy, and clinging to error. That is, there exists no obstacle preventing them from belief which would furnish them an excuse for it, but they went along the ways of those before them in error. This is a metonymy (kināya) for the negation of their belief until one of the two punishments befalls them.

In this metonymy there is threat, warning, admonition, and an incitement to hasten to seek forgiveness from disbelief. It is in the sense of God's words: ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yūnus 10:96].

"Qibalan" is a circumstantial qualifier of the punishment. It is pronounced with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the bāʾ according to the recitation of the majority, in the sense of "manifest confrontation." Ḥamza, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar, and Khalaf recited "qubulan" with two ḍammas, which is the plural of qabīl, meaning the punishment comes to them in kinds (anwāʿan).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 56:

﴿And We do not send the messengers except as bringers of good news and warners. And those who disbelieve argue with falsehood in order to refute thereby the truth, and they take My signs and that with which they were warned as a mockery.﴾

After he had pointed to their disputing over the guidance of the Qur'an, through what he prepared for it in His saying ﴿And man is ever most of anything given to dispute﴾ [al-Kahf: 54], and had pointed out that disputing about it is merely arrogance and obstinacy, and that there does not surround the Qur'an anything that prevents belief in it, just as there did not surround the guidance which He sent to the nations anything that prevented them from believing in it, he followed that with the fact that the function of the messengers is conveying with good news and warning, not confronting disputation; because it is a disputation from which guidance is not intended, rather its purpose is the nullification of the truth.

The exception (al-istithna') is from general omitted circumstances, meaning: We do not send the messengers in any state except in the state of their being bringers of good news and warners. By "the messengers" is meant all the messengers.

صفحة ٣٥٣
The clause ﴿And those who disbelieve argue with falsehood﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿We do not send the messengers except as bringers of good news and warners﴾, and both clauses are linked to the two clauses ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every [kind of] example, and man is ever most of anything given to dispute﴾ [al-Kahf: 54]. The arrangement of these clauses in mention follows the arrangement of their meanings in the mind, such that it suggests that each one of them arises in meaning from the one before it. Thus the clause ﴿And those who disbelieve argue with falsehood﴾ conveys the sense of contrast (al-istidrak): that is, We sent the messengers as bringers of good news and warners with that which contains persuasion for the seeker of guidance, but those who disbelieved argued with them with falsehood, in order to remove the truth, not for any other purpose. The choice of the present-tense verb (al-mudari'a) indicates the recurrence of the disputation, or to bring to mind the image of the disputation.

The word al-mujadila (disputation) has preceded in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They dispute with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74] in Surah Hud.

Al-idhah (refutation) means causing to slip. It is said: "the foot slipped" (dahadat al-qadam), when it slid. It is a metaphor for removal, because when a foot slips it moves away from the place where it stepped. God, Exalted, said: ﴿So he drew lots and was among the losers﴾ [al-Saffat: 141].

The clause ﴿and they take My signs﴾ is coordinated with the clause "they dispute," for they did not intend by the disputation to be guided, but intended to refute the truth; and they took the signs, all of them, and especially the signs of warning, as a mockery.

Al-huzu' (mockery) is a verbal noun of hazi'a, meaning they took that as an object of mockery. Mocking the signs is mocking them upon hearing them, as they do upon hearing the signs about the resurrection and upon hearing the signs of threat and warning of punishment.

The coordination of "wa ma undhiru" (and that with which they were warned) upon "the signs" is a coordination of the specific upon the general, because it is more eloquent in indicating the extent of their disbelief and the foolishness of their minds.

"Wa ma undhiru" is a masdar-type construction (masdariyya), meaning "and their warning," and the reporting of the verbal noun is for emphasis (al-mubalagha).

Al-Jumhur read (huzuan) with a damma on the zay, and Hamza read (huz'an) with a sukun on the zay.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 57:

Page 354
﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward? Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.﴾ When he (Allah) had made clear their condition in disputing with the Messengers out of ill intent, and in mocking the warning, and had hinted at their foolishness, He followed this by stating that it is the greatest injustice. That is because it is a person wronging himself, and it is the most astonishing kind of injustice. Those who were reminded of what they were heedless of, by means of the signs of Allah, turned away from reflecting upon them, although they warn them of an evil outcome. It is the way of the intelligent person, when he hears such things, to prepare himself for reflection and for taking precaution, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Quraysh: "If I told you that the enemy would attack you in the morning, would you believe me?" They said: "We have never found you to lie." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment."

The relative (man) in the genitive is a relative pronoun, and it is not restricted to a specific individual, as indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. The intended ones are the polytheists of the Arabs who were reminded by the Qur'an and turned away from it.

The conjunction of their turning away from the Remembrance to the reminding, with the fa' of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib), indicates that they hastened to turn away and did not allow themselves the respite of consideration and reflection.

The meaning of forgetting "what his hands have put forward" is that he did not present his state and deeds to examination and thought, to know whether they are good, with no fear of their consequences, or whether they are evil, of a kind that would mean the doer will not escape accountability. Good is clear and corruption is clear, and for this reason the first is called ma'ruf (recognized) and the second munkar (denounced). Especially after the reminder had come to them through the Messenger (ﷺ), they, by combining both states, are the most unjust of people. Had they reflected a little, they would have known that they will not escape encountering the recompense of their deeds.

Page 355
So "man" (who) is an interrogative used in the sense of denial, meaning: no one is more unjust than these people who have been spoken of.
Al-nisyan (forgetting) is used here for neglecting the deed. The true meaning of forgetting was discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of "what his hands have put forward" is the deeds he has sent ahead. This construction is used most often in the Qur'an for evil deeds, and it became like a proverb. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10], and He said: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30].

The verse is phrased in a general form, and its primary intended reference is the polytheists of Makkah.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from the clause ﴿and forgets what his hands have put forward﴾, meaning: if you do not know the cause of his forgetting what his hands have put forward, then know that We have placed over their hearts coverings. It conveys the sense of causation by outcome, and the clause does not occupy the position of a causal clause.

By "hearts" is meant: the faculties of knowledge.

Al-akinnah is the plural of kinan, which is a covering, because it covers the thing, that is, it screens it.

"An yafqahuhu" is in the genitive by a deleted preposition, meaning "from their understanding it," because "akinnah" is construed to imply the sense of a barrier or obstacle.

Al-waqr: heaviness of hearing that prevents the sound from reaching the ear canal.

The singular pronoun in "yafqahuhu" refers to the Qur'an, understood from the context and expressed by "the signs."

Page 356
The clause ﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts﴾, and it is a consequence of it, but it was not conjoined with fa', because the intent is to place that in an independent statement of information.

He emphasized the negation of their being guided by the negative particle of emphasis, which is (lan), and by the word (abadan), which reinforces the meaning of (lan), and by the conditional particle that indicates the answer's causation by the condition.

The sense of the conditional arises from considering the conditional clause as a consequence of the resumptive explanatory clause; that is, this is caused by the innate formation of their hearts toward not accepting the truth.

Your ﷾ Lord is the Oft-Forgiving, Possessor of mercy. Were He to take them to task for what they have earned, He would hasten their punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time, and they will never find, other than Him, a refuge. ﷿

Ibn 'Ashur: The Qur'an followed its usual practice of pairing warning (tarhib) with encouragement (targhib), and the reverse. When it had struck them with the calamities of threat and warning, it followed this allusion (ta'ridh) with a reminder of forgiveness, so that perhaps they would reflect on what pleases Him. Then it reminded them that His mercy encompasses creation at the very time of the warning, so He defers what He has threatened them with until a known limit, as a respite for people, perhaps they will turn back from their misguidance and reflect upon the blessings of God Most High in which they are, so that perhaps they will give thanks. The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), opening with the invocation of the majesty through the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) for the Prophet (ﷺ), as an indication that the content of the report is an honouring of him, like His saying ﴿But God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33].

The proper arrangement of the verse is that al-Ghafur be a qualifier (na't) of the subject (mubtada'), and dhu al-rahmah be the predicate (khabar), because it is suitable to the context and to what follows it, the clause "were He to take them to task" (law yu'akhidhuhum). Thus the mention of "al-Ghafur" is an insertion (idmaj) within the course of the intended meaning, and he singled out from the Names of God Most High the name al-Ghafur, as an allusion to encouragement to seek forgiveness.

Al-Ghafur: a name that includes intensive forgiveness (mubalaghat al-ghufran), because He is vast in forgiveness, for He forgives those who cannot be counted, and forgives sins that cannot be enumerated, if His servant comes to Him repentant and humbled. Moreover, His respite of the disbelievers and the disobedient is itself a effect of forgiveness, for it is a temporary forgiveness.

As for His saying ﴿dhu al-rahmah﴾, it is the intended meaning, as a preparation for the clause ﴿were He to take them to task for what they have earned﴾. Therefore that clause was an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿Your Lord is the Oft-Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾, considering "al-Ghafur" as the predicate, which is the second attribute.

The meaning: in what they have earned of shirk and obstinacy, they deserve the hastening of punishment, but God gives them respite until a determined, fixed term. In that deferral is mercy towards people, by enabling some of them to have a period for remedy, re-examination, and for a while preserving them in their state.

The description "dhu al-rahmah" is equivalent to the description (al-Rahim), because (dhu) denotes the firm establishment of the relation between what it describes and what it is attached to.

He departed from the description al-Rahim to "dhu al-rahmah" to draw attention to the fact that it is not a mere adjective (na't), by way of changing the style, for the name (al-Rahim) became similar to the rigid names (al-asma' al-jamidah), since it is formed in the pattern of the attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah), so it moved away from awareness of derivation in it, and drew close to the category of essential attribute (sifah dhatiyyah).

And (bal) is for the nullifying turn (al-idrab al-ibtali) away from the content of the answer of (law), meaning: He did not hasten the punishment for them, since for them there is an appointed time for punishment that is delayed. This is a threat of what will befall them on the day of Badr.

Al-mawil: a noun of place (maf'il) from (wa-la), meaning to take refuge, so it is a noun of place meaning a refuge.

He emphasised the negation with (lan) as a rejection of their denial, since they reckon that they will escape the punishment when they see that it has been delayed a long time. That is, they have no refuge from the punishment apart from the time of its promise or the place of its promise; He is their refuge. This is from the emphasis of a thing by means of what resembles its opposite, meaning they are not escaping from it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 59:

Page 358
﴿And those cities — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed for their destruction an appointed time.﴾
After their delusion about the delay of the punishment was removed, and the notion of escaping it was refuted by explaining that this respite is a result of the mercy of Allah toward His creation, He set forth for them the example of the people of the earlier cities, from whom the punishment was delayed for a period, and then they were not saved from it in the end. So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence "Nay, for them is an appointed time" (bal lahum mawid).

The demonstrative "tilka" (those) refers to something presumed in the mind. The address particle (kaf al-khitab) attached to the demonstrative is not intended to denote an addressee; rather, it is a completion of the demonstrative, and it follows what suits the state of the one addressed by the indication, whether singular or plural. The Arabs know the dwellings of 'Ad, Thamud and Madyan, and they hear of the people of Lut and the people of Pharaoh, so these were as if present at the time of the indication.

Al-zulm (wrongdoing) here is shirk and the denial of the messengers. Al-muhlak, with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam, is a mimi verbal noun from (ahlaka), meaning: We made for our destroying them a specific time in Our knowledge; when it comes, destruction befalls them. This is the reading of the majority. Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, as a noun of time on the pattern mafil. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a fatha on the mim and a fatha on the lam, as a mimi verbal noun from halaka.

[p. 359]

**Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat al-Kahf, verse 60 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿And when Moses said to his young man: I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas, or I will journey on for a long period.﴾

When the story of the creation of Adam was mentioned, along with God's command to the angels to prostrate to him, and what befell Satan of arrogance and of pride in his origin, out of ignorance of the causes of excellence, obstinacy in refusing to acknowledge them, and envy regarding nobility and virtue, God set this as an example for the people of misguidance, the slaves of desire, arrogance and envy, [p. 359 continues]

and then followed that story with another story that serves as an example of its opposite. This is because the seeking of one who has excellence and perfection, to increase in them, and his striving to attain one who can bring him greater perfection, is an acknowledgment by the one who seeks of the superior person's excellence. In this there is a display of the contrast between the two characters, and an establishment of proof regarding the similarity and difference between the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers. Within this there is also instruction, and an elevation of the status of knowledge and guidance, and an education for the God-fearing.

Because this sūrah was revealed on account of what the polytheists asked, and what some People of the Book had suggested to them, concerning two stories, the story of the People of the Cave and the story of Dhū al-Qarnayn, and since the answer to the first story and what was appended to it has been completed, it was time to move on to the answer concerning the second story, so that this sūrah, which was revealed to explain the two stories, would conclude with it. Before this second story there was placed a story that resembles it in that it is a wandering through the earth in search of a beneficial good, namely the story of the journey of Moses, peace be upon him, to seek the meeting with one who possesses a knowledge that Moses did not have. In recounting this story there is an indirect allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the People of the Book, to the effect that it would have been more fitting for them to direct people to the reports of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and to a journey undertaken for the sake of acquiring knowledge and wisdom, rather than a journey undertaken for the sake of extending dominion and power.

So the clause ﴿And when Moses said﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And when We said to the angels﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], a conjunction of one story to another story. The implied sense is: "And mention when Moses said to his young man," i.e., mention that time and what took place in it. The supposition of the verb "mention" fits here, because in this story there is an admonition and a reminder, as in the story of the creation of Adam.

So (idh) is placed in the accusative as the object of the verb.

*Fatā* (young man) means a young male, and the female is *fatāh*. It is used figuratively for a follower and a servant, and it was discussed earlier at the words of God, Exalted, ﴿Your young man is seeking to seduce her﴾ [Yūsuf: 30], in Sūrat Yūsuf.

The *fatā* of Moses was his servant and follower. The annexation of "young man" to the pronoun of Moses is for the sense of specification, as one says "his servant." The *fatā* of Moses was Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn, from the tribe of Ephraim (Ifrāyim). It has been said that he was the son of Moses' sister. His original name was Hūshaʿ, and Moses called him Yūshaʿ when he sent him to spy out the land of Canaan. Perhaps this change of name was a gentle kindness toward him, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abū Hurayrah: "O Abū Hirr" (father of the kitten). In the Torah it is reported that Abraham's name was Abram, and when God commanded him with the characteristics of the natural disposition (fiṭrah), He called him Abraham.

Perhaps these changes in Hebrew convey meanings other than the meanings of the original names, and so it is like what the Prophet (ﷺ) did when he called Zayd al-Khayl "Zayd al-Khayr" (Zayd of goodness).

Yūshaʿ was one of the twelve men whom Moses, peace be upon him, sent to spy in the land of Canaan, in the regions of Aleppo and Hebron, to test the might of its people and the bounty of its land. They remained forty days on the reconnaissance. He was one of the two men who encouraged the Children of Israel to enter the land of Canaan, the two whom the Qur'an mentioned in the verse ﴿Two men from among those who feared, upon whom God had bestowed favor, said: Enter upon them through the gate, and when you enter it, you will surely be victorious﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 23].

Yūshaʿ was born around the year 1463 BCE, and he died around the year 1353 BCE, having lived one hundred and ten years. Moses, peace be upon him, had brought him near to himself and taken him as a disciple and servant. Such a relationship is described by terms such as *fatā* or *ghulām* (servant/boy) for its possessor. From this usage is the description of Imam Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Muṭarriz, the grammarian and philologist, as "the *ghulām* of Thaʿlab," because of his close association with Imam Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Shaybānī, known as Thaʿlab.

Yūshaʿ was also one of the two men to whom Moses, peace be upon him, entrusted the task of dividing the land among the tribes of the Children of Israel after Moses' death. God commanded Moses to appoint Yūshaʿ to direct the affairs of the Israelite nation after Moses' death. So Moses appointed him to this, and from that day he became a prophet (nabiyy). He managed the affairs of the nation for twenty-seven years after Moses. The Book of Joshua (Yūshaʿ) is the first of the books of the prophets after Moses, peace be upon him.

The story begins with the report of Moses' words, peace be upon him, which imply a firm resolve not to turn away from what he is engaged in, meaning not to occupy himself with anything else until he reaches the junction of the two seas. [p. 361]

This is a wondrous opening in the matter of brevity (ījāz), for his statement indicates that he was engaged in an action whose end is reaching a place, and thus it is known that this action is the traveling of a journey.

It also indicates that his young man regarded this journey as great and feared that hardship might overtake them in it, obstructing them from completing it; or it indicates that he was of such a state that he regarded it as great, because of his knowledge that it was a distant journey. Such is the nature of the causes of important matters. It also indicates that the place to which he was traveling was a place where he would find what he sought.

*Abraḥu* is the present tense of *baraḥa* (with a kasra on the rāʾ), meaning "to cease" or "to depart," and it was discussed earlier in Sūrat Yūsuf, peace be upon him. The expression *lā abraḥu* is used metaphorically to mean "I will not leave off" or "I will not refrain from traveling until I reach the junction of the two seas." It is also possible that the present tense of *baraḥa*, which is a defective verb (fiʿl nāqiṣ) and is not used in the defective form except with negation, has its predicate omitted by the context, so that the meaning is "I will not cease traveling." According to al-Raḍī, the omission of its predicate is rare.

The omission of mention of the purpose for which Moses, peace be upon him, traveled is because it will be mentioned later. This is an omission for brevity (ījāz) and for creating suspense (tashwīq), which has a great effect in the narration of the story, in that it removes it from the familiar mode of stories to a style of wondrous wisdoms and parables, fulfilling the right of the eloquence of inimitability (iʿjāz).

The detailed account of this story appears in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*, from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Dīnār and Yaʿlā ibn Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Moses, peace be upon him, stood up to deliver a sermon to the Children of Israel, and he was asked: Who is the most knowledgeable of people? He said: I am. So God rebuked him, since he had not referred knowledge to Him. God revealed to him: Yes, [there is one], Our servant al-Khiḍr, who is more knowledgeable than you. He said: Where is he? [God] said: At the junction of the two seas. Moses, peace be upon him, said: O Lord, make for me a sign by which I may know it. [God] said: Take a fish with you in a basket, and wherever you lose the fish, he is there. So he took a fish and put it in a basket, and he said to his young man, Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn: I will not burden you except that you inform me when the fish leaves you. [The young man] said: 'You have not burdened me greatly.' Then he set out, and he set out with his young man until, when they came to the rock, they laid down their heads and slept. The fish stirred in the basket, [p. 362]

and it came out of it and fell into the sea, taking its path in the sea as a tunnel. Moses was asleep, and his young man, who had not slept, said: I will not wake him. God held back the flow of the water from the fish, so that the water above it became like an arch. When Moses awoke, his companion forgot to tell him about the fish. They traveled the rest of that day and night, until the next day, when Moses, peace be upon him, said to his young man: Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours. [The narrator] said: Moses did not feel the fatigue until he had passed the place which God had commanded him to reach, meaning that God makes the means of obedience easy for His friends. So his young man said to him: ﴿Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish, and none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it; and it took its path into the sea, in wonder﴾ [al-Kahf: 63]. [The narrator] said: So it was a tunnel for the fish, and a wonder for Moses and his young man. Moses said: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾, and they retraced their steps, following their tracks. [The narrator] said: They went back tracing their footprints until they reached the rock, and there was a man covered with a garment. Moses greeted him with peace, and al-Khiḍr said: 'And how is there peace in your land?'" The hadith continues.

His words, "And how is there peace in your land?", are an interrogative of wonder. The *kāf* (your) is addressed to the one who greeted him. Al-Khiḍr thought that this place had no people whose greeting is peace, either because the place was uninhabited, or because it was inhabited by a people whose greeting is not peace.

God held back the flow of the water from the fish only so that it would be a visible sign for Moses, peace be upon him, and his young man, increasing the means of strengthening their certainty. And because the place was a setting for the manifestation of the miracles of the knowledge of prophethood, it was fitting that it be surrounded by what is beyond the ordinary custom, as an honoring of the guests of that place.

The junction of the two seas is not to be disputed as being a place in the land of Palestine. The more evident view is that it is the outlet of the River Jordan into the lake of Tiberias (Ṭabariyyah), for it is the great river that passes beside the land in which Moses, peace be upon him, and his people settled. Among the Israelites it was called the Sea of Galilee (Baḥr al-Jalīl). Moses, peace be upon him, reached it after a day and a night of travel on foot, so we know that it was not a very distant place. Moses wished to reach that place because God had revealed to him that he would find there the servant who was more knowledgeable than he, so He made it an appointed meeting place for him. [p. 363]

The meaning of this servant being more knowledgeable than Moses, peace be upon him, is that he knew sciences of dealing with people that God had not taught to Moses. Thus the difference in knowledge in this context is a difference in the branches of knowledge, and it is a relative difference.

Al-Khiḍr is the name of a righteous man. It has been said that he was a prophet from among the descendants of ʿĀbir ibn Shālikh ibn Arpakhshad ibn Sām. He is thus al-Khiḍr ibn Malkān ibn Fāligh ibn ʿĀbir, and so he would be a paternal cousin of Abraham's second ancestor. It has also been said that "al-Khiḍr" is his epithet (laqab), and as for his name, it is (Balyā), with a single letter *b*, or (Ilyā) with a hamzah and a *yāʾ*.

People agree that he was among the long-lived, but they differ on whether he has remained alive, and this disagreement is not based on accepted and well-known proofs. Rather, it rests on the sayings of some Ṣūfīs, which should not be relied upon, because of the abundance of symbolic language in their speech, and their confusion between the spiritual and material lives, and between sensory and visionary observations. They have made him the symbol of the esoteric sciences, as will come later.

Some scholars claimed that al-Khiḍr is (Jirjis, Georgius). It has been said that he is from the offspring of ʿĪsū ibn Isḥāq, and it has been said that he is a prophet who was sent after Shuʿayb.

As for (Jirjis), he is the one known by the name (Mār Jirjis, Saint George), and the Arabs call him Mār Sarjis, as in the book of Sībawayh. He was from the people of Palestine, born in Ramla in the second half of the third century after the birth of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and died in the year 303, and he is among the martyrs. This contradicts his being in the time of Moses, peace be upon him.

"Al-Khiḍr" is a title for him, meaning one characterized by greenness, which is a symbol of blessing. It has been said that he was given the title "Khiḍr" because whenever he sat upon the earth, the surroundings became green, meaning they turned green with vegetation from the effect of his blessing. In the *Encyclopaedia of Islam* there are mentioned speculations that attach the story of al-Khiḍr to tales, some of them Persian and some Roman, and the only motive for this is the mere resemblance in some circumstances of the stories. Such resemblance is not free of myths and tales, so one should not indulge in fancies beyond such things.

The established view is that the story of al-Khiḍr and Moses is of Jewish origin, but it is not recorded in the books of the Jews that are called the Torah or the Old Testament. Perhaps the absence of mention of it in those books is what led Nawf al-Bikālī to say that the Moses mentioned in these verses is other than Moses of the Children of Israel, as was reported in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*, and that Ibn ʿAbbās denied Nawf, and he cited the hadith mentioned above.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 60 (part 2 of 2):

The reason for mentioning this in the Qur'an was the question posed to the Messenger ﷺ by a group of the Jews, or by those whom the Jews had taught to put the question about it, and God the Exalted alluded to this in His saying ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85].

The Jews differed as to whether the companion of al-Khidr was Musa ibn 'Imran, the Messenger, and whether his servant (fata) was Yusha' ibn Nun. It was said: yes. This has been strengthened by what Ubayy ibn Ka'b related from the Prophet ﷺ. It was also said: he is another man named Musa ibn Mikha, or Minsah ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub. Some scholars of Islam claimed that al-Khidr met the Prophet ﷺ and was counted among his Companions, but that is an illusion and a pursuit of the imaginings of the storytellers (al-qassasin). Al-Khidr was named Balya ibn Malkan, or Iliya, or Ilyas, and it was said that al-Khidr is the Ilyas mentioned in Surah Ya Sin.

It is not correct that al-Khidr was from the Children of Israel, for it is not permissible that he be obligated by the law of Musa while Musa would approve of him acting in ways that his law does not permit. Rather, it is necessary that he be a prophet to whom a special revelation was given. Musa knew that he was from a nation to which Musa had not been sent. When Musa knew this from what God revealed to him, namely the saying: "Rather, a servant of Ours, al-Khidr, is more knowledgeable than you," as in the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it did not deter him from it what he saw of his actions that contradicted the law of the Torah, because he was upon a different law ("a nation on his own"). As for his presence in the land of the Children of Israel, it was either from wandering (siyaha) in worship, or God commanded him to be present at the place He had determined for meeting Musa, out of gentleness toward Musa, peace be upon him.

Page 365

The meaning of "or I will continue on" (aw amdiya) is "or I will walk" (aw asir). Al-mudi means going and traveling, and al-huqub, with two dammas, is a name for a long period of time, not limited in measure; its plural is ahqab.

"Amdi" is coordinated with "ablugh" by "aw" (or), so the conjoined clause becomes one of two ends of ceasing the journey, that is: either I will reach the place, or I will continue for a long time. Since Musa had no doubt about the existence of a place that is the meeting point of the two seas, and that his request would be fulfilled there, because he knew this by revelation from God the Exalted, it became necessary that the purpose of the particle of alternation be the emphasis of his continuing for a period in which reaching the meeting point of the two seas is certain. The meaning is: I will not cease until I reach the meeting point of the two seas, by a short journey or I will travel for long periods; indeed I am certainly reaching the meeting point of the two seas. It seems he intended by this to make his servant despair of attempting their return, as indicated by his later saying, "Indeed we have met with fatigue from this our journey."

Or he intended to sharpen the resolve of his servant, so that he would match him in soundness of determination until they would be of one united resolve.

[Page 366]

The *fa'* here is *fa' al-tafri'* (the *fa'* of consequence) and *fa' al-fasihah* (the eloquent *fa'*), because it reveals an omitted statement. The meaning is: they set off until they reached the meeting point of the two seas. The pronoun in "بينهما" refers to the two seas, meaning a place where the two seas meet. The construct "مجمع" is annexed to "بين" in a broadened (*tawassu'*) usage, since "بين" is a noun denoting a place lying between two things. Its basic function in the language is to serve as an adverb of time or place for a verb, but it may also be used simply to denote an intermediate place, either through annexation as here, as in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, the testimony between you...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106]. This is equivalent to annexing a verbal noun or an active participle to its object. It may also occur without annexation, in a broadened usage, as in His saying: ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], according to the reading of those who read "بَيْنُكم" with a *raf'* (nominative vowel).

The fish was the one Allah commanded Musa to take with him, so that it would be a sign to the place where al-Khidr was, as has already been mentioned in the context of the hadith. The forgetting in His saying ﴿or cause it to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] is discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of their forgetting is that they forgot to watch its condition: was it still alive in its basket at that time? When they lost it at that spot, they realised that the place where it was lost was the place appointed to them by that sign, so they would not exert themselves further in walking. Attributing the forgetting to both of them is literal, because Yusha' (Joshua), although he was the one entrusted with guarding the fish and so was responsible for watching it, was not the one who had set out for this purpose; Musa was the one intending this task, so its care and supervision were his concern. This indicates that the owner of a task or need, if he delegates it to another, should not neglect following up on it. Then Musa, peace be upon him, slept, while his young companion remained awake, and the fish moved about and made for itself a path in the sea.

*Al-sarab* means a tunnel, and *al-ittikhadh* means making. "سربا" is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) from "سبيله", with the *hal* meant as a comparison, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

When the two of them stand, musk wafts from them,
like the breeze of the east bringing the scent of clove.

The explanation of how it took the sea as a tunnel has already passed in the earlier hadith transmitted from Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

The object of "جاوزا" is omitted because it is known, meaning: they passed the meeting place of the two seas.

*Al-ghada'* is the midday meal, derived from the word *al-ghudwah* (morning), because it is eaten at the time of the morning. Its opposite is *al-'asha'* (the evening meal). *Al-nasab* means exhaustion.

[Page 367]

*Al-sakhrah* refers to a particular rock known to them, since they had sheltered by it during their journey, sitting upon it. It was at the meeting place of the two seas. It has been said that its location was beside a river called the River of Oil, because of the abundance of olive trees around it.

His saying "نسيت الحوت" means: I forgot to keep watch over it and to notice its absence, that is, it slipped into the sea.

His saying ﴿and none but Satan caused me to forget it, that I should mention it﴾ refers to a different forgetting from the first one. This is the forgetting of mentioning and reporting it.

Hafs, from 'Asim, read ﴿وما أنسانيهُ﴾ with the pronoun's *ḍamma* (u-vowel) according to the original form of the pronoun, and this is a dialect. The *kasra* (i-vowel) is more common, because the *kasra* after the *ya'* is lighter.

"أن أذكره" is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive substitution) from the pronoun in "أنسانيه", not from the fish. The meaning is: none but Satan caused me to forget mentioning it to you. So the *dhikr* here is the *dhikr* of the tongue, that is, speech.

The reason for restricting the attribution of this causing to forget to Satan is that what befell him, namely forgetting to inform Musa of that incident, is a forgetting not normally expected to occur in a short time, given the intensity of his concern for the matter forgotten and his great care to inform his prophet of it. Moreover, the forgotten matter was a marvel, the kind that ought not to be forgotten. It is thus established that Satan is grieved by the meeting of these two righteous servants and by the influence they have in spreading beneficial knowledge; he therefore diverts it away from them, even if only by delaying its occurrence, hoping that obstacles will arise.

His saying ﴿and it made its way into the sea﴾ is a conjunction over the clause "فإني نسيت الحوت", and it is the continuation of the speech of Musa's young companion. That is, it made its way into the sea, that is, it swam in the sea after having been dead for a long time.

His saying "عجبا" is a new (*mustanaf*) clause, and it belongs to the report of the young man's words, meaning: I marvel at it with a marvel. It is therefore in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) that comes as a substitute for its verb.
