Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 64–70 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 368]
﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they returned, retracing their footsteps.﴾ ﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and had taught knowledge from Our presence.﴾ ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [for] right guidance?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me.﴾ ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"﴾ ﴿He said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in [any] matter."﴾ ﴿He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I mention to you about it [an explanation]."﴾.

"He said, 'That is what...'" and so on is a response to his statement, and for this reason it is separated (from what precedes), as we have explained more than once.

The reference of "That" is to what the account of the youth contained concerning the losing of the fish. The meaning of it being what they were seeking is that it was a means to the thing sought, whereas the real object sought was meeting the righteous servant at the place where the fish was lost.

"Nabgh" is written in the Mushaf without a yā' at its end. It was said: the scribes intended to observe the state of pausing, because the better practice in pausing on a defective noun's yā' is to stop by omitting it. It was also said: they intended to draw attention to the fact that it was transmitted without it in this verse, and the Arabs incline toward lightness. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read it with the yā' omitted in pause and with it present in continuation. 'Asim, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read it with the yā' omitted both in continuation and in pause. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read it with the yā' present in both states. The nūn is the nūn of the speaker who is joined with another, i.e., "what I and you seek," and both of them seek to meet the righteous servant.

"Irtidad" is the reflexive form (muta'wi') of "radd," as if a repeller had repelled them; what actually turned them back was their own intention. That is, they returned along the tracks of their journey, i.e., they went back along the path by which they had come.

[Page 369]
"Qasas" is the verbal noun of "qassa al-athar," when one aims to follow a trace closely so as not to miss the original path.

The "servant" is al-Khidr, and he is described as being "from among the servants of Allah" as an honour for him, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

The text departed from the idiom of the genitive construction (idafah) to indefiniteness and a descriptive phrase, because nothing preceding required his definition, and to indicate that this strange and great state mentioned in his story is only one of the states of many servants of Allah, and there is none of them but has a known station.

The granting of mercy may mean that he was made one who is shown mercy, by Allah being gentle with him in his circumstances; or it may mean that We made him a cause of mercy, by directing him in a manner that brings about general mercy. "Knowledge from the presence of Allah" is information conveyed by way of revelation.

"'Inda" and "ladun" both are originally names of a near place, and both are used figuratively to denote that what is ascribed to them is specific to the thing they qualify.

"Min" is for origin, meaning: We gave him mercy that issued from a place of nearness, i.e., of honour, namely the nearness of distinction through being attributed to Allah; and knowledge that also issued from Him. This is because what he was given of guardianship or prophethood is a rare mercy, or what he was given of knowledge is rare; thus both are things that are stored with Allah in the place of honourable nearness to Him, and are given only to the chosen.

The variation between "min 'indina" and "min ladunna" is for stylistic variety, to avoid repeating the same word. The sentence "Moses said to him" begins a dialogue, so it is a fresh, initiating resumption, and for this reason the speech is not introduced by "qala" without a conjunction.

The interrogative in His saying "Shall I follow you?" is used for asking permission, by the evidence that it asks about the action of the questioner himself. "Following" is metaphorical for accompaniment, as in His saying ﴿They follow only assumption﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

[Page 370]
"'Ala" is used in the sense of condition, since it is a figurative elevation: following is treated as if it were placed above teaching, because of the close connection between the two. So the formula "do such-and-such on condition of such-and-such" is among the expressions of obligation and contract.

From the verse it is derived that it is permissible to contract for the teaching of the Qur'an and knowledge, as in the hadith of the marriage of the woman who offered herself to the Prophet ﷺ, and he did not accept her, so he married her to the man who desired her on condition that he teach her what he had of the Qur'an.

In it there is also that it is an obligation that must be fulfilled, and from the ruling on the binding nature of obligations it follows that custom in such matters takes the place of explicit stipulation, so the one who has set himself up for teaching must deal with the students in accordance with what the custom of their regions has established.

'Iyad mentions, in the chapter on the description of Malik's gathering for knowledge in the book al-Madarik, that a Khurasani man came from Khurasan to Madinah to hear from Malik, and he found people presenting (their narrations) to him while he listened, and they did not hear a recitation from him to them. So he asked him to recite to them, but Malik refused. The Khurasani then summoned the judge of Madinah and said: "I have come from Khurasan, and we do not accept the method of presentation, and Malik refuses to recite to us." The judge then ruled against Malik that he should recite to him. It was said to Malik: "Did the judge hit the truth?" He said: "Yes."

In it there is also an indication that the right of the teacher over the student is that he be followed and emulated.

"Rushdan" is in the accusative as the object of "tu'allimani," meaning that by which there is guidance, i.e., goodness.

This knowledge which Moses asked to learn is of the beneficial knowledge that does not concern legislation for the Israelite community, for Moses was self-sufficient in legislative knowledge except through revelation from Allah directly to him, since that is why he was sent; and what lies beyond that is not required by his mission. "The Prophet ﷺ said concerning the people whom he found pollinating the palms: 'You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life'"; and on the Day of Badr he returned "to the opinion of al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith that the position where the Muslim army first camped at Badr was not the most suitable for war."

[Page 371]
Moses only desired to know something of the knowledge which Allah had specifically given to al-Khidr, because the increase of beneficial knowledge is of goodness, and Allah the Exalted has said, instructing His Prophet, ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. This knowledge that al-Khidr was given is a specific kind of governance, not general, concerned with particular persons, for the sake of bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm according to what the events and circumstances make available, not according to what suits the general public interest. Perhaps Allah facilitated it for the benefit of particular people from Him, just as He made Muhammad ﷺ a mercy for all mankind. From here it differs from the general legislative governance. Its parallel is the Prophet's ﷺ knowledge of the states of some of the polytheists and hypocrites, and his certainty that those polytheists would not believe, yet he would constantly call them to faith; and his certainty that those hypocrites were not believers, yet he treated them as believers. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman used to know them by their identities through the Prophet's ﷺ informing him about them.

The majority read "rushdan" with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the ra' and a fatha on the shin, like the two preceding readings; and both are dialectal forms, as was previously mentioned.

The sentence "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me" is emphasized by the particle "inna" and the particle "lan," to confirm its content, from the expectation of Moses's distress in accepting what he would show him; for he knew that actions would proceed from him whose outward appearance was reprehensible while their inner reality was good. It was preferred that it come in the form of a circumstantial clause, rather than being separated from the first clause and placed as a cause, even though causation is the intended meaning, in order to alert that its content is an inseparable cause of the content of the preceding clause, since it is a circumstance of the subject in the clause before it.

"Kayfa" is an interrogative of denial, meaning: "And you cannot have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge."

"Khubr," with a damma on the kha' and sukun on the ba', means knowledge. It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the attribution of encompassing in His saying "that which you do not encompass," i.e., encompassing in terms of knowledge.

"Ihatah" (encompassing) is metaphorical for mastery, likening the strength of the attribute's hold to the firm hold of an enclosing body upon what it encloses.

His saying ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, patient﴾ is more eloquent in establishing patience than saying "I will be patient," because it indicates the occurrence of an evident patience for his companion and follower. It is clear that the object of patience here is patience over what is of a nature to provoke distress or impatience: from the fatigue of following, from witnessing what one's perception cannot bear, and from awaiting the explanation of causes, reasons and purposes.

Since this complete patience requires obedience to the one who commands in what he commands, he joined to it what conveys obedience, to emphasize his attainment of the most perfect states of a seeker of knowledge.

Thus the clause ﴿and I will not disobey you in [any] matter﴾ is coordinated with the clause "you will find me," or it is the coordination of a verb onto a derived noun, coordinated onto "patient," and so it is interpreted as a verbal noun: "and not disobeying." In this is evidence that the most important quality of a seeker of knowledge is patience and obedience to the teacher.

In his affirming this by conditioning it on Allah's will, seeking His help and desiring that ease be preceded, out of courtesy with Allah, there is an indication that patience and obedience from a student who already possesses some knowledge are more difficult than the patience and obedience of a plain, unlearned student. This is because the emptiness of his mind from knowledge does not prevent him from witnessing marvels, since there is in his mind no store of knowledge that opposes accepting them. But the student who has a share of knowledge and comes seeking perfection in its sciences, when there appears to him from his teacher's knowledge something that contradicts what is established in his own learning, immediately moves to objection and dispute, and this may stir aversion between him and his teacher. To avoid this, al-Khidr feared that Moses would treat him in this way, so he said to him, ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me, and how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ Thereupon Moses affirmed to him that he would be patient and obey his command when commanded. Moses's commitment to this was based on his trust in the infallibility of the one he followed, since Allah had informed him that He had given him knowledge.

The "fa" in His saying ﴿So if you follow me﴾ is a consequence of Moses's promise that he would find him patient; upon this he based the prohibition against asking about anything he witnessed of his actions until he himself explained it from his own accord.

Ibn 'Ashur emphasized the prohibition with the particle of emphasis, to ensure the student achieves the most complete condition with the teacher, because the question may coincide with the time when the one questioned is busy completing his work, so that his soul becomes constricted. Thus the answer to it may come without any eagerness of the soul, while perhaps some anxiety mixes with it, so the answer is not fully satisfying. Al-Khadir therefore wanted to take upon himself the explanation of his deeds at the time he sees fit, so that the explanation would be more expansive and the attention more delightful, and thus the connection between the two companions would increase.

"Remembrance" here is remembrance by the tongue, which was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40] in Surat al-Baqarah. I mean by it the explanation of the causes and directions, and the uncovering of obscure matters.

"Iḥdath al-dhikr" (producing the remembrance) means originating it and bringing it forth, as in the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"We produced for its Creator thanks"

Nafi' recited ﴿fa-lā tas'alannī﴾ with a hamzah, with a fatḥah on the lam, and a shaddah on the nun, taking it as the imperfect of (sa'ala) with the hamzah, joined to the light nun of emphasis assimilated into the nun of protection, and with the first person ya' retained.

Ibn 'Amir recited the same, but with the first person ya' omitted. The rest recited ﴿tas'alnī﴾ with the hamzah, a sukun on the lam, and a light nun, and they retained the first person ya'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 71:

﴿So they set out, until when they boarded the ship, he damaged it. [Musa] said: "Have you damaged it in order to drown its people? You have certainly done a dreadful thing."﴾ That is, after that exchange, the two of them set out. Al-intilaq (setting out) means going away and walking; it is derived from al-itlaq, which is the opposite of restriction (al-taqyid), because when a beast's tether is untied it walks. Its root is thus the intransitive form (mutawi') of atlaqahu (he released it).

Hatta (until) marks the endpoint of the setting out, meaning: up to the point where they boarded the ship.

Hatta here is ibtida'iyyah (introducing a new clause), and the speech contains an ellipsis indicated by His words ﴿when they boarded the ship﴾. The underlying sense is: until they hired a ship and boarded it; then, when they had boarded the ship, he damaged it.

The definiteness of "the ship" (al-safinah) is the definiteness of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni), like the definiteness in His words ﴿and I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13].

Idha (when) is a adverb of past time here, and it is not implying the meaning of a conditional. This timing indicates that he undertook damaging the ship at the moment they boarded it, and this points to the fact that boarding it was for the sake of damaging it, since the intended object is pursued by the one who intends it, for he has already planned it and deliberated over it beforehand.

The structure of the speech is built on placing the adverbial phrase before its governing verb, to indicate that the damaging took place immediately upon boarding the ship, since fronting the adverb gives it emphasis, and so it shows that the moment of boarding is intended, for the act to be carried out in it.

Rukub (boarding) is construed with the meaning of entering (dukhul), since it is figurative boarding; therefore it is followed by the locative particle fi (in), like His words ﴿and he said: "Board in it"﴾ [Hud: 41], rather than the construction in His words ﴿and horses, mules and donkeys, that you may ride them﴾ [al-Nahl: 8]. This was already discussed in Surat Hud.

Kharq (damaging) means puncturing and splitting, and it is the opposite of mending (iltiam).

The interrogative in ﴿Have you damaged it﴾ expresses denial (inkar), and the object of the denial is the reason stated in ﴿in order to drown its people﴾, because the reason is inseparable from the act being questioned. Accordingly, Musa, peace be upon him, was directed to object to this outwardly disapproved act, and the emphasis of his denial is in His words ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing (shay'an imra)﴾.

Imr, with a kasra on the hamzah, means the great and appalling; it is said: amira (kafarihа) imran, when it became abundant in its kind. For this reason al-Raghib explained it as munkar (reprehensible). The situation indicates something harmful, and the position of the prophets in changing what is reprehensible is one of severity and frankness. He did not call it "nukr" (a denounced thing) as in the verse after it, because the action that al-Khidr performed was a means toward drowning, and drowning had not actually occurred.

Al-Jumhur read li-tughriqa with a feminine second-person verb (addressed as "you"), and Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read li-yaghraqa with a fatha-marked yā' and the raf' of "ahluha" (its people), attributing the verb of drowning to the people.

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 72:

[376]
﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir), and an indirect rebuke for not fulfilling what he had committed himself to. That is: Do you acknowledge that I said to you, "You will not be able to have patience with me"?

And "ma'iya" (with me) is an adverbial complement (zarf) related to "tastati'" (you are able). The inability to have patience that is negated is the one that occurs in his company, because he (Musa) sees strange matters whose interpretation he does not grasp.

The object of the verb of saying has been omitted, treating it as if it were intransitive (tanzilan lahu manzilat al-lazim). That is: Did there not occur from me a statement in which I addressed you with the inability (to be patient)?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 73:

﴿He said, "Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot, and do not overburden me in my affair with difficulty."﴾ Moses offered an excuse on the ground of forgetfulness, for he had forgotten his commitment because of what had overcome his mind from witnessing something he disapproved of.

The prohibition (al-nahy) is used here in the sense of seeking kindness (al-ta'attuf), and requesting that he not be held accountable. This is because he might hold him accountable for the forgetting in the manner of one who is not fit to be a companion, due to the danger arising from forgetfulness. Thus al-hazamah (prudence) is avoiding the company of one who is prone to forgetfulness. For this reason, Moses' speech was built upon a request that he not be held accountable for the forgetting, and was not built upon an excuse by forgetfulness, as though he saw himself as deserving of being held accountable. So it was a speech of wonderful weave in offering an excuse.

Al-mu'akhadhah (holding accountable) is a form of mufa'alah from al-akhdh (taking), and here it is for emphasis, since it is from one side only, like the saying of the Most High: ﴿And if Allah were to hold mankind accountable for their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Nahl: 61].

And "ma" (what) is a verbal-masdar particle, meaning: "Do not hold me accountable for my forgetting."

Page 377
Al-irhaq (overburdening) is the transitive form of rahiqa, when it overtakes and reaches, meaning: "Do not overtake me with difficulty." Here it is a metaphor for treatment with severity.
Al-irhaq is used figuratively for treatment and confrontation.

Al-'usr (difficulty) is hardship and the opposite of ease (al-yusr). The intended meaning here is the difficulty of treatment, that is, not being lenient with him regarding what he did, so he asks him for overlooking and pardon.

Al-amr (affair) is the matter or state of affairs.

The "min" (from) may be initial (ibtida'iyyah), so that what is meant by "his affair" is his forgetting, meaning: "Do not make my forgetting the cause of overburdening me with difficulty." It may also be explanatory (bayaniyyah), so that what is meant by "his affair" is his matter with him, meaning: "Do not make my matter with you one in which you overburden me with difficulty."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 74:

﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him. [Musa] said: "Have you killed a pure soul without it having killed anyone? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ The consequence expressed by His saying ﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy﴾ indicates that Musa's apology was accepted by al-Khadir, and that they set out together as companions.

The construction of His saying ﴿until, when they met a boy﴾ is the same as His saying ﴿until, when they boarded the ship﴾ [al-Kahf: 71].

His saying "he killed him" is a sequel to the act of "they met," emphasizing the immediacy implied by the fronting of the adverbial phrase. Thus the hastening to kill the boy upon meeting him was swifter than the hastening to damage the ship upon boarding it.

Musa's objection to this act follows the same pattern as his objection to the damaging of the ship, except that he described this act as ﴿nukr﴾ (terrible), which is with two dammas: that which reason rejects and finds repugnant. It is thus more severe than the ﴿imr﴾ (grave matter), because this is an actual corruption, whereas the other was a means leading to corruption, as has been previously explained. He described the soul as ﴿zakiyya﴾ (pure) because it was the soul of a boy who had not reached puberty, so he had not committed any sin; therefore he was pure and clean. And ﴿al-zaka'﴾ (purity) means increase in goodness.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ruways from Ya'qub read ﴿zakiyya﴾ with an alif after the zay, as an active participle from zaka. The rest read ﴿zakiyya﴾ (with a shaddah on the ya'), and both have the same meaning.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the nun in His saying ﴿nukran﴾ is the half of the Qur'an, i.e., the half of its letters. It has previously been mentioned that this contradicts the view of the majority, that the half of the Qur'an is the letter ta' in His exalted saying ﴿and let him be gentle﴾ [al-Kahf: 19] in this surah.

[Page 5]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surah al-Kahf

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me?"﴾ ﴿[Musa] said, "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion. You have indeed received an excuse from me."﴾

The reply of al-Khidr here follows the pattern of his earlier reply, except that he added the word (لَكَ, "to you") to what is related in the verse. This is an explicit statement of the object of the verb of saying. Since the one addressed was known from the context of the address, stating the object of the verb of saying confirms that the saying occurred, establishes it, and strengthens it. The reason for this is that [Musa] had neglected to act upon it.

The lam in his words (لَكَ) is the lam of tabligh (the lam of conveying, "lam al-tabligh"), which enters upon the noun or pronoun of the listener to a saying or what is similar to it, as in: "I said to him" (قُلْتُ لَهُ), "I permitted him" (أَذِنْتُ لَهُ), and "I explained to him" (فَسَّرْتُ لَهُ). This happens when the one addressed is known from the context, so mentioning the lam serves to add strength to the speech and to convey it to the listener. For this reason it is called the lam of tabligh. Do you not see that the lam was not needed in his first reply: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me?﴾ (Al-Kahf: 72)? So the affirmation and the rebuke, together with the mention of the lam that transmits the saying, were stronger and more forceful.

Here Musa did not offer the excuse of forgetfulness. Either because he had not forgotten, but he preferred to change a great wrong, which is the killing of a soul without cause, over the duty of keeping a commitment; or because he had forgotten, and he turned away from offering forgetfulness as an excuse because repeating that excuse would be shameful.

On both possibilities, he hastened to a condition that would reassure his companion's soul: that if he returned to asking about what his companion did not want, then his companion would be entitled not to keep him as a companion after that.

In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The first [objection] from Musa was forgetfulness, the second was a condition, and the third..." Thus the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) allow both of the two possibilities mentioned.

Musa was fair when he gave his companion the excuse for not keeping him as a companion in the third instance, to spare him embarrassment.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (لَدُنِّي) with a shadda on the nun. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ)," meaning that it has a specific chain of transmission reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), as was mentioned in the sixth of the introductory principles of this tafsir.

Nafi', Abu Bakr, and Abu Ja'far read (مِن لَدُنِي) without a shadda on the nun, on the basis that the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya, "nun al-wiqaya") was omitted from it for lightness, because (لَدُنْ) is heavier than (عَنْ) and (مِنْ), so lightening it was acceptable more than those two.

The meaning of ﴿you have indeed received an excuse from me﴾ is: you have indeed reached the excuse from my side. The verb (بَلَغْتَ, "you have reached") is used metaphorically for a meaning of (being decided and fixed), because its causes are present, by likening the excuse for ending the companionship to a place where the traveller arrives, in the manner of the metaphor by implication (al-makniyya).

He attributed reaching to it by imaginative representation (takhyil), or he used "reaching" metaphorically for the certainty of something occurring after delay.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 77:

Page 7
﴿So they went on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to entertain them. Then they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it up straight. [Moses] said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ The arrangement of His saying ﴿So they went on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾ is like the arrangement of its two preceding counterparts.

Al-istit'am (requesting food) means asking for food. The position of the clause "they asked its people for food" is like the position of the clause "he tore it" and the clause "so he killed him"; it is the complement of "idha" (when). The explicit repetition of the word "its people" instead of using a pronoun, saying "they asked them for food," serves to add emphasis, as a censure of them for their baseness, since they refused to entertain them. That is baseness, because hospitality was widespread among the nations from the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and it is one of the customary forms of generosity among people, carried out by whoever is designated for it from among those who pass by, and who asks them for hospitality, or by the noble men of the tribe who prepare themselves for it. So the refusal of all the people of a town to host them is baseness on the part of that town.

Al-Safadi raised a question to Shaykh Taqi al-Din al-Subki, in verses, about the subtle point of this explicit repetition. Al-Subki answered him with a long reply, both in prose and in verse, which is not convincing. Al-Alusi mentioned both of them.

The verse is evidence for the permissibility of a traveler requesting food, since it is the law of those before us, which the Qur'an related and against which no abrogating text has come.

Moses' rebuke of al-Khidr, for not taking a wage from the people of the town for setting up the wall, indicates that he intended to match their denial of the right of hospitality with their denial of the repair of the wall in their town.

Page 8
The verse also establishes the prescribed nature of hosting a traveler when he lodges with someone from the quarter or the town.

In the hadith of the Muwatta', the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest. His gift (jaizah) is one day and night (i.e., he should treat him generously and go to great lengths in his kindness), and his hospitality (diyafah) is three days (i.e., feeding and lodging with what is available, without excessive formality as is done on the first night). Whatever is beyond that is charity." The jurists differed about its obligation. The majority said: hospitality is among the noble characteristics, it is recommended and not obligatory. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i. Sahnun said: hospitality is incumbent upon the people of villages and quarters, and it was attributed to Malik. Sahnun said: as for the settled areas, the inn is where travelers stay. Al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam from the Malikis said: hospitality is a right upon the people of settled areas and the desert dwellers. Al-Layth and Ahmad said: hospitality is obligatory for one day and night.

It is said: "dayyafahu" and "adafahu," when one undertakes his hospitality. So the one who hosts is "mudayyif" with the doubled letter, and "mudif" without it. The one who seeks hospitality is "da'if" or "mutadayyif." It is said: "diftuhu" and "tadayyaftuhu," when one lodges with him and inclines towards him.

Al-jidar: the built wall.

The meaning of "yurid an yanqadda" is that it was on the verge of collapsing, i.e., falling down; that is, it was almost falling. This happened by it leaning. He expressed its being on the verge of collapse by the will to collapse, in the manner of explicit figurative metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah tab'iyyah), by likening the nearness of its collapse to the will of one who has intellect to do something, so that he is about to do it when he wills it.

Because will is the self's seeking the occurrence of something and the inclination of the heart towards it.

The setting up of the wall is the levelling of its lean. Its setting up was by a deed contrary to custom, in that he gestured to it with his hand, like one who levels a soft thing, as reported in some of the traditions.

Page 9
Moses' saying "﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾" is a rebuke, meaning: it was within your capacity to make a wage for yourself for setting up the wall, which you would take from those among the town's people who own it, and not set it up for free, because they did not fulfil the right of hospitality, and we are in need of what we spend on ourselves. In it is an indication that the expenses of the followers are upon the one followed.

This rebuke implies a question about the reason for leaving the negotiation of a fee for setting up the wall when there was need for the wage. It is not a rebuke merely for setting it up for free, because that is an act of goodness, and is not blameworthy.

Al-Jumhur read "la-ittakhadhta" with a hamzat al-wasl after the lam and with a doubled ta' (tashdid), as the past tense of (ittakhadha). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "latakhidhta" without a hamzah, as the past tense of (takhidha), which begins with a ta', i.e., it is from the pattern of (ʿalima).

[Page 10]

The referent of the word "this" (*hadha*) is understood in the mind. It results from Musa's condition that he made on himself: if he asks him about anything after his second question, the companionship between them ends. The meaning is: "What has now occurred is the parting between us," just as one says, "The condition is more binding on you, or for you." It is often the case that the referent is understood in the mind, as in His saying, ﴿That is the Last Abode﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. The idafa (genitive construction) of *firaq* ("parting") to *baynī* ("between me") is an idafa of a described noun to its description. The original form is *firaqun baynī*, meaning "a parting that has taken place between us." Alternatively, it is an idafa of a verbal noun that governs an adverbial complement to its object, as a verbal noun is annexed to its object. The departure of *bayn* from its adverbial usage has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿Then when they reached the junction of the two seas﴾ [al-Kahf: 61]. The clause *sa-unabbi'uka* ("I will inform you") is a resumptive clause of explanation (*isti'naf bayani*). It serves as an answer to a question that arises in the mind of Musa, peace be upon him, concerning the reasons for the actions that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, performed. Musa asked him about them, for he had promised him that he would give him a mention of what he would do.

*Ta'wil* (interpretation, explanation) is the explanation of something that is not clear. It is derived from *awwal*, which means "return." It likens the attainment of meaning through effort to returning to a place after traveling toward it. This was discussed in the first introduction of this tafsir, and also at His saying, ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge say﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran.

In the relative clause of the relative pronoun in His saying, ﴿what you could not bear with patience﴾, there is an allusion [Page 11] to blame for haste and for lack of patience until the mention is given to him, in accordance with what he promised him in His saying, ﴿So do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you﴾ [al-Kahf: 70].

*Al-masakin* ("the poor") here means those with little wealth who earn their livelihood through their own exertion, and for whom pity is felt because they toil their whole lives to obtain their sustenance. The intended meaning is not that they are in the most extreme poverty, as in His saying, ﴿The alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60]. Rather, what is meant by calling them "poor" is that pity is felt for them, as al-Hariri said in the forty-first *maqama*: "(... Pitiful is the son of Adam, and what a pitiful one he is!)."

The people of this ship were laborers who hired out their ship for carrying loads or for fishing.

The meaning of ﴿there was behind them a king﴾ is: he was the king of their land, lying in wait for them and for people like them, seizing every ship he found by force, that is, without compensation. This was for transporting construction materials or similar things that the king used for his own interests and desires, just as the Pharaohs used to compel people to labor in building the pyramids.

Had that been for the general benefit of the community, the compulsion would have been permissible according to each person's circumstances of need, because that is a communal obligation (*fard kifaya*) to the extent of the need and after it has been fulfilled.

*Wara'* ("behind") is the name of the direction that is behind the back of the one to whom that name is annexed. It is the opposite of *amama* and *quddama* ("in front").

The word *al-wara'* is used metaphorically for the state of one thing following another, for the state of persistently demanding something from something else by right, and for the state of a thing that will come soon. All of this is a likeness to what is behind a thing that will soon reach it, as in His saying, ﴿Hell is behind them﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] in Surat al-Jathiyah.

[Page 12] Labid said:

*Is it not that, behind me, my death has delayed, [and I am like] a staff on which the fingers bend?*

Some exegetes interpreted *wara'hum malik* ("behind them a king") to mean *amamahum malik* ("in front of them a king"). Hence some lexicographers thought that *wara'* is one of the words that have opposite meanings. Al-Farra' rejected this and said: "It is not permissible to say of what is in front of you that it is behind you. It is only permissible in the expressions of times of night. You say, *Wara'aka bardun shadid* ("behind you is intense cold") and *Bayna yadayka bardun shadid* ("in front of you is intense cold"). He means that this is figurative." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is not one of the opposites, as some lexicographers claimed."

The meaning of *kulla safina* ("every ship") is "every sound ship," as indicated by His saying, ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾. Scholars have mentioned, in identifying this king and the reason for his seizing ships, stories and opinions, none of which has been established with certainty, and no purpose relating to the lesson depends on them.

The clause ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾ is a consequence of each of the two clauses ﴿so it belonged to the poor﴾ and ﴿there was behind them a king﴾. Thus, according to the surface structure, it should have come after both clauses. But it was placed first, contrary to what the surface structure requires, to express concern and attention to the will to damage the ship. The act, whose outward appearance is objectionable but whose reality is good, is placed first to increase Musa's eagerness to learn its interpretation. For the fact that the ship belonged to the poor increases the hearer's surprise at the act of breaking it. The meaning is: "I wished to damage it, and I have done so." He did not say "I damaged it" in order to show that his act was done deliberately and after reflection. The word *irada* ("wish") is sometimes also used for intention. In *Lisan al-Arab*, this usage is attributed to Sibawayh.

Al-Khidr's disposal of the ship's affair was a disposal guided by the consideration of a particular benefit, by permission from Allah to act in the interests of the weak, since al-Khidr either knew the king's condition or Allah had informed him of his existence at that time. Al-Khidr's action took the place of a person's action with his own property, destroying part of it to preserve the remainder. Thus his outward action was corruption, but in reality it was correction, because it involved committing the lesser of two harms.

This is a hidden matter that none knew except al-Khidr. Therefore Musa rejected it.

As for his action concerning the killing of the boy, it was an action by revelation from Allah, aimed at cutting off a specific corruption that Allah knew and had informed al-Khidr of through revelation. Thus it does not belong to the station of legislation. Allah knew from the constitution of the boy's intellect and thinking that his intellect was aberrant and his thinking deviant, shaped by ordinary causes of distorted disposition and deficient perception. These are signs that lead that kind of soul and its owner to grow up as a tyrant and an unbeliever. Allah willed kindness to his parents by preserving their faith and protecting the world from this tyrant, a kindness that Allah willed as a miracle beyond the ordinary course, in accordance with the requirement of His prior knowledge. In this there is a benefit to the religion by preserving its followers from unbelief. It is a particular benefit that includes the preservation of religion, and a general benefit because it is a right of Allah, Exalted, and so it is like the ruling concerning the killing of an apostate.

*Zakah* means "purity," in observance of Musa's words, ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul?﴾ [al-Kahf: 74]. *Ruhm*, with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a sukun on the *ha'*, is like *kuthr* for *kathrah* ("abundance").

*Al-khashyah* ("fear") is the expectation of that happening if it were not forestalled by killing him.

The two plural pronouns in His saying, ﴿So we feared﴾ and His saying, ﴿So we wished﴾ refer to a single speaker, to show that he shares the act with others. This usage is from humility, not from self-exaltation, because the context is one of informing that Allah made him aware of this and commanded him. Humility was therefore appropriate, so he said, ﴿So we feared … so we wished.﴾ He did not say the same when he said, ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, because the cause of damaging the ship was his knowledge of the one who had knowledge of the condition of those regions. This was discussed earlier at His saying, [Page 14] ﴿He said: "Allah forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property; indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."﴾ [Yusuf: 79] in Surat Yusuf.

The majority read *an yubaddilahuma* with a *fatha* on the *ba'* and a shaddah on the *dal*, from *tabdil* ("replacement"). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *dal*, from *ibdal* ("substitution"). As for the wall, al-Khidr acted concerning its affair by the will of Allah to show kindness to the two orphans as a reward for their father's righteousness, since Allah knew that their father was concerned about their livelihood after him. He had deposited money under the wall. Perhaps he had asked Allah to inspire his two sons, when they reached maturity, to search for the place where the treasure was buried under the wall, either deliberately or by chance. If the wall had collapsed before they reached maturity, hands would have reached that place by digging and the like, and someone would have stumbled upon it. That too would be a kindness beyond the ordinary course. The will in the story of the wall was attributed to Allah, Exalted, and not to the two previous stories, because in those two cases the work was of a kind that anyone who was aware of its secret would strive to do, since they involved averting corruption from people. By contrast, the story of the wall is a favor from Allah to the father of the two boys.

His saying, ﴿a mercy from your Lord; and I did not do it of my own accord﴾, is an explicit statement that removes Musa's objection to these actions by showing that they were mercy and benefit, so there is no objection to them after understanding their interpretation.

He then added that he did it by revelation from Allah, because when he said, ﴿I did not do it of my own accord,﴾ Musa understood that it was by command from Allah, Exalted. This is because a prophet acts either by ijtihad (independent reasoning) or by revelation. So when he denied that his action was from his own command, it became certain that it was from the command of Allah, Exalted. He chose to deny that his action came from his own command instead of saying, "I did it by the command of my Lord," in order to complete the removal of Musa's bewilderment and objection. For when Musa objected to his three actions, he was supporting his objection with what implies that al-Khidr had acted from error.

*Rahmatan* ("as a mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). Thus it is governed by each of *aradtu* ("I wished"), *aradna* ("we wished"), and *arada rabbuka* ("your Lord wished"). The clause ﴿That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾ is a summary (*fadhlaka*) of the clauses before it, beginning from His saying, ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to the poor﴾. The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to what was mentioned in the previous speech, and it is a summary of the intended meaning, like the teacher's concluding recapitulation at the end of his lesson.

*Tasti'* is the imperfect of *istata'a* ("was able") in the sense of *istaṭa'a*. The *ta'* of the *istif'al* form was dropped for lightness, because it is close to the point of articulation of the *ta'* (*ṭa'*). The variation between this and His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾, is for stylistic variety, to avoid repeating the same word when a synonym exists. The first and more commonly used of the two was mentioned first, and the second was expressed with the lighter verb form, because lightness is more appropriate to it, since repeating *tasta'* would produce heaviness.

The first relative pronoun, occurring in His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾, was emphasized to reinforce the allusion to blame for lack of patience.

Know that the story of Musa and al-Khidr has been taken as a foundation by groups among the Islamic sects, on which they built false principles.

The first of what they established from it is that al-Khidr was not a prophet but only a righteous servant, that the knowledge he was given was not revelation but inspiration (*ilham*), that his actions in existing things are a basis for proving esoteric sciences, and that Allah granted al-Khidr life until the end of the world in order that he might be a source for receiving the esoteric sciences, and that he appears to people of the highest ranks among the saints, benefiting them with his knowledge to the extent that they are fit to receive it.

All of this is a likeness to what is behind a thing that will soon reach it, as in His saying, ﴿Hell is behind them﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] in Surat al-Jathiyah.

[Page 12] Labid said:

*Is it not that, behind me, my death has delayed, [and I am like] a staff on which the fingers bend?*

Some exegetes interpreted *wara'hum malik* ("behind them a king") to mean *amamahum malik* ("in front of them a king"). Hence some lexicographers thought that *wara'* is one of the words that have opposite meanings. Al-Farra' rejected this and said: "It is not permissible to say of what is in front of you that it is behind you. It is only permissible in the expressions of times of night. You say, *Wara'aka bardun shadid* ("behind you is intense cold") and *Bayna yadayka bardun shadid* ("in front of you is intense cold"). He means that this is figurative." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is not one of the opposites, as some lexicographers claimed."

The meaning of *kulla safina* ("every ship") is "every sound ship," as indicated by His saying, ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾. Scholars have mentioned, in identifying this king and the reason for his seizing ships, stories and opinions, none of which has been established with certainty, and no purpose relating to the lesson depends on them.

The clause ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾ is a consequence of each of the two clauses ﴿so it belonged to the poor﴾ and ﴿there was behind them a king﴾. Thus, according to the surface structure, it should have come after both clauses. But it was placed first, contrary to what the surface structure requires, to express concern and attention to the will to damage the ship. The act, whose outward appearance is objectionable but whose reality is good, is placed first to increase Musa's eagerness to learn its interpretation. For the fact that the ship belonged to the poor increases the hearer's surprise at the act of breaking it. The meaning is: "I wished to damage it, and I have done so." He did not say "I damaged it" in order to show that his act was done deliberately and after reflection. The word *irada* ("wish") is sometimes also used for intention. In *Lisan al-Arab*, this usage is attributed to Sibawayh.

Al-Khidr's disposal of the ship's affair was a disposal guided by the consideration of a particular benefit, by permission from Allah to act in the interests of the weak, since al-Khidr either knew the king's condition or Allah had informed him of his existence at that time. Al-Khidr's action took the place of a person's action with his own property, destroying part of it to preserve the remainder. Thus his outward action was corruption, but in reality it was correction, because it involved committing the lesser of two harms.

This is a hidden matter that none knew except al-Khidr. Therefore Musa rejected it.

As for his action concerning the killing of the boy, it was an action by revelation from Allah, aimed at cutting off a specific corruption that Allah knew and had informed al-Khidr of through revelation. Thus it does not belong to the station of legislation. Allah knew from the constitution of the boy's intellect and thinking that his intellect was aberrant and his thinking deviant, shaped by ordinary causes of distorted disposition and deficient perception. These are signs that lead that kind of soul and its owner to grow up as a tyrant and an unbeliever. Allah willed kindness to his parents by preserving their faith and protecting the world from this tyrant, a kindness that Allah willed as a miracle beyond the ordinary course, in accordance with the requirement of His prior knowledge. In this there is a benefit to the religion by preserving its followers from unbelief. It is a particular benefit that includes the preservation of religion, and a general benefit because it is a right of Allah, Exalted, and so it is like the ruling concerning the killing of an apostate.

*Zakah* means "purity," in observance of Musa's words, ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul?﴾ [al-Kahf: 74]. *Ruhm*, with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a sukun on the *ha'*, is like *kuthr* for *kathrah* ("abundance").

*Al-khashyah* ("fear") is the expectation of that happening if it were not forestalled by killing him.

The two plural pronouns in His saying, ﴿So we feared﴾ and His saying, ﴿So we wished﴾ refer to a single speaker, to show that he shares the act with others. This usage is from humility, not from self-exaltation, because the context is one of informing that Allah made him aware of this and commanded him. Humility was therefore appropriate, so he said, ﴿So we feared … so we wished.﴾ He did not say the same when he said, ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, because the cause of damaging the ship was his knowledge of the one who had knowledge of the condition of those regions. This was discussed earlier at His saying, [Page 14] ﴿He said: "Allah forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property; indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."﴾ [Yusuf: 79] in Surat Yusuf.

The majority read *an yubaddilahuma* with a *fatha* on the *ba'* and a shaddah on the *dal*, from *tabdil* ("replacement"). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *dal*, from *ibdal* ("substitution"). As for the wall, al-Khidr acted concerning its affair by the will of Allah to show kindness to the two orphans as a reward for their father's righteousness, since Allah knew that their father was concerned about their livelihood after him. He had deposited money under the wall. Perhaps he had asked Allah to inspire his two sons, when they reached maturity, to search for the place where the treasure was buried under the wall, either deliberately or by chance. If the wall had collapsed before they reached maturity, hands would have reached that place by digging and the like, and someone would have stumbled upon it. That too would be a kindness beyond the ordinary course. The will in the story of the wall was attributed to Allah, Exalted, and not to the two previous stories, because in those two cases the work was of a kind that anyone who was aware of its secret would strive to do, since they involved averting corruption from people. By contrast, the story of the wall is a favor from Allah to the father of the two boys.

His saying, ﴿a mercy from your Lord; and I did not do it of my own accord﴾, is an explicit statement that removes Musa's objection to these actions by showing that they were mercy and benefit, so there is no objection to them after understanding their interpretation.

He then added that he did it by revelation from Allah, because when he said, ﴿I did not do it of my own accord,﴾ Musa understood that it was by command from Allah, Exalted. This is because a prophet acts either by ijtihad (independent reasoning) or by revelation. So when he denied that his action was from his own command, it became certain that it was from the command of Allah, Exalted. He chose to deny that his action came from his own command instead of saying, "I did it by the command of my Lord," in order to complete the removal of Musa's bewilderment and objection. For when Musa objected to his three actions, he was supporting his objection with what implies that al-Khidr had acted from error.

*Rahmatan* ("as a mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). Thus it is governed by each of *aradtu* ("I wished"), *aradna* ("we wished"), and *arada rabbuka* ("your Lord wished"). The clause ﴿That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾ is a summary (*fadhlaka*) of the clauses before it, beginning from His saying, ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to the poor﴾. The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to what was mentioned in the previous speech, and it is a summary of the intended meaning, like the teacher's concluding recapitulation at the end of his lesson.

*Tasti'* is the imperfect of *istata'a* ("was able") in the sense of *istaṭa'a*. The *ta'* of the *istif'al* form was dropped for lightness, because it is close to the point of articulation of the *ta'* (*ṭa'*). The variation between this and His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾, is for stylistic variety, to avoid repeating the same word when a synonym exists. The first and more commonly used of the two was mentioned first, and the second was expressed with the lighter verb form, because lightness is more appropriate to it, since repeating *tasta'* would produce heaviness.

The first relative pronoun, occurring in His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾, was emphasized to reinforce the allusion to blame for lack of patience.

Know that the story of Musa and al-Khidr has been taken as a foundation by groups among the Islamic sects, on which they built false principles.

The first of what they established from it is that al-Khidr was not a prophet but only a righteous servant, that the knowledge he was given was not revelation but inspiration (*ilham*), that his actions in existing things are a basis for proving esoteric sciences, and that Allah granted al-Khidr life until the end of the world in order that he might be a source for receiving the esoteric sciences, and that he appears to people of the highest ranks among the saints, benefiting them with his knowledge to the extent that they are fit to receive it.

They built on this the claim that inspiration (al-ilham) is a kind of revelation (wahy), which they called "inspired revelation" (al-wahy al-ilhami), and that it comes through the tongue of an angel of inspiration. Shaykh Muhyi al-Din ibn al-'Arabi detailed this in the eighty-fifth chapter of his book al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, and he explained the difference between it and the revelation of the prophets through distinctions and signs that he set out in the chapters seventy-third, and two hundred and sixty-eighth, and three hundred and sixty-fourth. He asserted that this inspired revelation cannot contradict the Sharia, and he elaborated on this at length. What he said is not free from obscurity and symbolism. The scholars of theology (kalam) and the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) have taken a stand to refute the idea that what is called inspiration (ilham) can be a proof (hujja). They defined it as the placing of something in the heart by which the breast is set at ease, and they invalidated it as a proof because the thoughts of one who is not infallible (ma'sum) cannot be trusted, and because the levels of unveiling (kashf) differ among them. Al-Nasafi addressed this in his creed, and everything al-Nasafi said on this is correct. Legislation cannot be founded on imagined principles that cannot be pinned down.

The more evident view is that al-Khadir was a prophet, peace be upon him, and that he was receiving revelation for what was revealed to him, based on his saying ﴿and I did not do it of my own accord﴾. His account ended after the circumstances that are related in this surah, and he met the death that befalls all humans at the furthest limit of lifespan that can be supposed. As for what is attributed to him by some of the Sufis known for truthfulness, it should be understood as woven in the familiar symbolic idiom of their circle, or as the veil of imagination that may settle over them.

So be wary of anyone who says: "al-Khadir told me."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 83–85 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 17]
﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say, "I will recite to you about him a reminder."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him upon the earth and gave him of every thing a means.﴾ The opening of this story with "They ask you" indicates that the surah was revealed in answer to it, just as the beginning with the story of the People of the Cave was abrupt, as a call to attention to such matters.

When commenting on His saying, ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say, "The soul is of the affair of my Lord"﴾ [al-Isra: 85], in Surat al-Isra, we mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that "the polytheists in Makkah asked the Prophet ﷺ three questions, incited by rabbis of the Jews in Yathrib. They said: 'Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the soul. If he answers all of them, then he is not a prophet; and if he answers some and withholds from others, then he is a prophet.'" We explained there the reason for the hastening, in Surat al-Isra, which was revealed before Surat al-Kahf, in answering their question about the soul, and the delay of the answer about the People of the Cave and Dhu al-Qarnayn until Surat al-Kahf. We followed that with what we found to be the truth in the arrangement of these three questions in various places.

The questioners were, without doubt, the Quraysh. The matter asked about is the account of a man among the great figures of the world, known by the title Dhu al-Qarnayn, whose accounts of his life were obscure, general and closed, so they asked the Prophet to verify and detail them. Allah permitted him to make clear from them what is the subject of lesson for people concerning matters of righteousness and justice, and concerning the wondrous working of Allah Most High in the variation of the conditions of creation. The Jewish rabbis alone had a general knowledge of these three matters, and they were among their secrets; therefore they tested by them the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

[Page 18]
The Qur'an did not go beyond mentioning this man by the title for which he is famous, to specifying his name, land and people, because that belongs to the concerns of historians and storytellers and is not among the purposes of the Qur'an. So it confined itself to what benefits the community from this story as wisdom or moral lesson. Therefore Allah said: ﴿Say, "I will recite to you about him a reminder."﴾ The meaning of "asking about Dhu al-Qarnayn" is asking about his account; the modifier was elided for brevity, as the context indicates. Likewise the modifier was elided in His saying "from him," meaning from his account, and "from" (min) is partitive.

"Dhikr" means remembrance and reflection, i.e., "I will recite to you that by which there is remembrance." He made the recited thing itself a "reminder" as an intensification by describing it with the verbal noun. But the Qur'an came with the truth in which there is no confusion regarding the condition of the man described as Dhu al-Qarnayn, with what nullifies what people mixed together of the conditions of great men who lived in close eras, or whose stories were recounted as though they wandered through close and similar lands, and they distorted their confusion with falsehoods. The most prominent in this is the author of the Shahnameh, Firdawsi, who is known for falsehoods and fanciful legends.

The commentators differed greatly in identifying the one called Dhu al-Qarnayn, and reports of storytellers, historical reports and deductions from verbal derivations scattered them. Perhaps their disagreement about him is closely connected to the disagreement of the storytellers who were concerned with the conditions of conquerors with a concern of confusion rather than verification, so they sought to apply this story to them. What must be settled first of all is that his description as Dhu al-Qarnayn must be an intrinsic description of him, and it is an Arabic description which appears to have been known in its meaning among those who prompted the question about him, so they translated it with this expression.

[Page 19]
It is necessary that the two horns not be taken literally; rather they are either figurative or a matter of appearance. The most evident is that they were two locks of hair of the head hanging down, and the use of "horn" for a braid of hair is common in Arabic. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of her horns, drinking as one drinks wine, with the coolness of the water of al-Hashraj.

In the hadith of Umm 'Atiyya concerning the washing of the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, Umm 'Atiyya said: "We made her hair into three horns." So this king would have let his hair grow long and braided it into two plaits, and he was thus called Dhu al-Qarnayn, just as Khirbaq was called Dhu al-Yadayn.

It was also said: they were like the horns of a ram made of copper which were on this king's helmet, and he was described by them. It was also said: they were two blows on two places of a person's head which resemble the places where horns grow on horned animals.

From here the opinions regarding the identification of Dhu al-Qarnayn arise:

The first opinion: he is Alexander son of Philip the Macedonian. They mentioned as the reason for his title Dhu al-Qarnayn that he braided his hair into two horns; it was also said that he wore a helmet in battle with two horns on it; and it was also said that he depicted himself on some of his coins with two horns on his head, likening himself to the deity Amun, the god of the Egyptians, at the time he ruled Egypt.

The second opinion: he is a king of the kings of Himyar, Tubba' Abu Karib.

The third opinion: he is a king of the kings of Persia, and he is (Afridun son of Athfiyan son of Jamshid). These are the clearest of the opinions, and what lies beneath them should not be relied upon nor should its narration be authenticated.

Facing this disagreement, it is incumbent upon us to derive from his story in this verse conditions that bring his identification closer and refute what is other than it among the opinions. It is not necessary to restrict ourselves to identifying him among the holders of these opinions; rather the matter is broader.

[Page 20]
This Qur'anic story gives attributes from which there is no escape:
First: that he was a righteous, just king.
Second: that he was inspired by Allah.
Third: that his rule encompassed vast regions.
Fourth: that in his conquests he reached, from the direction of the west, a place that was unknown, namely a muddy spring (ʿaynun ḥamiʾah).
Fifth: that he reached the lands of Gog and Magog, and that they were in a direction of what his rule encompassed other than the eastern and western directions, so they were in the middle between them, as the inference from the extent of his means requires.
Sixth: that he built a barrier between Gog and Magog and other peoples.
Seventh: that these Gog and Magog were spreading corruption in the earth, and that they used to corrupt the lands of a people allied to this king.
Eighth: that with him was a people skilled in exact craftsmanship in iron and construction.
Ninth: that his story is obscure and subtle, known only to the rabbis in a general way, as the occasion of revelation indicates.

If you reflect on all these conditions, you will rule out that Dhu al-Qarnayn was Alexander the Macedonian, because he was not a righteous king but a idolater, and so he was not fit to receive revelation from Allah, even if he had certain perfections in general. Also, it is not known from his history that he built a barrier between two lands.

As for the attribution of the barrier separating China from the lands of Gog and Magog to him in the words of some historians, it arises from the fame of Alexander, so the storytellers imagined that that barrier could only be from his construction, just as the Arabs imagined that the city of Tadmur was built by Solomon, peace be upon him. Also, Herodotus the Greek historian mentioned that Alexander fought his mother (Scythus), and this name is the name of Magog, as will come shortly.

[Page 21]
I think that the composition of the story mentioned in this surah under the name of Alexander the Macedonian has an effect in spreading the attribution of the barrier to him. That is among the illusions of Muslim historians.

It is not known that Alexander's kingdom reached in the west to a muddy spring, nor in the east to unknown people who were naked or without dwellings, nor that his nation called him Dhu al-Qarnayn. Rather, this title was ascribed to him when they imagined that he was the one meant by Dhu al-Qarnayn in this verse. So bestowing this title upon him is an invention of Muslim historians, and depicting his face with two horns on coins is not of the kind that would give rise to such a title. Also, Alexander's reports were famous because he fought the Persians and the Copts, two nations neighboring the Arab nation.

Similar to these refutations we mentioned, the claim that the king referred to is Afridun can be refuted. As for the possibility that he was one of the Tubba'as of Himyar, it is possible that he lived in a very ancient era. Some commentators imagined that he was a contemporary of Abraham, peace be upon him, and that the lands he conquered were of unknown locations. But it is unlikely that he is the intended one, because the Arabs do not know of his story anything like this. It has become apparent from their statements that the cause of this imagining is the presence of the word (dhu), which is well known to appear in the titles of the kings of Yemen and their Tubba'as.

[Page 22]
What appears to me is that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a king of the kings of China, for several reasons:
One: the people of China have been known since antiquity as people of administration and crafts.
Two: most of their kings were people of justice and of good governance of the kingdom.
Three: among their characteristics is the lengthening of the hair of their heads and making it into two braids, so the reason he was described as Dhu al-Qarnayn becomes apparent.
Four: a great barrier and wall unmatched anywhere in the world exists between the lands of China and the lands of the Mongols. It is famous in books of geography and history as the Great Wall, and its description will come.
Five: what Umm Habiba related from Zaynab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ "went out one night and said: 'Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today there has been opened from the barrier of Gog and Magog such and such,'" and he gestured by forming ninety, meaning by placing the tip of the index finger on the tip of the thumb. The loss of the greatness of Arab rule came at the hands of the Mongols in Baghdad. Therefore it is established that Gog and Magog are the Mongols, and that the barrier mentioned in the Qur'an is the barrier separating the lands of the Mongols from the lands of China, and its builder was a king of theirs.

Also, its description in the Qur'an as Dhu al-Qarnayn is a descriptive designation, not a title; it is like the expression of Saul, king of Israel, by the name Talut. This king is the one who built the barrier separating China from Mongolia. His name is (Tsin-shi Huang-ti) or (Tsin Shi Hoang Ti). He existed around the year 247 BC, so he is about a century later than Alexander the Macedonian. The lands of China at that time followed the religion of (Confucius), the legislator and reformer. There is no doubt that the people of his law were righteous.

[Page 23]
It is taken from the history books that this king's condition deteriorated at the end of his life, he committed much corruption, killed scholars and burned books. Allah knows best the truth and its causes.

When many people thought that Dhu al-Qarnayn mentioned in the Qur'an was Alexander son of Philip, they attributed to him the building of the barrier, and considered it his work, just as they attributed to him the title Dhu al-Qarnayn. All of this is building illusions upon illusions, and there is no basis for any of them, and Alexander the Macedonian has no connection with the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn mentioned in this surah.

The command in His saying ﴿Say, "I will recite to you"﴾ is a permission from Allah to His Messenger to promise an answer to their question, in acting upon His saying ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [when adding], "If Allah wills"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23], according to one of the two interpretations of its meaning.

The "sa" (sin) in His saying ﴿I will recite to you﴾ is for affirming the promise, as in His Most High saying ﴿He said, "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Yusuf: 98] in Surat Yusuf.

The account of Dhu al-Qarnayn was made a recitation and a reminder to indicate that what is important of his accounts is what contains admonition and what is suitable to be a recitation according to the nature of the Qur'an, for it is recited for the sake of remembrance and is not presented in the manner of mere storytelling.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 83–85 (part 2 of 2):

His saying "from him a reminder" (min-hu dhikra) is an indication that his circumstances and reports are many, and that people are concerned only with some of his circumstances that are beneficial as a reminder and admonition. For this reason, in the story of the People of the Cave, He did not say, "We relate to you their news," because their story is confined to what was mentioned. The circumstances of Dhu al-Qarnayn are not confined to what is mentioned here.

The particle min in His saying "min-hu dhikra" is partitive (li-l-tab'id), with an elided noun understood, i.e., "from his report" (min khabarihi).

Al-tamkin (establishment) means making a thing firmly established (mutamakkinan), i.e., steadfast. It is a metaphor for the strength of disposal, such that no one can shake its strength. The original form of the verb makkana is transitive without a preposition, so it is said: makkanahu fi al-ard (We established him in the land), as in His saying ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. Thus the lam in His saying ﴿We established for him in the land﴾ is for emphasis, like the lam in the expressions "shakartu lahu" (I thanked him) and "nasahtu lahu" (I advised him), and combining the two is a stylistic variation (tafannun). Upon this came His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. So the meaning of tamkin in the land is giving the capability to dispose (of affairs).

By "the land" is meant either its people, or a specific land, which is the land of his dominion. This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

The sabab (means) is in its real sense a rope, and here it is applied, by way of metaphor, to whatever one uses to reach a thing, whether knowledge, capability, or instruments of control, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the means were cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqara: 166], in Surat al-Baqara.

"Kull shay'" (everything/every thing) is used here for many things, as has been mentioned in its similar occurrences more than once, among them His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and even if every sign had come to them﴾ [Yunus: 97], meaning: We gave him means of many great things.

So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of her horns, drinking as one drinks wine, with the coolness of the water of al-Hashraj.

In the hadith of Umm 'Atiyya concerning the washing of the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, Umm 'Atiyya said: "We made her hair into three horns." So this king would have let his hair grow long and braided it into two plaits, and he was thus called Dhu al-Qarnayn, just as Khirbaq was called Dhu al-Yadayn.

It was also said: they were like the horns of a ram made of copper which were on this king's helmet, and he was described by them. It was also said: they were two blows on two places of a person's head which resemble the places where horns grow on horned animals.

From here the opinions regarding the identification of Dhu al-Qarnayn arise:

The first opinion: he is Alexander son of Philip the Macedonian. They mentioned as the reason for his title Dhu al-Qarnayn that he braided his hair into two horns; it was also said that he wore a helmet in battle with two horns on it; and it was also said that he depicted himself on some of his coins with two horns on his head, likening himself to the deity Amun, the god of the Egyptians, at the time he ruled Egypt.

The second opinion: he is a king of the kings of Himyar, Tubba' Abu Karib.

The third opinion: he is a king of the kings of Persia, and he is (Afridun son of Athfiyan son of Jamshid). These are the clearest of the opinions, and what lies beneath them should not be relied upon nor should its narration be authenticated.

Facing this disagreement, it is incumbent upon us to derive from his story in this verse conditions that bring his identification closer and refute what is other than it among the opinions. It is not necessary to restrict ourselves to identifying him among the holders of these opinions; rather the matter is broader.

[Page 20]
This Qur'anic story gives attributes from which there is no escape:
First: that he was a righteous, just king.
Second: that he was inspired by Allah.
Third: that his rule encompassed vast regions.
Fourth: that in his conquests he reached, from the direction of the west, a place that was unknown, namely a muddy spring (ʿaynun ḥamiʾah).
Fifth: that he reached the lands of Gog and Magog, and that they were in a direction of what his rule encompassed other than the eastern and western directions, so they were in the middle between them, as the inference from the extent of his means requires.
Sixth: that he built a barrier between Gog and Magog and other peoples.
Seventh: that these Gog and Magog were spreading corruption in the earth, and that they used to corrupt the lands of a people allied to this king.
Eighth: that with him was a people skilled in exact craftsmanship in iron and construction.
Ninth: that his story is obscure and subtle, known only to the rabbis in a general way, as the occasion of revelation indicates.

If you reflect on all these conditions, you will rule out that Dhu al-Qarnayn was Alexander the Macedonian, because he was not a righteous king but a idolater, and so he was not fit to receive revelation from Allah, even if he had certain perfections in general. Also, it is not known from his history that he built a barrier between two lands.

As for the attribution of the barrier separating China from the lands of Gog and Magog to him in the words of some historians, it arises from the fame of Alexander, so the storytellers imagined that that barrier could only be from his construction, just as the Arabs imagined that the city of Tadmur was built by Solomon, peace be upon him. Also, Herodotus the Greek historian mentioned that Alexander fought his mother (Scythus), and this name is the name of Magog, as will come shortly.

[Page 21]
I think that the composition of the story mentioned in this surah under the name of Alexander the Macedonian has an effect in spreading the attribution of the barrier to him. That is among the illusions of Muslim historians.

It is not known that Alexander's kingdom reached in the west to a muddy spring, nor in the east to unknown people who were naked or without dwellings, nor that his nation called him Dhu al-Qarnayn. Rather, this title was ascribed to him when they imagined that he was the one meant by Dhu al-Qarnayn in this verse. So bestowing this title upon him is an invention of Muslim historians, and depicting his face with two horns on coins is not of the kind that would give rise to such a title. Also, Alexander's reports were famous because he fought the Persians and the Copts, two nations neighboring the Arab nation.

Similar to these refutations we mentioned, the claim that the king referred to is Afridun can be refuted. As for the possibility that he was one of the Tubba'as of Himyar, it is possible that he lived in a very ancient era. Some commentators imagined that he was a contemporary of Abraham, peace be upon him, and that the lands he conquered were of unknown locations. But it is unlikely that he is the intended one, because the Arabs do not know of his story anything like this. It has become apparent from their statements that the cause of this imagining is the presence of the word (dhu), which is well known to appear in the titles of the kings of Yemen and their Tubba'as.

[Page 22]
What appears to me is that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a king of the kings of China, for several reasons:
One: the people of China have been known since antiquity as people of administration and crafts.
Two: most of their kings were people of justice and of good governance of the kingdom.
Three: among their characteristics is the lengthening of the hair of their heads and making it into two braids, so the reason he was described as Dhu al-Qarnayn becomes apparent.
Four: a great barrier and wall unmatched anywhere in the world exists between the lands of China and the lands of the Mongols. It is famous in books of geography and history as the Great Wall, and its description will come.
Five: what Umm Habiba related from Zaynab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ "went out one night and said: 'Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today there has been opened from the barrier of Gog and Magog such and such,'" and he gestured by forming ninety, meaning by placing the tip of the index finger on the tip of the thumb. The loss of the greatness of Arab rule came at the hands of the Mongols in Baghdad. Therefore it is established that Gog and Magog are the Mongols, and that the barrier mentioned in the Qur'an is the barrier separating the lands of the Mongols from the lands of China, and its builder was a king of theirs.

Also, its description in the Qur'an as Dhu al-Qarnayn is a descriptive designation, not a title; it is like the expression of Saul, king of Israel, by the name Talut. This king is the one who built the barrier separating China from Mongolia. His name is (Tsin-shi Huang-ti) or (Tsin Shi Hoang Ti). There is no doubt that the people of his law were righteous.

[Page 23]
