The "sa" (sin) in His saying ﴿I will recite to you﴾ is for affirming the promise, as in His Most High saying ﴿He said, "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Yusuf: 98] in Surat Yusuf.

The account of Dhu al-Qarnayn was made a recitation and a reminder to indicate that what is important of his accounts is what contains admonition and what is suitable to be a recitation according to the nature of the Qur'an, for it is recited for the sake of remembrance and is not presented in the manner of mere storytelling.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 83–85 (part 2 of 2):

His saying "from him a reminder" (min-hu dhikra) is an indication that his circumstances and reports are many, and that people are concerned only with some of his circumstances that are beneficial as a reminder and admonition. For this reason, in the story of the People of the Cave, He did not say, "We relate to you their news," because their story is confined to what was mentioned. The circumstances of Dhu al-Qarnayn are not confined to what is mentioned here.

The particle min in His saying "min-hu dhikra" is partitive (li-l-tab'id), with an elided noun understood, i.e., "from his report" (min khabarihi).

Al-tamkin (establishment) means making a thing firmly established (mutamakkinan), i.e., steadfast. It is a metaphor for the strength of disposal, such that no one can shake its strength. The original form of the verb makkana is transitive without a preposition, so it is said: makkanahu fi al-ard (We established him in the land), as in His saying ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. Thus the lam in His saying ﴿We established for him in the land﴾ is for emphasis, like the lam in the expressions "shakartu lahu" (I thanked him) and "nasahtu lahu" (I advised him), and combining the two is a stylistic variation (tafannun). Upon this came His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We had established them in the land as We had not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. So the meaning of tamkin in the land is giving the capability to dispose (of affairs).

By "the land" is meant either its people, or a specific land, which is the land of his dominion. This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

The sabab (means) is in its real sense a rope, and here it is applied, by way of metaphor, to whatever one uses to reach a thing, whether knowledge, capability, or instruments of control, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the means were cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqara: 166], in Surat al-Baqara.

"Kull shay'" (everything/every thing) is used here for many things, as has been mentioned in its similar occurrences more than once, among them His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and even if every sign had come to them﴾ [Yunus: 97], meaning: We gave him means of many great things.

We followed that with what we found to be the truth in the arrangement of these three questions in various places.

The questioners were, without doubt, the Quraysh. The Jewish rabbis alone had a general knowledge of these three matters, and they were among their secrets; therefore they tested by them the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

The most prominent in this is the author of the Shahnameh, Firdawsi, who is known for falsehoods and fanciful legends.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 86–89:

﴿So he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 85] ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring, and found near it a people. We said: "O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness."﴾ ﴿He said: "As for him who wrongs, we shall punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment. As for him who believes and does righteous deeds, he shall have a good reward, and we shall speak to him of Our command with ease."﴾

Al-sabab (السبب) means the means or the way. Here it is used in a figurative sense, namely "the road," because a road is a means to the intended place. The indicator of the figurative usage is the mention of "following" (al-ittiba') and "reaching" (al-bulugh).

In His saying "So he followed a way until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun," the evidence that a meaning other than the primary sense of sabab is intended is found in His saying, "And We gave him of every thing a means (sabab)" [al-Kahf: 84]. The name sabab is made explicit rather than replaced by a pronoun, because it is used here with a meaning different from the first occurrence; the explicit repetition draws attention to the difference between the two meanings. That is, he followed a path for travel, and his journey was for the sake of military campaign, as indicated by His saying, "until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun." The lexicographers did not count the meaning "road" among the meanings of the word sabab, perhaps because they regarded it as not frequent or widespread in speech. It appears that His saying "the means (asbab) of the heavens" [Ghafir: 37] is of this meaning, and likewise the verse of Zuhayr:

"And whoever fears the means (asbab) of death, death will seize him,"

that is, whoever fears the roads of death to travel them, death will seize him, meaning it will come to him; this is a figurative usage by virtue of the indicator.

By "the setting-place of the sun" is meant the place of the sun's setting, from the point where setting appears from the directions of the inhabited world, along the route of his campaign or his kingdom. That is where it appears that there is no land beyond it, such that the horizon appears from an expansive direction, since the sun has no true setting except as it appears to imagination. It is most likely that Dhu'l-Qarnayn reached the Caspian Sea, which is the Lake of Qazvin, for it is the western extremity of the lands of China.

The discussion of the construction "until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun" is like the discussion of His saying "until, when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it" [al-Kahf: 71]. The 'ayn (عين) is a source of water. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read "in a spring of hami'a (حمئة)," with hamza, derived from al-hama'a (الحمأة), which is black mud. The meaning is: a spring whose water is mixed with mud, so it is not clear.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read "in a spring of hamiya (حامية)," with an alif after the ha' and a ya' after the mim, meaning hot, from al-humuww, which is heat; that is, its water was heated.

It appears that this spring is one of the oil springs situated on the shore of the Caspian Sea, where the city of Baku is located, and in which there are oil sources now, though this was not known at that time. The Muslim historians called it "the stinking lands."

The indefinite form of qawman (قومًا) indicates that they were a nation not known or familiar in terms of their beliefs and conduct.

Therefore, the phrase "We said: O Dhu'l-Qarnayn" is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) answering what the indefiniteness of qawman suggests, namely a question about their condition and what Dhu'l-Qarnayn encountered from them.

His saying "either punish them or treat them with kindness" indicates that they deserved punishment, and thus that their condition was one of corruption, both of disbelief and of corrupt deeds.

The attribution of the saying to the Divine Name may be a saying of inspiration (qawl ilham), that is, We cast into his soul a hesitation between hastening to exterminate them and granting them respite and calling them to faith and good conduct. *Matla' al-shams* (the rising place of the sun) means the direction of the east within its dominion and realm. He reached a remote part of the east, where one would suppose there was no inhabited land beyond it. Thus *al-matla'* is the place of rising.

The apparent meaning is that he reached the coast of the Sea of Japan, within the borders of Manchuria or Korea to the east, and found a people on whom the sun rises and who are not shielded from its heat. That is, there is no mountain there for them to shelter in its shade, nor any trees; it is an land exposed to the sun. It is also possible that the meaning is that they were a naked people, who protected themselves from the rays of the sun in caves or in burrows they dug in the earth. Thus *al-sitr* (the shield) refers to whatever covers the body.

They had become accustomed to facing the heat of the sun, and perhaps they would expose themselves to the sun so as to ward off from themselves the cold they encountered at night.

In this condition there is a lesson concerning the difference among nations in their natures, customs and ways of life, according to the nature of their climate.

The *kaf* and its genitive complement may be a prepositional phrase (*shibh jumla*) functioning as a qualifier of a deleted verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that the context indicates, meaning: a comparison similar to what you have heard.

The demonstrative refers to the deleted element, since it is treated as if it were mentioned, the knowledge of it being firmly established. The meaning is: whoever wishes to compare it cannot compare it with anything more than itself, in the manner already stated in His words, ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143], in Surat al-Baqara.

It may also be a part of a sentence in which one of its two components has been deleted, the deleted component being the subject (*mubtada'*). The estimate would be: the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn is thus, meaning, as you have heard.

It may also be a qualifier of *qawman* (a people), meaning: a people such as those people whom he found at the setting place of the sun, that is, in their being disbelievers, and in his being given the choice to deal with their affair by punishment or by respite. It may also be that the genitive phrase is a part of a sentence, introduced to shift from one speech to another, so that it is a decisive statement (*faṣl al-khiṭāb*), as one says: this matter is such-and-such.

In all these aspects, it is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*) between the sentence ﴿Then he followed a way until, when he reached the rising place of the sun﴾ [al-Kahf: 89], etc., and the sentence ﴿Then he followed a way until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾, etc.

**Al-Sudd** (the barrier), with a *ḍamma* or a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, means a mountain. It is also applied to a dividing wall, because space is blocked (*yusaddu*) with it. It was said that the *ḍamma* is used for a mountain and the *fatḥa* for a barrier.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim), Abū Jaʿfar, Khalaf and Yaʿqūb read it with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ (from ʿĀṣim) read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, following the dialect that does not distinguish between them. Here, "the two barriers" (*al-saddayn*) means two mountains, and "a single barrier" (*al-sadd al-mufrad*) means a dividing wall. The context is what specifies the intended meaning of this shared term.

The definite article in *al-saddayn* is the article of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), meaning "between two specific barriers", that is, he followed another route on a campaign until he reached between two known mountains.

It appears that he headed in a direction other than east or west, so it may be north or south. The commentators specified that it was north, and they based this on the view that Dhū al-Qarnayn was Alexander the Macedonian. They said that the location of the two barriers was between Armenia and Azerbaijan. We build on what we have identified concerning the one called Dhū al-Qarnayn, and we say that the site of the two barriers is the north-west of the Gobi Desert, which separates China from the lands of the Mongols, north of China and south of Mongolia. The barrier was found there, and its traces remain to this day. Geographers and travellers have seen it, and it has been photographed in modern geography and history books.

The meaning of ﴿who scarcely understand any speech﴾ is that they do not know any of the speech of others. Their language differs from the languages of the known nations, to the extent that the interpreters of Dhū al-Qarnayn do not know it. This is because it is the custom of kings to employ interpreters to translate the languages of the peoples with whom they need to communicate. These people spoke a strange language because their lands were cut off from the known regions, so there was no one who could make them understand the king's meaning, nor could they make themselves understood.

It is also possible that the meaning is that they are a people deeply immersed in primitiveness and foolishness, so they do not understand what the one addressing them intends.

Page 32

Al-Jumhūr read *yafqahūna* with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* (the letter with two dots below) and a *fatḥa* on the *qāf*, meaning they do not understand the speech of others. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a *kasra* on the *qāf*, meaning they cannot make others understand their speech. The two meanings are mutually implied. This is like the hadith about faith: "We hear the buzzing of his voice but do not understand what he says."

These people were neighbours of Yājūj and Mājūj. They were weaker than them, so they asked Dhū al-Qarnayn to protect them from the corruption of Yājūj and Mājūj. The commentators did not mention the identification of these people, nor the names of their tribe, except that they said they were in the remote region of the Turks towards the east, and that they were righteous people. There is no doubt that they were among the tribes of the lands of China, which border the lands of the Mongols and the Tatars.

The sentence ﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*) introducing the dialogue. We have explained elsewhere that sentences reporting speech in dialogues are not connected by a conjunction, as in His saying, ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who will spread corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. According to the first of the two possibilities regarding the meaning of ﴿who scarcely understand any speech﴾, they do not grasp what is required of them in terms of obedience and order, yet they express what is in their souls of desires in the manner of children's expression. According to the second possibility, it was possible for their meaning to be understood after some difficulty.

Their opening of the speech with a call (*nidāʾ*) means that they called him with the call of those seeking help who are in distress. Their addressing him with the title Dhū al-Qarnayn indicates that this title was well known among the nations bordering his lands, with its meaning.

Yājūj and Mājūj are a people of great numbers. It is possible that the *wāw* between the two names is a conjunction, so they would be one nation consisting of two peoples. They are the Mongols and some categories of the Tatars. This is the most fitting for the original form of the word, especially on the view that the two are Arabic names, as will come. The two groups were neighbours.

Page 33

Historians and genealogists have differed over the application of the names Mongols and Tatars, each applying to the other, because it is difficult to distinguish between two closely related groups. Some scholars have said that the Mongols are Mājūj, with a *mīm*, the name of their ancestor, also called Sikīshūs. The general name that gathered the two tribes was Mājūj. Then the nation divided and its branches were given specific names. Among them are Mājūj, Yājūj, Tatar, then the Turkmen, then the Turks. It is possible that the *wāw* mentioned is not a conjunction, but it came in the form of one, so the expression is a single compound word formed by fusion (*tarkīb mazjī*). Thus it forms the name of one nation, namely the Mongols.

What must be relied upon is that Yājūj and Mājūj are the Mongols and the Tatars.

Abū al-Fidāʾ mentioned that Mājūj are the Mongols, so Yājūj are the Tatars. The Tatars greatly outnumbered the Mongols, so the Mongols merged into the Tatars, and the name Tatar prevailed over the two tribes. The clearest evidence for this is what came in the hadith of Umm Ḥabībah from Zaynab bint Jaḥsh: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her in alarm, saying: 'There is no god but Allah. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today a gap has been opened in the barrier of Yājūj and Mājūj like this,' and he made a circle with his thumb and the finger next to it." This has been mentioned earlier.

The exact time of their departure from their lands is not known, nor the reason for it. It is estimated that their departure was towards the end of the sixth century AH. The dispersal of the Arab kingdom at the hands of the Mongols and Tatars came with the emergence of Genghis Khan the Mongol and his seizure of Bukhara in the year 616 AH. They reached Diyar Bakr in the year 628 AH, then came the destruction of Baghdad, capital of the Arab kingdom, by Hulagu in the year 660 AH.

A parallel to applying two names to one tribal group formed of two tribes is the application of Tasm and Jadīs to an extinct Arab nation. Also the application of al-Sakākik and al-Sakaran to Yemeni tribes, and of Hilāl and Zighbah to the Bedouin of Ifriqiya who came from the Upper Egypt region. Also the application of Awlād Yaḥyā to a clan in Tunisia in the south-west, and Murādah and Farjān to a clan from the land of Nābul in Tunisia.

Al-Jumhūr read *Yājūj wa-Mājūj* both times with an *alif* after the *yāʾ* (the letter with two dots below), without a hamza. ʿĀṣim read it with a hamza.

The commentators differed over whether it is an Arabic name or an Arabicised foreign word (*muʿarrab*). My strong opinion is that it is a name that the Qur'an created, through which it reproduced its meaning in the language of that nation, appropriate to the condition of their society. Thus the two names were derived from the root *ajj*, which means mixing, since you know that this nation was a mixture of categories.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Shall We then set up for you﴾ is used for offering (*ʿarḍ*).

*Kharj* is the money paid to the king. It is pronounced with a *fatḥa* on the *khāʾ* (with a dot) and a sukūn on the *rāʾ* in the reading of al-Jumhūr. It is also said *kharāj*, with an *alif* after the *rāʾ*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it this way.

Al-Jumhūr read *saddan* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*.

His saying ﴿What my Lord has established me in is better﴾ means: what Allah has given me of wealth and power is better than the tribute you have offered, from the barrier you have asked for. That is, what my Lord has established me in is better than what you ask, for it occurred to him that if he blocked their passage between the two cliffs, they would find a way, climb the mountains and enter the land of China. So he intended to build a wall extending along the mountains along the length of the borders of the land, so that it would be impossible for them to climb those mountains.

For this reason he called it a *radm* (barrier).

Page 35

The *radm* is a built structure that has been packed (*murddam*). It is likened to a patched garment composed of pieces upon pieces, that is, a doubled barrier. Perhaps he built two walls far apart and filled the gap between them with mixed earth, so that it could not be breached.

Since that required many workers, he said to them ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is, with bodily strength. He intended to conscript them for the work to ward off harm from them.

Dhū al-Qarnayn, who is Qin Shi Huang, the emperor of China, built this barrier in a remarkable manner in the third century BC, and millions of labourers worked on it. He made its length three thousand three hundred kilometres. Some say it was twelve hundred miles, depending on differences in the standard of the mile. He made its starting point at the sea, that is the Yellow Sea, east of the city of Beijing, the capital of China, in the line of direction of the famous city of Mukden. That is at latitude 40.4° north and longitude 120.2° east. It meets the Yellow River where the longitude is 111.50° east and the latitude 39.50° north, and also at latitude 37° north. From there it turns towards the north-west and ends near longitude 99° east and latitude 40° north.

It is built of stone and brick, and part of it of clay alone.

Its thickness at the base is about 25 feet and at the top about 15 feet, and its height ranges between 15 and 20 feet. On it are towers built of tiles, some of which are about 40 feet high.

It is now in a state of ruin, so it has no defensive value.

However, it has remained a marker of the dividing line between the administrative regions of the land, so it separates China from Mongolia. It cuts through the Babulony mountains, which are a natural border between China and the land of Mongolia, so its far end is at the north-west of the Gobi Desert.

Al-Jumhūr read *makkannī* with an assimilated nūn. Ibn Kathīr read it with the nūn unassimilated, according to the original form.

His saying ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ is a command to them to hand him blocks of iron. Here the verb *ātā* (bring) is used in its literal meaning, which is handing over, and it is not an obligation on the people to bring the iron from its mines, because that would contradict His saying (﴿What my Lord has established me in is better, so help me with strength﴾), meaning that he was independent of their obligation to spend on building the barrier. This was for the purpose of constructing iron doors at the entrances of the barrier, so that the floodwaters flowing through the mountain gullies would not demolish the structure. The iron doors were like grilles, preventing people from passing through but not preventing the water from flowing between their bars. He made the iron bars supported by molten copper poured over the iron.

Al-Zubar: the plural of zubrah, which is a large piece of iron. Iron is one of the metals of the earth; it occurs in pieces like pebbles, and in its lesser forms it has hardness. It is initially classified into two types: soft, which is called the female iron (al-hadid al-unthā), and hard, which is called the male (al-dhakar). Then it is classified into eighteen types. Its colours are close to one another: it is grey-blue (sinjabi), and some of it tends toward red while some tends toward white. When it is smelted with a strong fire in a closed furnace (utun), its parts join together and gather in the middle of the fire like a sponge, and its hardness increases, because by smelting it expels the earthy parts it contains, which are called rust (sada') and dross (khabath), and those parts rise to its surface, and this is the scum (zabad). The hadith, "Indeed, Madinah expels its dross as the bellows expels the dross of iron" [Khabath al-hadid], is relevant here; accordingly, in proportion as those foreign, impure parts float off, the iron part becomes pure and clear and becomes zubar. From these zubar are made iron objects such as swords, glass (zujaj), armour (durū') and coats of mail (la'amat). There is no way to make it except also by smelting with fire, to the point that the zubrah becomes like glowing embers; then it is shaped into the intended form by means of iron hammers.

The era in which mankind was guided to the craft of iron-working is called in history the Iron Age.

His saying ﴿until, when he had made level between the two cliffs﴾ — the word "until" (ḥattā) indicates something preceding it that is implied, and this is an omitted clause whose estimated meaning is: "So they brought him the zubar of iron, and he arranged them and built them, until, when he had placed [it] between the two cliffs." This is from the conciseness of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf). Equalising (al-musāwāt) is making things equal, that is, similar in quantity or description.

"Al-ṣadafayn," with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the dāl, is the reading of the majority, and it is the best known. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and the dāl, and this is a dialectal form (lughah). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a sukun on the dāl.

Al-ṣadaf: the side of a mountain. The two sides of the two mountains are the two barriers (al-saddān). Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qazwini in al-Kashf said: it is only said "ṣadafān" in the dual, and one of them is not called ṣadaf, because each of them faces (yuṣādif) the other; so "al-ṣadafān" is the name for the combined two sides, like "al-miqaṣṣān" (the scissors) for that by which cloth or the like is cut.

From Abu 'Isa: al-ṣadaf is every great, high structure.

The address in His saying "blow" (unfukhū) and His saying "bring me" (ātūnī) is addressed to the workers. The object of "blow" is omitted because it is evident from the fact that the work is the making of iron. The estimated meaning is: "Blow into the bellows arranged along the length of what lies between the two cliffs of iron zubar."

The majority read "ātūnī" like the first.

Ḥamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ī'tūnī" (i'tūnī), as an imperative from al-ityān, meaning: he ordered them to attend to the work.

Al-qiṭr, with a kasrah on the qāf: molten copper.

The pronoun in "isṭā'ū" and "istaṭā'ū" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

Al-ẓuhūr: ascending. Al-naqb: breaking through the barrier. Their inability to do that is due to its height and hardness.

"Isṭā'ū" is a lightened form of "istaṭā'ū." Combining the two is a variation in eloquent speech, out of dislike of repeating the same word. The lighter of the two is mentioned first, because it is followed by the hamzah, which is a heavy letter as it comes from the throat, unlike the second, since it is followed by the lām, which is light.

The apparent requirement would be to begin with the verb "istaṭā'ū" and follow it with "isṭā'ū," because the latter is heavy when repeated, as occurred in His saying earlier: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Among the distinctive features of departing here from the apparent requirement is the preference for a verb with an added element in its form in a position where an added meaning is intended, because the ability to breach the barrier is stronger than the ability to scale it; this is therefore one of the instances where added form indicates added meaning.

Ḥamzah alone read "fa-mā 'sṭṭā'ū" (famā 'sṭṭā'ū), the first with a shaddah on the ṭā', the tā' being assimilated into it.

His saying ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafah) of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), because when the discourse signalled the end of the description of the barrier, this prompted the question of someone asking: "What did Dhu al-Qarnayn say when he completed this great work?" It is answered by the sentence "He said, 'This is a mercy from my Lord.'" The demonstrative "this" refers to the barrier. It is a mercy to people, because in it there is the averting of the corruption of the nation of Ya'juj and Ma'juj from another righteous nation.

The "min" is for origin (ibtidā'iyyah). It is attributed to God because God inspired him to that and made easy for him what was difficult.

On this is based His saying ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakkā)﴾, as a statement of wisdom, because he knows that every occurrence passes into cessation. And because he knew that a great work like that requires care and preservation against collapse. And he knew that this cannot be achieved in some periods of the decline of the kingdom, which is unavoidable for every holder of authority.

"Al-wa'd" (promise) is the announcement of a future matter, and by it he meant the term that is in God's knowledge, at which the continuance of that barrier will end. So the name "promise" was borrowed for it. It is also possible that God revealed to him, if he was a prophet, or inspired him, if he was a righteous man, that the barrier has a specific term at which it ends.

The beginning of that promise was the day the Prophet ﷺ said: "The barrier of Ya'juj has been opened today this much," and he made a ring with his thumb and forefinger, as previously mentioned.

The word "dakk" in the reading of the majority is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle for emphasis, meaning: He made it levelled (madkūk), that is, made level with the ground after being raised. 'Asim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "ja'alahu dakkā'" with a long vowel. "Dakkā'" is the name for a she-camel without a hump, and this is an eloquent comparison.

His saying ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyīl) affirming the knowledge that it must have a term at which it ends, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every term there is a decree, and for every nation there is a term﴾. That is, God's appointing of terms for things is ever a firm truth that does not fail. This sentence, in its generality and in the wisdom it contains, is a wonderful concluding sentence.

﴿And We left some of them on that day surging over one another﴾ [al-Kahf: 99]. Al-tark (leaving): its literal meaning is parting from a thing that was near to one, and it is used figuratively for placing a thing in a state different from a previous state, by way of likening the state of its being left in a condition to the state of one who was near a thing and then departed from it. This figurative use is restricted only by a state in which the object of "tark" was, so it indicates that this is the last stage of the connection, and this implies that it remains in the state in which it was left, by the context.

The sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence preceding it, beginning from His saying ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. So this sentence mentions the act of God Exalted in this third story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, when He inspired him to repel the corruption of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. It is in the same position as the sentence ﴿We said, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness"﴾ [al-Kahf: 86] in the first story, and the sentence ﴿Thus, and We had encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], so the manner of narrating these three stories follows one pattern.

"Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is the day of completing the construction of the barrier, which is understood from His saying ﴿so they were not able to scale it﴾, the verse.

"Yamūj" means: to be in turmoil, likened to the surging of the sea.

The sentence "yamūju" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "baʿḍihim," or a second object of "taraknā," according to its interpretation as "ja'alnā" (We made). That is: We made Ya'juj and Ma'juj on that day turbulent among themselves, so their corruption became confined to themselves and was averted from others.

Fire devours itself if it finds nothing to devour.

For when they do not find what they were accustomed to, namely raiding the neighbouring nations, the strong among them turn upon the weak by aggression.

Al-Zubar: the plural of zubrah, which is a large piece of iron. Iron is one of the metals of the earth; it occurs in pieces like pebbles, and in its lesser forms it has hardness. It is initially classified into two types: soft, which is called the female iron (al-hadid al-unthā), and hard, which is called the male (al-dhakar). Then it is classified into eighteen types. Its colours are close to one another: it is grey-blue (sinjabi), and some of it tends toward red while some tends toward white. When it is smelted with a strong fire in a closed furnace (utun), its parts join together and gather in the middle of the fire like a sponge, and its hardness increases, because by smelting it expels the earthy parts it contains, which are called rust (sada') and dross (khabath), and those parts rise to its surface, and this is the scum (zabad). The hadith, "Indeed, Madinah expels its dross as the bellows expels the dross of iron" [Khabath al-hadid], is relevant here; accordingly, in proportion as those foreign, impure parts float off, the iron part becomes pure and clear and becomes zubar. From these zubar are made iron objects such as swords, glass (zujaj), armour (durū') and coats of mail (la'amat). There is no way to make it except also by smelting with fire, to the point that the zubrah becomes like glowing embers; then it is shaped into the intended form by means of iron hammers.

The era in which mankind was guided to the craft of iron-working is called in history the Iron Age.

This is from the conciseness of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf). Equalising (al-musāwāt) is making things equal, that is, similar in quantity or description.

From Abu 'Isa: al-ṣadaf is every great, high structure.

The address in His saying "blow" (unfukhū) and His saying "bring me" (ātūnī) is addressed to the workers. The object of "blow" is omitted because it is evident from the fact that the work is the making of iron. The majority read "ātūnī" like the first.

Ḥamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ī'tūnī" (i'tūnī), as an imperative from al-ityān, meaning: he ordered them to attend to the work.

Al-qiṭr, with a kasrah on the qāf: molten copper.

The pronoun in "isṭā'ū" and "istaṭā'ū" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

Al-ẓuhūr: ascending. Al-naqb: breaking through the barrier. Their inability to do that is due to its height and hardness.

"Isṭā'ū" is a lightened form of "istaṭā'ū." Combining the two is a variation in eloquent speech, out of dislike of repeating the same word. The lighter of the two is mentioned first, because it is followed by the hamzah, which is a heavy letter as it comes from the throat, unlike the second, since it is followed by the lām, which is light.

The apparent requirement would be to begin with the verb "istaṭā'ū" and follow it with "isṭā'ū," because the latter is heavy when repeated, as occurred in His saying earlier: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Among the distinctive features of departing here from the apparent requirement is the preference for a verb with an added element in its form in a position where an added meaning is intended, because the ability to breach the barrier is stronger than the ability to scale it; this is therefore one of the instances where added form indicates added meaning.

Ḥamzah alone read "fa-mā 'sṭṭā'ū" (famā 'sṭṭā'ū), the first with a shaddah on the ṭā', the tā' being assimilated into it.

His saying ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafah) of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), because when the discourse signalled the end of the description of the barrier, this prompted the question of someone asking: "What did Dhu al-Qarnayn say when he completed this great work?" It is answered by the sentence "He said, 'This is a mercy from my Lord.'" The demonstrative "this" refers to the barrier. It is a mercy to people, because in it there is the averting of the corruption of the nation of Ya'juj and Ma'juj from another righteous nation.

The "min" is for origin (ibtidā'iyyah). It is attributed to God because God inspired him to that and made easy for him what was difficult.

On this is based His saying ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakkā)﴾, as a statement of wisdom, because he knows that every occurrence passes into cessation. And because he knew that a great work like that requires care and preservation against collapse. And he knew that this cannot be achieved in some periods of the decline of the kingdom, which is unavoidable for every holder of authority.

"Al-wa'd" (promise) is the announcement of a future matter, and by it he meant the term that is in God's knowledge, at which the continuance of that barrier will end. So the name "promise" was borrowed for it. It is also possible that God revealed to him, if he was a prophet, or inspired him, if he was a righteous man, that the barrier has a specific term at which it ends.

The beginning of that promise was the day the Prophet ﷺ said: "The barrier of Ya'juj has been opened today this much," and he made a ring with his thumb and forefinger, as previously mentioned.

The word "dakk" in the reading of the majority is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle for emphasis, meaning: He made it levelled (madkūk), that is, made level with the ground after being raised. 'Asim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "ja'alahu dakkā'" with a long vowel. "Dakkā'" is the name for a she-camel without a hump, and this is an eloquent comparison.

His saying ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyīl) affirming the knowledge that it must have a term at which it ends, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every term there is a decree, and for every nation there is a term﴾. That is, God's appointing of terms for things is ever a firm truth that does not fail. This sentence, in its generality and in the wisdom it contains, is a wonderful concluding sentence.

﴿And We left some of them on that day surging over one another﴾ [al-Kahf: 99]. Al-tark (leaving): its literal meaning is parting from a thing that was near to one, and it is used figuratively for placing a thing in a state different from a previous state, by way of likening the state of its being left in a condition to the state of one who was near a thing and then departed from it. This figurative use is restricted only by a state in which the object of "tark" was, so it indicates that this is the last stage of the connection, and this implies that it remains in the state in which it was left, by the context.

The sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence preceding it, beginning from His saying ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. "Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is the day of completing the construction of the barrier, which is understood from His saying ﴿so they were not able to scale it﴾, the verse.

"Yamūj" means: to be in turmoil, likened to the surging of the sea.

The sentence "yamūju" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "baʿḍihim," or a second object of "taraknā," according to its interpretation as "ja'alnā" (We made). He made the iron bars supported by molten copper poured over the iron.

Al-Zubar: the plural of zubrah, which is a large piece of iron. Iron is one of the metals of the earth; it occurs in pieces like pebbles, and in its lesser forms it has hardness. It is initially classified into two types: soft, which is called the female iron (al-hadid al-unthā), and hard, which is called the male (al-dhakar). Then it is classified into eighteen types. Its colours are close to one another: it is grey-blue (sinjabi), and some of it tends toward red while some tends toward white. When it is smelted with a strong fire in a closed furnace (utun), its parts join together and gather in the middle of the fire like a sponge, and its hardness increases, because by smelting it expels the earthy parts it contains, which are called rust (sada') and dross (khabath), and those parts rise to its surface, and this is the scum (zabad). The hadith, "Indeed, Madinah expels its dross as the bellows expels the dross of iron" [Khabath al-hadid], is relevant here; accordingly, in proportion as those foreign, impure parts float off, the iron part becomes pure and clear and becomes zubar. From these zubar are made iron objects such as swords, glass (zujaj), armour (durū') and coats of mail (la'amat). There is no way to make it except also by smelting with fire, to the point that the zubrah becomes like glowing embers; then it is shaped into the intended form by means of iron hammers.

The era in which mankind was guided to the craft of iron-working is called in history the Iron Age.

His saying ﴿until, when he had made level between the two cliffs﴾ — the word "until" (ḥattā) indicates something preceding it that is implied, and this is an omitted clause whose estimated meaning is: "So they brought him the zubar of iron, and he arranged them and built them, until, when he had placed [it] between the two cliffs." This is from the conciseness of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf). Equalising (al-musāwāt) is making things equal, that is, similar in quantity or description.

"Al-ṣadafayn," with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the dāl, is the reading of the majority, and it is the best known. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and the dāl, and this is a dialectal form (lughah). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a sukun on the dāl.

Al-ṣadaf: the side of a mountain. The two sides of the two mountains are the two barriers (al-saddān). Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qazwini in al-Kashf said: it is only said "ṣadafān" in the dual, and one of them is not called ṣadaf, because each of them faces (yuṣādif) the other; so "al-ṣadafān" is the name for the combined two sides, like "al-miqaṣṣān" (the scissors) for that by which cloth or the like is cut.

From Abu 'Isa: al-ṣadaf is every great, high structure.

The address in His saying "blow" (unfukhū) and His saying "bring me" (ātūnī) is addressed to the workers. The object of "blow" is omitted because it is evident from the fact that the work is the making of iron. The estimated meaning is: "Blow into the bellows arranged along the length of what lies between the two cliffs of iron zubar."

The majority read "ātūnī" like the first.

Ḥamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ī'tūnī" (i'tūnī), as an imperative from al-ityān, meaning: he ordered them to attend to the work.

Al-qiṭr, with a kasrah on the qāf: molten copper.

The pronoun in "isṭā'ū" and "istaṭā'ū" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

Al-ẓuhūr: ascending. Al-naqb: breaking through the barrier. Their inability to do that is due to its height and hardness.

"Isṭā'ū" is a lightened form of "istaṭā'ū." Combining the two is a variation in eloquent speech, out of dislike of repeating the same word. The lighter of the two is mentioned first, because it is followed by the hamzah, which is a heavy letter as it comes from the throat, unlike the second, since it is followed by the lām, which is light.

The apparent requirement would be to begin with the verb "istaṭā'ū" and follow it with "isṭā'ū," because the latter is heavy when repeated, as occurred in His saying earlier: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Among the distinctive features of departing here from the apparent requirement is the preference for a verb with an added element in its form in a position where an added meaning is intended, because the ability to breach the barrier is stronger than the ability to scale it; this is therefore one of the instances where added form indicates added meaning.

Ḥamzah alone read "fa-mā 'sṭṭā'ū" (famā 'sṭṭā'ū), the first with a shaddah on the ṭā', the tā' being assimilated into it.

His saying ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafah) of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), because when the discourse signalled the end of the description of the barrier, this prompted the question of someone asking: "What did Dhu al-Qarnayn say when he completed this great work?" It is answered by the sentence "He said, 'This is a mercy from my Lord.'" The demonstrative "this" refers to the barrier. It is a mercy to people, because in it there is the averting of the corruption of the nation of Ya'juj and Ma'juj from another righteous nation.

The "min" is for origin (ibtidā'iyyah). It is attributed to God because God inspired him to that and made easy for him what was difficult.

On this is based His saying ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakkā)﴾, as a statement of wisdom, because he knows that every occurrence passes into cessation. And because he knew that a great work like that requires care and preservation against collapse. And he knew that this cannot be achieved in some periods of the decline of the kingdom, which is unavoidable for every holder of authority.

"Al-wa'd" (promise) is the announcement of a future matter, and by it he meant the term that is in God's knowledge, at which the continuance of that barrier will end. So the name "promise" was borrowed for it. It is also possible that God revealed to him, if he was a prophet, or inspired him, if he was a righteous man, that the barrier has a specific term at which it ends.

The beginning of that promise was the day the Prophet ﷺ said: "The barrier of Ya'juj has been opened today this much," and he made a ring with his thumb and forefinger, as previously mentioned.

The word "dakk" in the reading of the majority is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle for emphasis, meaning: He made it levelled (madkūk), that is, made level with the ground after being raised. 'Asim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "ja'alahu dakkā'" with a long vowel. "Dakkā'" is the name for a she-camel without a hump, and this is an eloquent comparison.

His saying ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyīl) affirming the knowledge that it must have a term at which it ends, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every term there is a decree, and for every nation there is a term﴾. That is, God's appointing of terms for things is ever a firm truth that does not fail. This sentence, in its generality and in the wisdom it contains, is a wonderful concluding sentence.

﴿And We left some of them on that day surging over one another﴾ [al-Kahf: 99]. Al-tark (leaving): its literal meaning is parting from a thing that was near to one, and it is used figuratively for placing a thing in a state different from a previous state, by way of likening the state of its being left in a condition to the state of one who was near a thing and then departed from it. This figurative use is restricted only by a state in which the object of "tark" was, so it indicates that this is the last stage of the connection, and this implies that it remains in the state in which it was left, by the context.

The sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence preceding it, beginning from His saying ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. So this sentence mentions the act of God Exalted in this third story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, when He inspired him to repel the corruption of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. It is in the same position as the sentence ﴿We said, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness"﴾ [al-Kahf: 86] in the first story, and the sentence ﴿Thus, and We had encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], so the manner of narrating these three stories follows one pattern.

"Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is the day of completing the construction of the barrier, which is understood from His saying ﴿so they were not able to scale it﴾, the verse.

"Yamūj" means: to be in turmoil, likened to the surging of the sea.

The sentence "yamūju" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "baʿḍihim," or a second object of "taraknā," according to its interpretation as "ja'alnā" (We made). That is: We made Ya'juj and Ma'juj on that day turbulent among themselves, so their corruption became confined to themselves and was averted from others.

Fire devours itself if it finds nothing to devour.

For when they do not find what they were accustomed to, namely raiding the neighbouring nations, the strong among them turn upon the weak by aggression.

Page 31

**Al-Sudd** (the barrier), with a *ḍamma* or a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, means a mountain. It is also applied to a dividing wall, because space is blocked (*yusaddu*) with it. It was said that the *ḍamma* is used for a mountain and the *fatḥa* for a barrier.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim), Abū Jaʿfar, Khalaf and Yaʿqūb read it with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ (from ʿĀṣim) read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, following the dialect that does not distinguish between them. Here, "the two barriers" (*al-saddayn*) means two mountains, and "a single barrier" (*al-sadd al-mufrad*) means a dividing wall. The context is what specifies the intended meaning of this shared term.

The definite article in *al-saddayn* is the article of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), meaning "between two specific barriers", that is, he followed another route on a campaign until he reached between two known mountains.

It appears that he headed in a direction other than east or west, so it may be north or south. The commentators specified that it was north, and they based this on the view that Dhū al-Qarnayn was Alexander the Macedonian. They said that the location of the two barriers was between Armenia and Azerbaijan. We build on what we have identified concerning the one called Dhū al-Qarnayn, and we say that the site of the two barriers is the north-west of the Gobi Desert, which separates China from the lands of the Mongols, north of China and south of Mongolia. The barrier was found there, and its traces remain to this day. Geographers and travellers have seen it, and it has been photographed in modern geography and history books.

The meaning of ﴿who scarcely understand any speech﴾ is that they do not know any of the speech of others. Their language differs from the languages of the known nations, to the extent that the interpreters of Dhū al-Qarnayn do not know it. This is because it is the custom of kings to employ interpreters to translate the languages of the peoples with whom they need to communicate. These people spoke a strange language because their lands were cut off from the known regions, so there was no one who could make them understand the king's meaning, nor could they make themselves understood.

It is also possible that the meaning is that they are a people deeply immersed in primitiveness and foolishness, so they do not understand what the one addressing them intends.

Page 32

Al-Jumhūr read *yafqahūna* with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* (the letter with two dots below) and a *fatḥa* on the *qāf*, meaning they do not understand the speech of others. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a *kasra* on the *qāf*, meaning they cannot make others understand their speech. The two meanings are mutually implied. This is like the hadith about faith: "We hear the buzzing of his voice but do not understand what he says."

These people were neighbours of Yājūj and Mājūj. They were weaker than them, so they asked Dhū al-Qarnayn to protect them from the corruption of Yājūj and Mājūj. The commentators did not mention the identification of these people, nor the names of their tribe, except that they said they were in the remote region of the Turks towards the east, and that they were righteous people. There is no doubt that they were among the tribes of the lands of China, which border the lands of the Mongols and the Tatars.

The sentence ﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*) introducing the dialogue. We have explained elsewhere that sentences reporting speech in dialogues are not connected by a conjunction, as in His saying, ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who will spread corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. According to the first of the two possibilities regarding the meaning of ﴿who scarcely understand any speech﴾, they do not grasp what is required of them in terms of obedience and order, yet they express what is in their souls of desires in the manner of children's expression. According to the second possibility, it was possible for their meaning to be understood after some difficulty.

Their opening of the speech with a call (*nidāʾ*) means that they called him with the call of those seeking help who are in distress. Their addressing him with the title Dhū al-Qarnayn indicates that this title was well known among the nations bordering his lands, with its meaning.

Yājūj and Mājūj are a people of great numbers. It is possible that the *wāw* between the two names is a conjunction, so they would be one nation consisting of two peoples. They are the Mongols and some categories of the Tatars. This is the most fitting for the original form of the word, especially on the view that the two are Arabic names, as will come. The two groups were neighbours.

Page 33

Historians and genealogists have differed over the application of the names Mongols and Tatars, each applying to the other, because it is difficult to distinguish between two closely related groups. Some scholars have said that the Mongols are Mājūj, with a *mīm*, the name of their ancestor, also called Sikīshūs. The general name that gathered the two tribes was Mājūj. Then the nation divided and its branches were given specific names. Among them are Mājūj, Yājūj, Tatar, then the Turkmen, then the Turks. It is possible that the *wāw* mentioned is not a conjunction, but it came in the form of one, so the expression is a single compound word formed by fusion (*tarkīb mazjī*). Thus it forms the name of one nation, namely the Mongols.

What must be relied upon is that Yājūj and Mājūj are the Mongols and the Tatars.

Abū al-Fidāʾ mentioned that Mājūj are the Mongols, so Yājūj are the Tatars. The Tatars greatly outnumbered the Mongols, so the Mongols merged into the Tatars, and the name Tatar prevailed over the two tribes. The clearest evidence for this is what came in the hadith of Umm Ḥabībah from Zaynab bint Jaḥsh: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her in alarm, saying: 'There is no god but Allah. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today a gap has been opened in the barrier of Yājūj and Mājūj like this,' and he made a circle with his thumb and the finger next to it." This has been mentioned earlier.

The exact time of their departure from their lands is not known, nor the reason for it. It is estimated that their departure was towards the end of the sixth century AH. The dispersal of the Arab kingdom at the hands of the Mongols and Tatars came with the emergence of Genghis Khan the Mongol and his seizure of Bukhara in the year 616 AH. They reached Diyar Bakr in the year 628 AH, then came the destruction of Baghdad, capital of the Arab kingdom, by Hulagu in the year 660 AH.

A parallel to applying two names to one tribal group formed of two tribes is the application of Tasm and Jadīs to an extinct Arab nation. Also the application of al-Sakākik and al-Sakaran to Yemeni tribes, and of Hilāl and Zighbah to the Bedouin of Ifriqiya who came from the Upper Egypt region. Also the application of Awlād Yaḥyā to a clan in Tunisia in the south-west, and Murādah and Farjān to a clan from the land of Nābul in Tunisia.

Al-Jumhūr read *Yājūj wa-Mājūj* both times with an *alif* after the *yāʾ* (the letter with two dots below), without a hamza. ʿĀṣim read it with a hamza.

The commentators differed over whether it is an Arabic name or an Arabicised foreign word (*muʿarrab*). My strong opinion is that it is a name that the Qur'an created, through which it reproduced its meaning in the language of that nation, appropriate to the condition of their society. Thus the two names were derived from the root *ajj*, which means mixing, since you know that this nation was a mixture of categories.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Shall We then set up for you﴾ is used for offering (*ʿarḍ*).

*Kharj* is the money paid to the king. It is pronounced with a *fatḥa* on the *khāʾ* (with a dot) and a sukūn on the *rāʾ* in the reading of al-Jumhūr. It is also said *kharāj*, with an *alif* after the *rāʾ*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it this way.

Al-Jumhūr read *saddan* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*.

His saying ﴿What my Lord has established me in is better﴾ means: what Allah has given me of wealth and power is better than the tribute you have offered, from the barrier you have asked for. That is, what my Lord has established me in is better than what you ask, for it occurred to him that if he blocked their passage between the two cliffs, they would find a way, climb the mountains and enter the land of China. So he intended to build a wall extending along the mountains along the length of the borders of the land, so that it would be impossible for them to climb those mountains.

For this reason he called it a *radm* (barrier).

Page 35

The *radm* is a built structure that has been packed (*murddam*). It is likened to a patched garment composed of pieces upon pieces, that is, a doubled barrier. Perhaps he built two walls far apart and filled the gap between them with mixed earth, so that it could not be breached.

Since that required many workers, he said to them ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is, with bodily strength. He intended to conscript them for the work to ward off harm from them.

Dhū al-Qarnayn, who is Qin Shi Huang, the emperor of China, built this barrier in a remarkable manner in the third century BC, and millions of labourers worked on it. He made its length three thousand three hundred kilometres. Some say it was twelve hundred miles, depending on differences in the standard of the mile. He made its starting point at the sea, that is the Yellow Sea, east of the city of Beijing, the capital of China, in the line of direction of the famous city of Mukden. That is at latitude 40.4° north and longitude 120.2° east. It meets the Yellow River where the longitude is 111.50° east and the latitude 39.50° north, and also at latitude 37° north. From there it turns towards the north-west and ends near longitude 99° east and latitude 40° north.

It is built of stone and brick, and part of it of clay alone.

Its thickness at the base is about 25 feet and at the top about 15 feet, and its height ranges between 15 and 20 feet. On it are towers built of tiles, some of which are about 40 feet high.

It is now in a state of ruin, so it has no defensive value.

However, it has remained a marker of the dividing line between the administrative regions of the land, so it separates China from Mongolia. It cuts through the Babulony mountains, which are a natural border between China and the land of Mongolia, so its far end is at the north-west of the Gobi Desert.

This figurative use is restricted only by a state in which the object of "tark" was, so it indicates that this is the last stage of the connection, and this implies that it remains in the state in which it was left, by the context.

The sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence preceding it, beginning from His saying ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. So this sentence mentions the act of God Exalted in this third story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, when He inspired him to repel the corruption of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. It is in the same position as the sentence ﴿We said, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness"﴾ [al-Kahf: 86] in the first story, and the sentence ﴿Thus, and We had encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], so the manner of narrating these three stories follows one pattern.

"Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is the day of completing the construction of the barrier, which is understood from His saying ﴿so they were not able to scale it﴾, the verse.

"Yamūj" means: to be in turmoil, likened to the surging of the sea.

The sentence "yamūju" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "baʿḍihim," or a second object of "taraknā," according to its interpretation as "ja'alnā" (We made). That is: We made Ya'juj and Ma'juj on that day turbulent among themselves, so their corruption became confined to themselves and was averted from others.

Fire devours itself if it finds nothing to devour.

For when they do not find what they were accustomed to, namely raiding the neighbouring nations, the strong among them turn upon the weak by aggression.

**Al-Sudd** (the barrier), with a *ḍamma* or a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, means a mountain. It is also applied to a dividing wall, because space is blocked (*yusaddu*) with it. It was said that the *ḍamma* is used for a mountain and the *fatḥa* for a barrier.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim), Abū Jaʿfar, Khalaf and Yaʿqūb read it with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Here, "the two barriers" (*al-saddayn*) means two mountains, and "a single barrier" (*al-sadd al-mufrad*) means a dividing wall. The context is what specifies the intended meaning of this shared term.

The definite article in *al-saddayn* is the article of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), meaning "between two specific barriers", that is, he followed another route on a campaign until he reached between two known mountains.

It appears that he headed in a direction other than east or west, so it may be north or south. The commentators specified that it was north, and they based this on the view that Dhū al-Qarnayn was Alexander the Macedonian. They said that the location of the two barriers was between Armenia and Azerbaijan. We build on what we have identified concerning the one called Dhū al-Qarnayn, and we say that the site of the two barriers is the north-west of the Gobi Desert, which separates China from the lands of the Mongols, north of China and south of Mongolia. The barrier was found there, and its traces remain to this day. Geographers and travellers have seen it, and it has been photographed in modern geography and history books.

The meaning of ﴿who scarcely understand any speech﴾ is that they do not know any of the speech of others. Their language differs from the languages of the known nations, to the extent that the interpreters of Dhū al-Qarnayn do not know it. This is because it is the custom of kings to employ interpreters to translate the languages of the peoples with whom they need to communicate. These people spoke a strange language because their lands were cut off from the known regions, so there was no one who could make them understand the king's meaning, nor could they make themselves understood.

It is also possible that the meaning is that they are a people deeply immersed in primitiveness and foolishness, so they do not understand what the one addressing them intends.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a *kasra* on the *qāf*, meaning they cannot make others understand their speech. The two meanings are mutually implied. These people were neighbours of Yājūj and Mājūj. They were weaker than them, so they asked Dhū al-Qarnayn to protect them from the corruption of Yājūj and Mājūj. The commentators did not mention the identification of these people, nor the names of their tribe, except that they said they were in the remote region of the Turks towards the east, and that they were righteous people. There is no doubt that they were among the tribes of the lands of China, which border the lands of the Mongols and the Tatars.

The sentence ﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*) introducing the dialogue. We have explained elsewhere that sentences reporting speech in dialogues are not connected by a conjunction, as in His saying, ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who will spread corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. According to the first of the two possibilities regarding the meaning of ﴿who scarcely understand any speech﴾, they do not grasp what is required of them in terms of obedience and order, yet they express what is in their souls of desires in the manner of children's expression. According to the second possibility, it was possible for their meaning to be understood after some difficulty.

Their opening of the speech with a call (*nidāʾ*) means that they called him with the call of those seeking help who are in distress. Their addressing him with the title Dhū al-Qarnayn indicates that this title was well known among the nations bordering his lands, with its meaning.

Yājūj and Mājūj are a people of great numbers. It is possible that the *wāw* between the two names is a conjunction, so they would be one nation consisting of two peoples. Historians and genealogists have differed over the application of the names Mongols and Tatars, each applying to the other, because it is difficult to distinguish between two closely related groups. Some scholars have said that the Mongols are Mājūj, with a *mīm*, the name of their ancestor, also called Sikīshūs. The general name that gathered the two tribes was Mājūj. Then the nation divided and its branches were given specific names. Among them are Mājūj, Yājūj, Tatar, then the Turkmen, then the Turks. It is possible that the *wāw* mentioned is not a conjunction, but it came in the form of one, so the expression is a single compound word formed by fusion (*tarkīb mazjī*). Thus it forms the name of one nation, namely the Mongols.

What must be relied upon is that Yājūj and Mājūj are the Mongols and the Tatars.

Abū al-Fidāʾ mentioned that Mājūj are the Mongols, so Yājūj are the Tatars. The Tatars greatly outnumbered the Mongols, so the Mongols merged into the Tatars, and the name Tatar prevailed over the two tribes. The clearest evidence for this is what came in the hadith of Umm Ḥabībah from Zaynab bint Jaḥsh: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her in alarm, saying: 'There is no god but Allah. This has been mentioned earlier.

The exact time of their departure from their lands is not known, nor the reason for it. It is estimated that their departure was towards the end of the sixth century AH. The dispersal of the Arab kingdom at the hands of the Mongols and Tatars came with the emergence of Genghis Khan the Mongol and his seizure of Bukhara in the year 616 AH. They reached Diyar Bakr in the year 628 AH, then came the destruction of Baghdad, capital of the Arab kingdom, by Hulagu in the year 660 AH.

A parallel to applying two names to one tribal group formed of two tribes is the application of Tasm and Jadīs to an extinct Arab nation. Also the application of al-Sakākik and al-Sakaran to Yemeni tribes, and of Hilāl and Zighbah to the Bedouin of Ifriqiya who came from the Upper Egypt region. Also the application of Awlād Yaḥyā to a clan in Tunisia in the south-west, and Murādah and Farjān to a clan from the land of Nābul in Tunisia.

Al-Jumhūr read *Yājūj wa-Mājūj* both times with an *alif* after the *yāʾ* (the letter with two dots below), without a hamza. ʿĀṣim read it with a hamza.

The commentators differed over whether it is an Arabic name or an Arabicised foreign word (*muʿarrab*). My strong opinion is that it is a name that the Qur'an created, through which it reproduced its meaning in the language of that nation, appropriate to the condition of their society. Thus the two names were derived from the root *ajj*, which means mixing, since you know that this nation was a mixture of categories.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Shall We then set up for you﴾ is used for offering (*ʿarḍ*).

*Kharj* is the money paid to the king. It is pronounced with a *fatḥa* on the *khāʾ* (with a dot) and a sukūn on the *rāʾ* in the reading of al-Jumhūr. It is also said *kharāj*, with an *alif* after the *rāʾ*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it this way.

Al-Jumhūr read *saddan* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*.

His saying ﴿What my Lord has established me in is better﴾ means: what Allah has given me of wealth and power is better than the tribute you have offered, from the barrier you have asked for. That is, what my Lord has established me in is better than what you ask, for it occurred to him that if he blocked their passage between the two cliffs, they would find a way, climb the mountains and enter the land of China. So he intended to build a wall extending along the mountains along the length of the borders of the land, so that it would be impossible for them to climb those mountains.

For this reason he called it a *radm* (barrier).

Page 35

The *radm* is a built structure that has been packed (*murddam*). It is likened to a patched garment composed of pieces upon pieces, that is, a doubled barrier. Perhaps he built two walls far apart and filled the gap between them with mixed earth, so that it could not be breached.

Since that required many workers, he said to them ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is, with bodily strength. He intended to conscript them for the work to ward off harm from them.

Dhū al-Qarnayn, who is Qin Shi Huang, the emperor of China, built this barrier in a remarkable manner in the third century BC, and millions of labourers worked on it. He made its length three thousand three hundred kilometres. Some say it was twelve hundred miles, depending on differences in the standard of the mile. He made its starting point at the sea, that is the Yellow Sea, east of the city of Beijing, the capital of China, in the line of direction of the famous city of Mukden. That is at latitude 40.4° north and longitude 120.2° east. It meets the Yellow River where the longitude is 111.50° east and the latitude 39.50° north, and also at latitude 37° north. From there it turns towards the north-west and ends near longitude 99° east and latitude 40° north.

It is built of stone and brick, and part of it of clay alone.

Its thickness at the base is about 25 feet and at the top about 15 feet, and its height ranges between 15 and 20 feet. On it are towers built of tiles, some of which are about 40 feet high.

It is now in a state of ruin, so it has no defensive value.

However, it has remained a marker of the dividing line between the administrative regions of the land, so it separates China from Mongolia. It cuts through the Babulony mountains, which are a natural border between China and the land of Mongolia, so its far end is at the north-west of the Gobi Desert.

Al-Jumhūr read *makkannī* with an assimilated nūn. Ibn Kathīr read it with the nūn unassimilated, according to the original form.

His saying ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ is a command to them to hand him blocks of iron. Here the verb *ātā* (bring) is used in its literal meaning, which is handing over, and it is not an obligation on the people to bring the iron from its mines, because that would contradict His saying (﴿What my Lord has established me in is better, so help me with strength﴾), meaning that he was independent of their obligation to spend on building the barrier. This was for the purpose of constructing iron doors at the entrances of the barrier, so that the floodwaters flowing through the mountain gullies would not demolish the structure. The iron doors were like grilles, preventing people from passing through but not preventing the water from flowing between their bars. He made the iron bars supported by molten copper poured over the iron.

Al-Zubar: the plural of zubrah, which is a large piece of iron. Iron is one of the metals of the earth; it occurs in pieces like pebbles, and in its lesser forms it has hardness. It is initially classified into two types: soft, which is called the female iron (al-hadid al-unthā), and hard, which is called the male (al-dhakar). Then it is classified into eighteen types. Its colours are close to one another: it is grey-blue (sinjabi), and some of it tends toward red while some tends toward white. When it is smelted with a strong fire in a closed furnace (utun), its parts join together and gather in the middle of the fire like a sponge, and its hardness increases, because by smelting it expels the earthy parts it contains, which are called rust (sada') and dross (khabath), and those parts rise to its surface, and this is the scum (zabad). The hadith, "Indeed, Madinah expels its dross as the bellows expels the dross of iron" [Khabath al-hadid], is relevant here; accordingly, in proportion as those foreign, impure parts float off, the iron part becomes pure and clear and becomes zubar. From these zubar are made iron objects such as swords, glass (zujaj), armour (durū') and coats of mail (la'amat). There is no way to make it except also by smelting with fire, to the point that the zubrah becomes like glowing embers; then it is shaped into the intended form by means of iron hammers.

The era in which mankind was guided to the craft of iron-working is called in history the Iron Age.

His saying ﴿until, when he had made level between the two cliffs﴾ — the word "until" (ḥattā) indicates something preceding it that is implied, and this is an omitted clause whose estimated meaning is: "So they brought him the zubar of iron, and he arranged them and built them, until, when he had placed [it] between the two cliffs." This is from the conciseness of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf). Equalising (al-musāwāt) is making things equal, that is, similar in quantity or description.

"Al-ṣadafayn," with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the dāl, is the reading of the majority, and it is the best known. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and the dāl, and this is a dialectal form (lughah). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a sukun on the dāl.

Al-ṣadaf: the side of a mountain. The two sides of the two mountains are the two barriers (al-saddān). Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qazwini in al-Kashf said: it is only said "ṣadafān" in the dual, and one of them is not called ṣadaf, because each of them faces (yuṣādif) the other; so "al-ṣadafān" is the name for the combined two sides, like "al-miqaṣṣān" (the scissors) for that by which cloth or the like is cut.

From Abu 'Isa: al-ṣadaf is every great, high structure.

The address in His saying "blow" (unfukhū) and His saying "bring me" (ātūnī) is addressed to the workers. The object of "blow" is omitted because it is evident from the fact that the work is the making of iron. The estimated meaning is: "Blow into the bellows arranged along the length of what lies between the two cliffs of iron zubar."

The majority read "ātūnī" like the first.

Ḥamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ī'tūnī" (i'tūnī), as an imperative from al-ityān, meaning: he ordered them to attend to the work.

Al-qiṭr, with a kasrah on the qāf: molten copper.

The pronoun in "isṭā'ū" and "istaṭā'ū" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

Al-ẓuhūr: ascending. Al-naqb: breaking through the barrier. Their inability to do that is due to its height and hardness.

"Isṭā'ū" is a lightened form of "istaṭā'ū." Combining the two is a variation in eloquent speech, out of dislike of repeating the same word. The lighter of the two is mentioned first, because it is followed by the hamzah, which is a heavy letter as it comes from the throat, unlike the second, since it is followed by the lām, which is light.

The apparent requirement would be to begin with the verb "istaṭā'ū" and follow it with "isṭā'ū," because the latter is heavy when repeated, as occurred in His saying earlier: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Among the distinctive features of departing here from the apparent requirement is the preference for a verb with an added element in its form in a position where an added meaning is intended, because the ability to breach the barrier is stronger than the ability to scale it; this is therefore one of the instances where added form indicates added meaning.

Ḥamzah alone read "fa-mā 'sṭṭā'ū" (famā 'sṭṭā'ū), the first with a shaddah on the ṭā', the tā' being assimilated into it.

His saying ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafah) of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), because when the discourse signalled the end of the description of the barrier, this prompted the question of someone asking: "What did Dhu al-Qarnayn say when he completed this great work?" It is a mercy to people, because in it there is the averting of the corruption of the nation of Ya'juj and Ma'juj from another righteous nation.

The "min" is for origin (ibtidā'iyyah). It is attributed to God because God inspired him to that and made easy for him what was difficult.

On this is based His saying ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakkā)﴾, as a statement of wisdom, because he knows that every occurrence passes into cessation. And he knew that this cannot be achieved in some periods of the decline of the kingdom, which is unavoidable for every holder of authority.

So the name "promise" was borrowed for it.
