The exact time of their departure from their lands is not known, nor the reason for it. It is estimated that their departure was towards the end of the sixth century AH. The dispersal of the Arab kingdom at the hands of the Mongols and Tatars came with the emergence of Genghis Khan the Mongol and his seizure of Bukhara in the year 616 AH. They reached Diyar Bakr in the year 628 AH, then came the destruction of Baghdad, capital of the Arab kingdom, by Hulagu in the year 660 AH.

A parallel to applying two names to one tribal group formed of two tribes is the application of Tasm and Jadīs to an extinct Arab nation. Also the application of al-Sakākik and al-Sakaran to Yemeni tribes, and of Hilāl and Zighbah to the Bedouin of Ifriqiya who came from the Upper Egypt region. Also the application of Awlād Yaḥyā to a clan in Tunisia in the south-west, and Murādah and Farjān to a clan from the land of Nābul in Tunisia.

Al-Jumhūr read *Yājūj wa-Mājūj* both times with an *alif* after the *yāʾ* (the letter with two dots below), without a hamza. ʿĀṣim read it with a hamza.

The commentators differed over whether it is an Arabic name or an Arabicised foreign word (*muʿarrab*). My strong opinion is that it is a name that the Qur'an created, through which it reproduced its meaning in the language of that nation, appropriate to the condition of their society. Thus the two names were derived from the root *ajj*, which means mixing, since you know that this nation was a mixture of categories.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Shall We then set up for you﴾ is used for offering (*ʿarḍ*).

*Kharj* is the money paid to the king. It is pronounced with a *fatḥa* on the *khāʾ* (with a dot) and a sukūn on the *rāʾ* in the reading of al-Jumhūr. It is also said *kharāj*, with an *alif* after the *rāʾ*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it this way.

Al-Jumhūr read *saddan* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*.

His saying ﴿What my Lord has established me in is better﴾ means: what Allah has given me of wealth and power is better than the tribute you have offered, from the barrier you have asked for. That is, what my Lord has established me in is better than what you ask, for it occurred to him that if he blocked their passage between the two cliffs, they would find a way, climb the mountains and enter the land of China. So he intended to build a wall extending along the mountains along the length of the borders of the land, so that it would be impossible for them to climb those mountains.

For this reason he called it a *radm* (barrier).

Page 35

The *radm* is a built structure that has been packed (*murddam*). It is likened to a patched garment composed of pieces upon pieces, that is, a doubled barrier. Perhaps he built two walls far apart and filled the gap between them with mixed earth, so that it could not be breached.

Since that required many workers, he said to them ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is, with bodily strength. He intended to conscript them for the work to ward off harm from them.

Dhū al-Qarnayn, who is Qin Shi Huang, the emperor of China, built this barrier in a remarkable manner in the third century BC, and millions of labourers worked on it. He made its length three thousand three hundred kilometres. Some say it was twelve hundred miles, depending on differences in the standard of the mile. He made its starting point at the sea, that is the Yellow Sea, east of the city of Beijing, the capital of China, in the line of direction of the famous city of Mukden. That is at latitude 40.4° north and longitude 120.2° east. It meets the Yellow River where the longitude is 111.50° east and the latitude 39.50° north, and also at latitude 37° north. From there it turns towards the north-west and ends near longitude 99° east and latitude 40° north.

It is built of stone and brick, and part of it of clay alone.

Its thickness at the base is about 25 feet and at the top about 15 feet, and its height ranges between 15 and 20 feet. On it are towers built of tiles, some of which are about 40 feet high.

It is now in a state of ruin, so it has no defensive value.

However, it has remained a marker of the dividing line between the administrative regions of the land, so it separates China from Mongolia. It cuts through the Babulony mountains, which are a natural border between China and the land of Mongolia, so its far end is at the north-west of the Gobi Desert.

Page 36

Al-Jumhūr read *makkannī* with an assimilated nūn. Ibn Kathīr read it with the nūn unassimilated, according to the original form.

His saying ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ is a command to them to hand him blocks of iron. Here the verb *ātā* (bring) is used in its literal meaning, which is handing over, and it is not an obligation on the people to bring the iron from its mines, because that would contradict His saying (﴿What my Lord has established me in is better, so help me with strength﴾), meaning that he was independent of their obligation to spend on building the barrier. This was for the purpose of constructing iron doors at the entrances of the barrier, so that the floodwaters flowing through the mountain gullies would not demolish the structure. The iron doors were like grilles, preventing people from passing through but not preventing the water from flowing between their bars. He made the iron bars supported by molten copper poured over the iron.

Al-Zubar: the plural of zubrah, which is a large piece of iron. Iron is one of the metals of the earth; it occurs in pieces like pebbles, and in its lesser forms it has hardness. It is initially classified into two types: soft, which is called the female iron (al-hadid al-unthā), and hard, which is called the male (al-dhakar). Then it is classified into eighteen types. Its colours are close to one another: it is grey-blue (sinjabi), and some of it tends toward red while some tends toward white. When it is smelted with a strong fire in a closed furnace (utun), its parts join together and gather in the middle of the fire like a sponge, and its hardness increases, because by smelting it expels the earthy parts it contains, which are called rust (sada') and dross (khabath), and those parts rise to its surface, and this is the scum (zabad). The hadith, "Indeed, Madinah expels its dross as the bellows expels the dross of iron" [Khabath al-hadid], is relevant here; accordingly, in proportion as those foreign, impure parts float off, the iron part becomes pure and clear and becomes zubar. From these zubar are made iron objects such as swords, glass (zujaj), armour (durū') and coats of mail (la'amat). There is no way to make it except also by smelting with fire, to the point that the zubrah becomes like glowing embers; then it is shaped into the intended form by means of iron hammers.

The era in which mankind was guided to the craft of iron-working is called in history the Iron Age.

His saying ﴿until, when he had made level between the two cliffs﴾ — the word "until" (ḥattā) indicates something preceding it that is implied, and this is an omitted clause whose estimated meaning is: "So they brought him the zubar of iron, and he arranged them and built them, until, when he had placed [it] between the two cliffs." This is from the conciseness of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf). Equalising (al-musāwāt) is making things equal, that is, similar in quantity or description.

"Al-ṣadafayn," with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the dāl, is the reading of the majority, and it is the best known. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and the dāl, and this is a dialectal form (lughah). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a sukun on the dāl.

Al-ṣadaf: the side of a mountain. The two sides of the two mountains are the two barriers (al-saddān). Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qazwini in al-Kashf said: it is only said "ṣadafān" in the dual, and one of them is not called ṣadaf, because each of them faces (yuṣādif) the other; so "al-ṣadafān" is the name for the combined two sides, like "al-miqaṣṣān" (the scissors) for that by which cloth or the like is cut.

From Abu 'Isa: al-ṣadaf is every great, high structure.

The address in His saying "blow" (unfukhū) and His saying "bring me" (ātūnī) is addressed to the workers. The object of "blow" is omitted because it is evident from the fact that the work is the making of iron. The estimated meaning is: "Blow into the bellows arranged along the length of what lies between the two cliffs of iron zubar."

The majority read "ātūnī" like the first.

Ḥamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ī'tūnī" (i'tūnī), as an imperative from al-ityān, meaning: he ordered them to attend to the work.

Al-qiṭr, with a kasrah on the qāf: molten copper.

The pronoun in "isṭā'ū" and "istaṭā'ū" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

Al-ẓuhūr: ascending. Al-naqb: breaking through the barrier. Their inability to do that is due to its height and hardness.

"Isṭā'ū" is a lightened form of "istaṭā'ū." Combining the two is a variation in eloquent speech, out of dislike of repeating the same word. The lighter of the two is mentioned first, because it is followed by the hamzah, which is a heavy letter as it comes from the throat, unlike the second, since it is followed by the lām, which is light.

The apparent requirement would be to begin with the verb "istaṭā'ū" and follow it with "isṭā'ū," because the latter is heavy when repeated, as occurred in His saying earlier: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Among the distinctive features of departing here from the apparent requirement is the preference for a verb with an added element in its form in a position where an added meaning is intended, because the ability to breach the barrier is stronger than the ability to scale it; this is therefore one of the instances where added form indicates added meaning.

Ḥamzah alone read "fa-mā 'sṭṭā'ū" (famā 'sṭṭā'ū), the first with a shaddah on the ṭā', the tā' being assimilated into it.

His saying ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafah) of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), because when the discourse signalled the end of the description of the barrier, this prompted the question of someone asking: "What did Dhu al-Qarnayn say when he completed this great work?" It is answered by the sentence "He said, 'This is a mercy from my Lord.'" The demonstrative "this" refers to the barrier. It is a mercy to people, because in it there is the averting of the corruption of the nation of Ya'juj and Ma'juj from another righteous nation.

The "min" is for origin (ibtidā'iyyah). It is attributed to God because God inspired him to that and made easy for him what was difficult.

On this is based His saying ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakkā)﴾, as a statement of wisdom, because he knows that every occurrence passes into cessation. And because he knew that a great work like that requires care and preservation against collapse. And he knew that this cannot be achieved in some periods of the decline of the kingdom, which is unavoidable for every holder of authority.

"Al-wa'd" (promise) is the announcement of a future matter, and by it he meant the term that is in God's knowledge, at which the continuance of that barrier will end. So the name "promise" was borrowed for it. It is also possible that God revealed to him, if he was a prophet, or inspired him, if he was a righteous man, that the barrier has a specific term at which it ends.

The beginning of that promise was the day the Prophet ﷺ said: "The barrier of Ya'juj has been opened today this much," and he made a ring with his thumb and forefinger, as previously mentioned.

The word "dakk" in the reading of the majority is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle for emphasis, meaning: He made it levelled (madkūk), that is, made level with the ground after being raised. 'Asim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "ja'alahu dakkā'" with a long vowel. "Dakkā'" is the name for a she-camel without a hump, and this is an eloquent comparison.

His saying ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyīl) affirming the knowledge that it must have a term at which it ends, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every term there is a decree, and for every nation there is a term﴾. That is, God's appointing of terms for things is ever a firm truth that does not fail. This sentence, in its generality and in the wisdom it contains, is a wonderful concluding sentence.

﴿And We left some of them on that day surging over one another﴾ [al-Kahf: 99]. Al-tark (leaving): its literal meaning is parting from a thing that was near to one, and it is used figuratively for placing a thing in a state different from a previous state, by way of likening the state of its being left in a condition to the state of one who was near a thing and then departed from it. This figurative use is restricted only by a state in which the object of "tark" was, so it indicates that this is the last stage of the connection, and this implies that it remains in the state in which it was left, by the context.

The sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence preceding it, beginning from His saying ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. So this sentence mentions the act of God Exalted in this third story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, when He inspired him to repel the corruption of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. It is in the same position as the sentence ﴿We said, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or treat them with kindness"﴾ [al-Kahf: 86] in the first story, and the sentence ﴿Thus, and We had encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], so the manner of narrating these three stories follows one pattern.

"Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is the day of completing the construction of the barrier, which is understood from His saying ﴿so they were not able to scale it﴾, the verse.

"Yamūj" means: to be in turmoil, likened to the surging of the sea.

The sentence "yamūju" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "baʿḍihim," or a second object of "taraknā," according to its interpretation as "ja'alnā" (We made). That is: We made Ya'juj and Ma'juj on that day turbulent among themselves, so their corruption became confined to themselves and was averted from others.

Fire devours itself if it finds nothing to devour.

For when they do not find what they were accustomed to, namely raiding the neighbouring nations, the strong among them turn upon the weak by aggression.

[p. 42]

This is a transition (*takhallus*) from the purposes of reflection on what the story contains, namely the establishment of worldly interests at the hands of those whom God chose from among His close friends to establish them, to the purpose of reminding the listener through admonition about the conditions of the Hereafter. This transition indicates a comparison between the state of their surging with the state of people surging at the place of assembly. It serves to remind the listeners of the matter of the Gathering (*hashr*) and to bring its occurrence closer to the imagination of the polytheists. The One who is able to gather a whole nation behind this barrier, through the act of those among His creatures whom He facilitated for that purpose, is more able to gather the nations at the Gathering by His power, because the objects of power in the world of the Hereafter are more wondrous. It has already been stated that among the most important purposes of this surah is establishing the Resurrection (*al-ba'th*).

The past tense is used in place of the present to emphasize that the event will certainly take place.

The blowing into the Trumpet (*al-nafkh fi al-sur*) is a metaphorical allegory (*tamthiliyyah makniyyah*), comparing the state of the one who calls and is obeyed, and the state of the many-numbered callees who respond swiftly, with the state of soldiers who carry out the commander's order to mobilize by blowing the horn of mobilization, and with the state of the remaining soldiers when they hear the horn of mobilization and hasten to go out. However, it is also permissible that the Trumpet is one of the created things of the Hereafter.

The allegorized condition is a strange state whose details none knows except God, exalted is He.

The emphasis of the two verbs *jama'nahum* ("We gathered them") and *'aradna* ("We presented") by their verbal nouns (*masdar*) is to affirm that the gathering is a true gathering and the presentation is a true presentation, not figurative usage (*majaz*). The indefinite form of *jam'* ("gathering") and *'ard* ("presentation") conveys awe (*tahwil*).

Describing the disbelievers by the relative clause ﴿those whose eyes were under a veil﴾ serves to draw attention to the fact that the content of the relative clause is the cause of Hell being presented to them, meaning: those who were known for this in the world.

*Al-ghita'* ("veil") is used metaphorically for the failure to benefit from sight as an indicator of God's oneness in divinity. The particle *min* here denotes figurative containment, which is the firm settling of the veil over their eyes such that it is as if the eyes were enclosed by the veil.

*'An* here denotes separation, i.e., away from looking at that by which My remembrance is achieved.

The negation of their ability to hear indicates that, because of the intensity of their disbelief, their souls do not comply with listening. The object of *sam'an* ("hearing") is omitted, because the phrase *'an dhikri* ("from My remembrance") indicates it. The estimated meaning is: hearing My signs. Thus, the negation of ability is used to negate desire and to express aversion, as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you call us, and in our ears is deafness."﴾

The presentation of Hell is used to mean displaying it when they overlook it, having been driven toward it, and they know that it is what has been prepared for them. This was likened to a presentation mockingly directed at them, because a presentation is the display of something that arouses desire and appetite.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 102:

[Page 43]

﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants as protectors instead of Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.﴾ This follows the description of their deprivation of benefiting from the evidences of observable things pointing to Allah's oneness, and their turning away from hearing the verses. It comes by way of a consequential denunciation (tafri' al-inkar) of their taking protectors besides Allah, whom they believe to be beneficial to them and to be their helpers. It is a consequential denunciation following the relative clause "those whose eyes were in a covering from My remembrance," because their supposing this arose from the fact that their eyes were in a covering and that they were unable to hear. That is, they supposed a false supposition, so what they supposed did not avail them anything. And because of it, their eyes were in a covering from My remembrance, and they were unable to hear.

The interrogative particle has been placed before the conjunctive fa' because the interrogative holds the beginning of the sentence, and this is common in its like. The disagreement is well known among the scholars of Arabic grammar as to whether the interrogative is moved from a later position (taqdim min ta'khir), or whether the conjunction is upon what follows the interrogative after the deletion of the object of the interrogation, because the conjoined element indicates it. Thus it is estimated here: "Were they secure from My punishment, so they supposed that they might take..." etc. The first of the two opinions is more preferable. Similar instances of this have preceded, such as His saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe for you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The interrogation is denunciatory (inkari). The denunciation against them concerning what they suppose requires that what they assumed is false. A parallel is His saying ﴿Do the people think that they will be left alone?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. The clause "an yattakhidhu" (that they take) takes the place of the two objects of "hasiba" (supposed), because it contains what indicates the two objects, so it resolves into two objects. The estimated meaning is: "Did those who disbelieve suppose My servants to be taking protectors for themselves besides Me?"

The denunciation applies to the second object's complement, namely "awliya'" (protectors), the complement of "yattakhidhu" (take), by virtue of the indication given by the verb "hasiba" that there is a supposed thing that is false. That is, their being protectors in terms of what the true meaning of protection entails, namely protection and help.

[Page 44]

"My servants" applies to the angels, the jinn, the devils, and those of the righteous whom they worshipped, such as 'Isa (peace be upon him). It also applies to the idols by way of predominance (taghlib).

"Min dूनi" (besides Me) is connected to "awliya'" either by making "dūnī" a noun meaning "around" (hawl), i.e., "from around My punishment," and interpreting "awliya'" as meaning "helpers," that is, those who stand between them and My punishment and prevent them from it. Or by making "dūnī" mean "other than Me," i.e., "Did they suppose that they would be independent by means of their protection?"

The verb of taking is put in the present form to indicate its renewal from them and that they do not desist from it.

In the Kashshaf, the verb "yattakhidhu" was taken as referring to the future, i.e., "Did they suppose that they would take My servants as protectors on the Day of Resurrection as they took them in the world?" This is what is indicated by His saying ﴿And We will present Hell on that Day to the disbelievers, a presentation﴾ [al-Kahf: 100], and he compared it to His saying ﴿And on the Day We gather them all, then We say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40], they say, "Glory be to You, You are our Protector, not them." The mention of "those who disbelieve" explicitly, rather than saying "Did they suppose," by repeating the pronoun referring to the disbelievers in the preceding verse, is for the purpose of making the sentence independent in its indication and for increasing the rebuke directed at them.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers﴾ confirms the denial of their benefiting from their protectors, so it affirms that Hell has been prepared for them as a lodging, and there is no escape for them from it. For this reason it is emphasized with the particle "inna."

[Page 45]

"A'tadna" means "a'dadna" (We have prepared); the first dal was changed to ta' because the two letters are close in articulation. "I'dad" means preparation, and it has already been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. The subject was made the pronoun of majesty (Allah) in order to introduce awe into the hearts of the polytheists.

"Nuzul" with two dammas is what is prepared for a guest and visitor of hospitality. The application of the term "nuzul" to punishment is a metaphor whose relation is sarcasm (tahakkum), like the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hosted you, then we hastened your hospitality before dawn, a fierce and crushing one."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 103–104:

﴿Say, "Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in their deeds?"﴾ ﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing good work.﴾ This is an interjected statement (i'tiraD) in an independent initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), prompted by the content of the sentence ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants as protectors instead of Me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 102], and so on. For when they took as protectors those who could not benefit them, and chose idols and worshipped them, and drew near to them by whatever means they could, deluded into thinking that they would ward off harm from them, while in fact they could not avail them anything, their deed was a loss and their effort was vain. The purpose of this sentence is therefore His words ﴿while they think﴾ . . . and so on.

Beginning the sentence with the command to say ("Say") serves to draw the listeners' attention to what is to be said, since such an opening signals that the matter concerns them. Likewise, opening with a question about whether they wish to be informed is a question used in the sense of an offer (istifham musta'mal fi al-'ard), meaning: Would you like us to inform you of the greatest losers in their deeds? It is an offer made in mockery, since He informs them of this without waiting for their consent.

In His words ﴿the greatest losers in their deeds﴾ to the end there is an allusion (tamlih), in that He shifts from the mode of address, which would have been to say to them, "Shall We inform you that you are the greatest losers in deeds?", to the mode of third person, so that they become eager to know who these greatest losers are, and what alarms them is only to learn that the one being spoken of is themselves.

The one being addressed: the polytheists, as a rebuke to them and a warning about what they have neglected of the futility of their effort.

The first-person plural "We" in His words ﴿We inform you﴾ may be the majestic "We" referring to the Essence of God, in the manner of iltifat (shift) within the narration. The apparent requirement would be to say, "Will God inform you," meaning He will inform you. It may also be the plural of the speaker referring to the Messenger ﷺ and to God Exalted, since he informs them of what is revealed to him by his Lord. It may also refer to the Messenger and the Muslims.

His words ﴿those whose effort is lost﴾ are a substitution (badal) for ﴿the greatest losers in their deeds﴾. In this elaboration there is additional excitement toward knowing who these greatest losers are, since He attributes to them descriptions and states which increase the listener's eagerness to know those so described.

Dalal (ḍalāl) means straying from the right path. Their unfruitful effort is likened to walking on a road that does not lead to its destination.

Sa'y (effort) means walking with vigour; here it is a metaphor for action, as was previously mentioned at His words ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving﴾ in Surah al-Isra', that is, they performed deeds by which they drew near to the idols, thinking that these would deliver them to their goals, but they missed the mark, while they thought they were doing good.

Attributing dalal to their effort is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). The meaning is: those who went astray in their effort.

Between yahsabuna (they think) and yuhsinuna (they do well) there is a paronomasia (jinas musahhaf, a near-homophonic pun differing by a diacritic), and both have been cited as examples in the section on jinas.

**Translation:**

﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, so their deeds have become void, and We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection.﴾

This sentence is an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a clause that answers an implied question) following His words ﴿Shall We inform you...﴾ [al-Kahf: 103]. The demonstrative *ism al-ishāra* ("those") is used to distinguish them most fully, so that they are not confused with others, as in His words ﴿And those are the successful ones﴾. It also signals that the people referred to deserve what follows the demonstrative, namely the ruling, because of the attributes that have been ascribed to them.

*Al-āyāt* ("the signs") means the Qur'an and the miracles.

*Al-ḥabṭ* ("voiding") means invalidation and nullification.

The phrase *rabbihim* ("their Lord"), according to the first aspect regarding the *nūn* in ﴿Shall We inform you﴾ [al-Kahf: 103], is an *iẓhār* (explicit noun) in the place of an *iḍmār* (pronoun). The expected form by the apparent rule would be: "Those who disbelieved in Our signs." According to the second and third aspects, it conforms to the apparent rule.

The *nūn* in ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is, according to the first aspect regarding the *nūn* in ﴿Say: Shall We inform you﴾ [al-Kahf: 103], in accordance with the apparent rule.

However, according to the third and fourth aspects, it is an *iltifāt* (shift in grammatical person) from His words *bi-āyāti rabbihim* ("in the signs of their Lord"), and the expected form by the apparent rule would be: "So He will not assign them..."

The negation of assigning weight is used in the sense of not giving any consideration to a thing, and of its insignificance, because people weigh things whose quantities they compete for, while a trivial thing is not weighed. Thus they are likened to despised things by way of *makniyya* (an implicit metaphor), and non-weight is attributed to them as *takhyīl* (imaginative representation).

The non-assigning of weight is made a consequence of the voiding of their deeds, because by the voiding of their deeds they have become despised, having nothing of righteous deeds.

**[p. 48]**

That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers either to what preceded in their threat, in His words ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 102], meaning: that preparation is their recompense.

His words "their recompense" (jaza'uhum) are the predicate (khabar) of the demonstrative. His words "Hell" (jahannam) are a substitute (badal, a substituting apposition) for "their recompense," a "congruent substitute" (badal mutabiq), because the preparation of Hell is the very same as Hell. Repeating the word "Hell" gave it the force of emphasis.

Or the demonstrative refers to something implied in the mind that the context indicates, which the following words clarify, in the manner of using the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) with an implied subject (mubtada'). The sense is: The matter is that: their recompense is Hell.

The "ba'" (bi) is causal (sababiyya), and "ma" is verbal (masdariyya, forming a verbal noun with the following verb), meaning: because of their disbelief.

His words "and they took" (wa-ittakhadhu) are coordinated (ataf) with "they disbelieved," so it belongs to the clause of the verbal "ma." The sense is: and because they took My signs and My messengers in mockery, that is, by their taking of that in this way.

"The messengers" (al-rusul) may be meant literally as the plural, so that it informs about the state of the disbelievers of Quraysh and of the disbelieving nations before them. It may also be meant as the Messenger who was sent to all people, and the plural form is used for him out of exaltation, as in His words ﴿We will answer your call and follow the messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 44].

"Huzu'" (with two dammas) is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), and it is more emphatic than describing with the passive participle form. The sense is: they were very much given to mocking them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verses 107–108:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds – for them will be the Gardens of Firdaws as a lodging﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever; they will not desire any change from them﴾. This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 102], in accordance with the Qur'an's custom of mentioning good tidings after warning.

The emphasis of the sentence (ta'kid) is for the sake of giving it importance, since it came in contrast to the sentence ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 102], which is itself emphasized, lest someone suppose that the reward of the believers is not of equal concern and so not equally emphasized. Along with that, the two emphases strengthen both the warning and the good tidings.

Placing the subject (al-musnad ilayhi), the relative pronoun, with the attribute of faith and doing righteous deeds is for the sake of giving importance to their deeds. For this reason the structure of the sentence corresponding to it was varied, so it did not say: "Their reward is the Garden." A similar style has already occurred in the contrast between the descriptions of the two rewards in the saying of God, Exalted, in this surah: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], then His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds – indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who has done well in deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 30]. In the use of "kānat" (they were) there is an indication that their being entitled to the Gardens is a settled matter from before, prepared for them.

The lam of entitlement (lam al-istihqaq) is used to honor them, that they attained the Garden through the entitlement of their faith and deeds, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 72]. The plural "Gardens" (jannat) signals the vastness of their bliss and that they are many gardens, as came in the hadith: "Indeed, they are many gardens" (innaha jinan kathirah). Firdaws (al-Firdaws): a garden comprising everything found in orchards. On the authority of Mujahid, it is an arabicized word (mu'arrab) from Greek (al-Rumiyyah). It was said to be from Syriac. Al-Farra' said: it is Arabic, i.e., not arabicized. Its mention is not found in the speech of the Arabs before the Qur'an.

The people of al-Sham call vineyards and orchards "al-faradis." In the city of Aleppo there is a gate called Bab al-Faradis.

The construction of "the Gardens" annexed to "Firdaws" is explicative (bayaniyyah), i.e., gardens that are of the kind of Firdaws. It is reported in a hadith that "Firdaws is the highest part of the Garden, or the middle of the Garden." That is another usage for this specific place, which goes back to its being a proper noun by predominance (ʿalam bil-ghalabah).

If this verse is understood in that sense, then the annexation of "gardens" to "Firdaws" is a true annexation (idafah haqiqiyyah), i.e., the gardens of this place.

al-Nuzul (the lodging): already discussed shortly before.

His saying ﴿they will not desire any change from them﴾ means: there is nothing beyond what those gardens contain of kinds of pleasures and enjoyment for which souls yearn, so that they would wish to leave what they are in for something better than it. That is, they find in them everything that arises in their souls of desire.

al-Hiwal: a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern of al-'iwaj and al-sighar. The weak letter (harf al-'illah) remains sound in this form, but most of what is on this pattern as a masdar keeps the sound form, like al-hiwal, while what is among them as a plural takes the altered form, such as al-hiyal, the plural of hilah. It is derived from the root of the waw, from al-tahawwul (change).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 109:

﴿Say: "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would surely be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement."﴾

This surah began by emphasizing the status of the Qur'an, then proceeded to elaborate on various modes of guidance, warning, promise and threat, and mentioned among its narratives the finest stories containing lessons and admonition, and what is hidden of the conditions of past nations. The discourse then turned to the notification that all of that is but a little of the immense knowledge of God Most High.

This is a fresh, initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), and it is a transition to highlighting the knowledge of God Most High, who bestows knowledge upon His Messenger ﷺ. For when the polytheists asked him about things they thought would silence the Messenger, and that he would have no means of knowing them, God taught him them, informed him of them with the most truthful report, and explained them to the utmost extent that their understandings could accept, and in a manner that the knowledge of those who incited the polytheists to ask about them falls short of. The last of these was the account of Dhu al-Qarnayn. He followed that with what makes known the vastness of God Most High's knowledge and the vastness of what proceeds in accordance with His knowledge of revelation, when He wills to convey some of what is in His knowledge to one of His messengers. In this there is a response of the end of the surah to its beginning.

It was said: it was revealed on account of the saying of the Jews to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "How do you say," i.e., in Surat al-Isra', ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra': 85], "and we have been given the Torah, and whoever is given the Torah has been given much good." This has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra': 85] in Surat al-Isra'.

Al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas: Huyayy ibn Akhtab, the Jew, said: "In your Book is ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269], then you recite ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra': 85]." So there was revealed His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾, the verse.

The "words of God" (kalimat Allah) are that which indicates some of His knowledge which He reveals to His messengers to convey. Thus every known thing can be told. When it is told, it becomes a word. For this reason the known things are called "words," because God has informed of many of them, and had He willed, He would have informed of others. So applying the term "words" to them is a metaphor by the relation of what is to become (ʿalaqat al-ma'al). A parallel is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And if whatever is on the earth of trees were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it, the words of God would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27]. In this there is evidence for affirming the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi) and for affirming the potential relation (al-ta'alluq al-sulluhi) of the attribute of knowledge. Few are those who notice this relation.

Since what God informs of through one of His messengers is customarily written down, to preserve it within the community, the known things of God which are told and called "words" were likened to written things, and the likened-to was alluded to by one of its necessary attributes, which is the ink by which writing is done, in the manner of the metaphor (al-makniyya). The affirmation of ink is an imaginative representation (takhyil), like the imagining of claws for the Maniyya. So what is here is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And if whatever is on the earth of trees were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it, the words of God would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27], for the mention of pens is fitting only to ink in the sense of writing fluid.

It is also permissible that there is here a likening of the words of God to a shining lamp, because it guides to what is sought, just as the light of God and His guidance was likened to a lamp in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. Then "ink" would be an imaginative representation by the oil with which the lamp is fed.

"Midad" is applied to ink, because the inkwell is replenished with it, i.e., what is in it of its kind is replenished with it. "Midad" is also applied to the oil with which a lamp is fed, but its application to ink became predominant. In this verse it admits of both meanings, so the verse contains two metaphors according to the two possibilities.

The lam in His saying "for the words of my Lord" (li-kalimat) is the lam of cause, i.e., for the sake of the words of my Lord. The statement implies an omitted modifier, its estimate being: "for the writing of the words of my Lord," since ink is intended for writing, and the sea is not something written with, but the statement was built on the supposed condition by means of "law" (lau). "Midad" is a noun for what a thing is replenished with, i.e., something is added to what it has. He did not say "midadan" (as a predicate), since the intention is not to liken it to ink, as this is achieved by the likening that precedes it; rather what is intended here is that its like replenishes it.

"Al-Nafad" means perishing and dissolution. The exhaustion of the sea is rationally possible.

As for the exhaustion of the words of God in the sense of the objects of His knowledge (ta'alluqat 'ilmihi), it is impossible. Thus one does not understand from restricting the exhaustion of the words of God by the temporal clause "before" that the exhaustion of the words of God is possible. But since the statement was built on supposition and hypothesis, by what "law" indicates, the meaning is: "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, and the words of my Lord were of what can be exhausted, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted."

This statement is a kinayah (allusive expression) for the non-finitude of the known things of God Most High, among which are those three questions which they asked the Prophet ﷺ about. Therefore His saying "before the words of my Lord are exhausted" does not imply that the words of God Most High are subject to exhaustion, as you have understood.

The clause ﴿and if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

"Law" here is the law of conjunction (wasliyya), which indicates a state which is most unlikely to coincide with the content of the preceding statement, so the hearer is alerted that the content of the preceding statement is realized along with it. This has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran. This is a second intensification.

"Madadan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) explaining the ambiguity in the word "mithlihi," i.e., the like of the sea in replenishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 18, verse 110:

﴿Say: "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord."﴾ This is a second resumptive statement (istinaf). It moves from emphasizing the vastness of God's knowledge, and that He is not unable to reveal to His Messenger knowledge of everything he is asked about, to informing them that the Messenger was not sent to report past events and bygone generations. Nor does the requirement of prophethood entail that the Messenger's knowledge encompass all things, so that he would take it upon himself to answer questions put to him. Rather, he is a human being whose knowledge is like human knowledge, and he was revealed to what God willed to convey to His servants of monotheism and the law. And he has no knowledge except what his Lord taught him, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."﴾ [al-A'raf: 203]. The restriction in His words ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾ confines the described (the Prophet) to the attribute (humanity), and it is a relative restriction (qasr idafi) of the corrective type (lil-qalb), meaning: I am nothing but a human being; I do not go beyond humanity to knowledge of the unseen.

Included within this is the most important thing revealed to him and the purpose for which he was sent, namely the oneness of God and striving for what brings safety at the meeting with God the Exalted. This is an instance of radd al-ajuz 'ala al-sadr (returning the end of a passage to its beginning), from His words at the beginning of the surah: ﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾ [al-Kahf: 2] up to His words ﴿They say nothing but a lie﴾ [al-Kahf: 5]. The clause "It has been revealed to me" is either a new resumptive clause or a second attribute of "a human being." "Anna-ma" with a fatha on the hamza is a sister of "inna-ma" with a kasra on the hamza, and it is composed of "anna" with a fatha on the hamza and "ma" (the kaffah, the particle that removes the governing effect), just as "inna-ma" with a kasra on the hamza was composed. It conveys what "anna" with a fatha conveys of the verbal-source meaning, and what "inna-ma" conveys of restriction. The restriction derived from it here is a relative restriction of the corrective type.

The meaning: God reveals to me the oneness of the Deity and that His attribute is confined to the attribute of unity, without partnership.

The consequence expressed in ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾ is part of what is revealed to him. That is, it is revealed to me: the oneness of the Deity, the affirmation of resurrection, and righteous deeds.

Thus the composition came in a wondrous manner in conveying the three foundations: it made monotheism the root of them, and the other two were made branches of it. It reinforced the report of oneness by the prohibition against associating anyone in the worship of God the Exalted. Along with this, the return of the end to the beginning was achieved, which is a wondrous style.

Surah Maryam

The name of this surah in the mushafs, in books of tafsir, and in most books of Sunnah is Surah Maryam. This naming is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) in a hadith transmitted by al-Tabarani, al-Daylami, Ibn Mandah, Abu Nu'aym, and Abu Ahmad al-Hakim, from Abu Bakr ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Maryam al-Ghassani, from his father, from his grandfather Abu Maryam, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, a girl was born to me last night.' He said: 'And last night Surah Maryam was revealed to me, so name her Maryam.'" He was thus called Abu Maryam and became known by his kunya. His name was Nadhir, and it appears that he was an Ansari.

Ibn 'Abbas called it Surah Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad, and this naming also occurs in Sahih al-Bukhari in the Book of Tafsir in most and the most accurate copies. Jalal al-Din (al-Suyuti) did not count it in al-Itqan among the surahs known by two names, and perhaps he did not regard the second as a name.

It is Meccan according to the majority. It is reported from Muqatil that the verse of prostration is Medinan. This view is not sound, since that verse is connected to the verses before it, unless it was appended to them in revelation, which is far-fetched.

Al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Itqan an opinion that His words ﴿There is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71], the verse, is Medinan, and he did not attribute it to any speaker.

It is the forty-fourth surah in order of revelation; it was revealed after Surah Fatir and before Surah Ta-Ha. Surah Ta-Ha was revealed before the conversion of Umar ibn al-Khattab, as is understood from the story of his conversion. So the revelation of this surah would have been during the fourth year of the Prophethood, even though the surah is Meccan. Abu Maryam is not counted among the early Muslims, so I do not consider the hadith transmitted from him acceptable.

The reason for the naming is that the story of Maryam, her son, and her family is elaborated in it before it is detailed in other surahs. Only Surah Al 'Imran, which was revealed in Medina, resembles it in this respect.

Its verses are counted as ninety-nine according to the counts of the people of Medina and Mecca, and ninety-eight according to the counts of the people of Syria and Kufa.

* * *

It appears that this surah was revealed in refutation of the Jews for the vile speech they had fabricated about Maryam and her son. So it contains a clarification of the purity and sanctity of the family of 'Imran.

"Does the straight spear-shaft remain firm except by its own wood?"

Then (it contains) the honoring of a group of prophets and messengers from the ancestors of these (people) and their relatives, and the rebuke of some of their descendants who did not follow their righteous ways, from among the People of the Book and the polytheists, who uttered a monstrous statement when they attributed a son to God. Some of the polytheists among them denied resurrection, and the Christians affirmed that God has a son.

The surah also honors the Quran in its giving good news and warning, and that God made it easy by making it in Arabic, to ease that language.

The warning concerns what befell the nations that denied before them, of annihilation.

It includes the miracle (karama) of Zakariyya, when God answered his supplication and granted him a son in old age and when his wife was barren.

And the miracle of Maryam, through a supernatural event in her pregnancy and the sanctity of her son, which is an irhas (a pre-prophetic sign) for the prophethood of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Similar to it is his speech in the cradle.

And the honoring of Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Musa, Isma'il, and Idris, peace be upon them all.

And the description of Paradise and its people.

And the recounting of the denial of resurrection by the polytheists in the words of Ubayy ibn Khalaf and al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their boasting over the Muslims about their station and gatherings.

And the warning to the polytheists that the idols in which they took pride will regret their being taken as gods.

And the promise to the Messenger of victory over his enemies.

And the mention of a kind of their disbelief in attributing a child to God the Exalted.

And the honoring of the Quran and of its Arabic community, and that it is a bringer of good news to its allies and a warner of the destruction of its opponents, just as generations before them were destroyed.

The attribute "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) is repeated in this surah sixteen times, and the name "mercy" (al-rahmah) is mentioned four times. This indicates that one of its aims is to affirm God the Exalted by the attribute of al-Rahman, and to refute the polytheists who were arrogant in denying this attribute, as God the Exalted related of them in His words in Surah al-Furqan: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]. In this surah there also occurs an istitrad (digression) with the verse ﴿We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64].
